#3562. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

Taylor Swift and Brittany Mahomes prove it’s nice to have a friend on NFL game days.

Brittany, who is married to Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, sparked a friendship with Swift during the 2023-2024 season after the pop star began dating Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce.

“They have a really genuine friendship and love hanging out at the games together and cheering on their men,” a source exclusively told Us Weekly in January 2024. “Brittany loves that Taylor is dating Travis, and she’s so supportive of their relationship. They have a very similar sense of humor and are always cracking jokes and laughing.”

Brittany has frequently been seated next to Swift at Chiefs home and away games, with the two women enthusiastically cheering (and sharing secret handshakes) whenever their partners caught a pass or scored a touchdown.

Their friendship also extends well beyond the NFL gridiron with Brittany even receiving several invitations to Swift’s star-studded girls’ nights. Swift even made Brittany and her husband a “sentimental” gift after their third baby arrived in January 2025.

I don't know how you follow a $1.8 billion trip through Greek mythology, but Steven Spielberg apparently has an idea. Christopher Nolan is still taking a victory lap for The Odyssey, one of the biggest hits on the 2026 movie schedule, and the Jaws director just floated a follow-up I'd pay good money to see. The way he brought it up made me laugh, too. Even Hollywood legends know how to suggest another movie without sounding too pushy.

The moment came Tuesday, Nov. 17, at an awards-season screening of The Odyssey in Los Angeles. Spielberg moderated a Q&A with Nolan at the Directors Guild of America theater, where he praised the filmmaker's latest blockbuster before slipping in one more suggestion. As Gizmodo's Germain Lussier reported from the event, Spielberg told him:

The only other thing I want to say, not to challenge you or anything, but there’s always The Iliad.

I love how politely Spielberg slid that into the conversation. It's the cinematic equivalent of complimenting somebody's enormous Thanksgiving dinner and then asking what they're making next year. He even followed it up by insisting there was no pressure. Nolan, understandably, joked that Spielberg seemed to be speaking for Universal Pictures. Spielberg admitted the studio would probably appreciate it, but he was interested himself.

The idea makes a lot of sense. Homer's The Iliad takes place during the Trojan War, before Odysseus spends years trying to get home in The Odyssey. It wouldn't be a straightforward sequel, since we'd be going backward in the timeline, but the stories share a world. Imagine Nolan using his massive practical sets and IMAX cameras to tackle the conflict between Achilles and Hector. I'm already looking for a seat.

Here's what really makes the suggestion fun: Nolan almost got his shot at The Iliad decades ago. He was originally hired to direct Troy, the 2004 movie that eventually went to Wolfgang Petersen and starred Brad Pitt as Achilles. Nolan has since explained that he carried ideas from that unrealized project into The Odyssey, including the impressive Trojan Horse sequence.

Nolan has already explained why he chose The Odyssey. He considers The Iliad more grounded, while the later poem's monsters and stranger adventures offered something he hadn't seen done the way he envisioned. That doesn't mean he couldn't change his mind, especially after his latest movie has reportedly earned more than $1.8 billion worldwide.

There's also something delightful about Spielberg being the person to make this pitch. He helped develop Interstellar before Nolan took over, and Nolan consulted him while preparing Dunkirk. Watching Spielberg praise Nolan as a fellow filmmaker and then immediately ask for another movie feels like the most recognizable fan behavior imaginable.

For now, Nolan hasn't announced his next directing project. He told the crowd that he tends to focus on one film at a time and figures out the next one only after he's finished. So nobody should start booking tickets for The Iliad just yet. But if the man who gave us Jaws, Raiders of the Lost Ark, and Jurassic Park is personally asking for another giant Homer adaptation, I think somebody at Universal should at least write that suggestion down. Maybe keep the IMAX cameras handy.

In the meantime, The Odyssey is now available to rent or buy digitally, as well as on Blu-ray and 4K Blu-ray.

#3559. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3558. Luca Guadagnino and Andrew Garfield Get Real About 'Artificial'

Ask a large language model the same question twice, and you will get two different answers. Like this one: Have Andrew Garfield and Sam Altman ever met?

In an interview with Vanity Fair global editorial director Mark Guiducci this fall, Altman claimed he waved to Garfield while Garfield was shooting Luca Guadagnino’s new film, Artificial, near Altman’s house. Garfield—who plays Altman in the movie—remembers things differently.

“All I know is that I was looking out for him on that day when we were shooting. I was really looking out for him,” Garfield tells me in October, shortly after Artificial’s premiere at the New York Film Festival. “And I was looking at every single tinted car window. I was looking in the windows of the house. I was checking to see the security guard. No, I didn’t see him. I wish I had.”

It’s a question that reverberates both through and around Artificial. From the start, the film has been an intriguing mash-up: a marriage between cinema’s great sensualist and the nerd kingdom of Silicon Valley. Artificial tells the story of the OpenAI CEO’s rise and fall and rise; it was cast and shot in record time to keep pace with the drumbeat of AI doomsday headlines. Then the movie became the headlines after Amazon MGM abruptly dropped Artificial from its slate—a few months after the studio’s parent company, Amazon, invested $50 billion in OpenAI.

A24 declined to rescue Artificial. So did Netflix, Focus Features, and Clockwork, the new specialty arm of Warner Bros. Finally, the lightning bolt of a feature got picked up by Neon, the distributor that’s won six consecutive Palmes d’Or at Cannes.

The film’s electric relationship to the very recent past makes it the most zeitgeist-nailing tech blockbuster since The Social Network. The difference is that back in 2010, Facebook was where you made friends on the internet. Artificial, by contrast, is a film about a self-teaching, self-aware robot that’s getting smarter by the minute and might destroy the human world. And it’s happening in real time.

“You see, we were very prescient with things,” Guadagnino tells me. “I know my subject. I studied my subject very, very much.”

HERE TO MAKE FRIENDS Artificial ends with a heartbreaking act of betrayal—but Guadagnino, Borisov, and Garfield left the project with their bond intact.

Artificial also has a button-pushing relationship with the truth as it endeavors to tell the real story of how OpenAI was born and investigate how reliable the people behind OpenAI are. If Altman can’t be trusted with small details—about, say, whether he ever aimed a friendly wave at Garfield—can he be trusted with the most important technology of our time?

“I question the validity of his statement about being there while we were filming,” Monica Barbaro, who plays former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati in the film, tells me. “I mean, we don’t know if that’s true. And that feels textbook to me.”

In 2024, Amazon bought a script by Simon Rich about Sam Altman and the formation of OpenAI—one of many ChatGPT-related projects then getting passed around town. Rich’s take had the backing of hit-churning producer David Heyman—the man behind Paddington and the Harry Potter series—and his script pulled no punches. To write it, Rich mined details from a childhood friend who had a job at OpenAI (and, as of now, still works there). By the end of the process, Rich was terrified of the power his friend’s colleagues commanded.

“I came up with this last-ditch effort to warn mankind,” Rich said. He’s a comedy writer, but here he isn’t joking. “And I hope to God that it helps people pay attention.”

After shopping the film around to directors, the studio landed on Guadagnino. To some, the Call Me by Your Name director seemed like a strange choice for a film about scientists, coders, and start-up bros. The director barely uses AI himself, or even thinks about it.

ARTIFICIAL RECKONING Garfield’s first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network.

“I think we should not let ourselves give AI such an important role. I think for me, AI is a prop, a gadget,” Guadagnino tells me. “Definitely AI has high-end worth [for], I don’t know, the military, medicine. But in general, as a sort of everyday life usage of AI, I think it’s just a little gadget. And I don’t believe that we should ever consider the possibility that it can equal whatever we can do as people.”

Garfield approached the material from a different vantage. By the time he got his hands on the script, the actor had been deeply invested in the Silicon Valley origin-story mythos for years—ever since he starred in that other major movie about a world-changing digital platform. His first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network. “And I thought, Oh my God,” says the actor, sitting in a suite at the Carlyle Hotel. But the movie also had its own gloss. “Simon’s script was so funny—like a stone being skimmed a thousand times across, and then a couple of really deep dives in the midst.”

Making Artificial would allow Garfield to scratch an old itch. “In The Social Network, I was auditioning for [Mark] Zuckerberg. Then they found Jesse [Eisenberg],” who was much better for the role, Garfield says. “But it left this little dangling thread, because I started to imagine how I would play Zuckerberg: how I would try and enter that ambition and that drive and that responsibility. A kind of ability to make huge global decisions that are going to have potentially really positive effects on humanity, but inevitably, really, really heavily negative effects on humanity.”

THE ENGINEER “I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews,” says Borisov.

Garfield is not actually the lead in Artificial. The movie is focused less on Altman than on slightly naive genius coder Ilya Sutskever, played heroically by Oscar nominee Yura Borisov. Borisov has definitively never met the man he’s depicting in the film. But from afar, he can relate to Sutskever. Neither of them is quite comfortable in the spotlight.

“I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews because I’m every time very...I know what to say because I feel a lot about this,” the Russian actor says from a couch at the Carlyle next to Garfield. “I can see the same in his public speeches, because I’m really nervous during some public stuff.”

Though there’s a translator next to him, Borisov soldiers through the interview with just one request for a lifeline. He adds that by cosmic coincidence, he and Sutskever have the same birthday.

Guadagnino was fully aware of the breakneck clip of the developing OpenAI saga. He cast his leads in days and began shooting the film in late July 2025. Artificial wrapped just two months later. As he spent the winter hunkered down in the editing room, word about the film got out. While Rich’s original script was hardly a puff piece, rumor had it that the final film leaned even harder into a negative portrayal of Altman.

There’s no proof that a Jeff Bezos deal had any direct effect on decisions made by Bezos’s movie studio. But for whatever reason, late last spring, Guadagnino learned Amazon would be cutting the film loose.

All of a sudden, the speedily assembled project was in a holding pattern. The trades speculated that Amazon was deliberately killing the film to protect Altman; others wondered if the movie was being dropped not due to a conflict of interest but because it hadn’t played well in early screenings.

Barbaro pushes back on that notion. “I did believe in Luca and the film, and I had already heard really positive things from people who had seen it—really interesting positive reviews,” she says. “There is a thing these companies can do—any production company—which is to essentially build the release and squash a film. And Amazon is not a company that I think necessarily needs to make its money back on an investment like this.”

Either way, it was unclear if Artificial would ever see the light of day. “It’s a dialogue between our fields: tech and art,” Borisov says. “And I don’t know what sells, what will happen. It’s unpredictable.”

In the end, the film was picked up by Neon—an outcome Garfield finds surprising for a few reasons. “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film, and very impressed again when they decided [that while] they didn’t want to release it, they didn’t kill it,” he says. He pauses for a second. “They could have killed it.”

Garfield’s thrilled about the film’s eventual home too. Neon, he says pointedly, is “a place for artists to be free artists.” Guadagnino feels similarly, though he claims to have zero ill will toward the studio that threw his movie to the wolves.

“I had went through a process with Amazon that I loved. They were fantastic in making this movie with me. I owe them a lot,” says Guadagnino, who’d done four films with the studio prior to Artificial: Bones and All, Challengers, Suspiria, and After the Hunt.

But what was it like to watch his film fall into limbo while the trades salivated over its demise? Here too, Guadagnino is blissfully zen: “Once the thing happened, I deferred to the thing. Meaning if that was the case, that was the case.”

Even after watching the film twice, I am still pleasantly surprised that Artificial actually exists in the world—that Guadagnino was able to capture the man-child bonhomie of coder bros through his fabulous scrim of art film wooziness. I ask Garfield, now a two-time vet of the director’s films, to sum up the full Guadagnino psychedelic experience.

“Humanity and bodies and interpersonal dynamics and relationship and sexuality, sensuality, Eros, love, the muck and the mire of being human, ambition, drive, greed, power, love, brotherhood, connection,” he says. Guadagnino’s movies are about “his curiosity and love for people: wanting to skin, flay, open up, crack the ribs, and show the insides of these human beings.”

To Garfield this is the key to understanding the director’s vision for Artificial. Robots didn’t build the robots that might destroy humanity: People did. And people still control them—for now.

Artificial inspires a lot of comparisons. Barbaro likens it to Invasion of the Body Snatchers; Garfield compares its climactic confrontation scene to West Side Story. Guadagnino, the actor says, gave another point of reference. Then he does a spot-on, peak-Sicilian impression of the director: “I want this to be like a John Hughes movie.”

Guadagnino himself is reluctant to name any films that may have inspired this one. But he does name one filmmaker—someone who, as he notes, balanced indie flicks with blockbusters all while building the world’s greatest collection of Haitian art: Jonathan Demme.

“Jonathan was a humanist, and he had this very profound capacity of eviscerating dynamics of humanism in America,” Guadagnino says. “He did some great movies about the dynamics of corporations versus individual freedom,” like Fighting Mad and Philadelphia.

Barbaro says the film’s secret sauce is that it’s up for interpretation. It’s possible to come away from it celebrating the AI bros as heroes or decrying them as villains.

“It’s a bit of a Rorschach test,” she says. “Some people come out shaking, terrified. And I think some people are like, ‘Wow, what a good time!’ I also think that you have to hide the medicine in the food a little bit. I don’t think a purely doomsday story is going to reach many people.”

UNDER PRESSURE “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film,” Garfield says. “They didn’t kill it. They could have killed it.”

Garfield, meanwhile, may leave the film eternally bonded with Altman—the role that could help him finally clinch the Oscar. (Garfield’s been nominated twice but hasn’t won yet.) Before making Artificial, Garfield says, he had a positive impression of Altman. He seemed friendly, “like maybe we would’ve been buddies on the kibbutz.”

As he dove deeper, though, Garfield’s feelings about Altman got stranger and more complicated in ways that the film addresses both head-on and obliquely. Is Altman someone who habitually tells tall tales? Uses lies to say what needs to be said, as Sam tells Ilya in the movie? Imagines anecdotes about waving to the A-lister who’s playing him in a biopic?

Whatever Altman’s relationship with reality is, the version of him we see in Artificial is charming, ingratiating, prone to grandiose hallucinations and to telling people exactly what they want to hear—then doing what he was going to do anyway. He’s not far off from an AGI approaching a real human consciousness, art imitating a machine imitating life.

“There are certain threads that feel consistent, which is a questioning of his ability to tell or his commitment to the truth,” Garfield says. “How often is he telling the truth to himself? How often is he telling the truth to others? And how many versions of the truth are there, and how is he utilizing that in order to...”

“Because I ultimately do believe that Sam feels, in our film and in life, that he is serving the good of mankind.”

#3556. Meta's VR Glasses Could Be The Future Of Home Viewing (But They Probably Won't)

In stark contrast to the dire straits that the movie theater industry was in just a few years ago, 2026 has been especially encouraging to those of us who adore going to the movies. A big part of why that's changed lies in the industry's embrace of unique Premium Large Formats, with numerous releases this year having been shown in formats like IMAX, 4DX, Screen X, Dolby Cinema, and so on. Along the way, screening on celluloid (70mm in particular) have become a draw unto themselves, and some cities are home to even more specialized formats, among them Las Vegas' immersive Sphere and the Cosm experience. And while the biggest draw to movie theaters will always be good films, it's clear that audiences also enjoy an experience they can't get elsewhere.

As usual, however, the tech industry isn't far behind to try and stoke the competition between theaters and home viewing. While most consumers have been content with things like big screen 4K TV's or even their handheld devices for watching at home or on the go, the latest attempt to leap forward from these is just around the corner, in the form of Meta's VR Glasses. It's important to note that these are not the latest version of the smart glasses that have existed on the market since 2021, as they're explicitly not designed to be used while engaged in other activity. Instead, they're a cutting edge virtual/augmented reality system intended to bring together multiple work and entertainment options while idle.

I recently had the opportunity to try these glasses for myself, and their potential, especially for home viewing, is amazing. That said, there are some restrictions to them which, unless changed, mean they won't be replacing our existing personal devices anytime soon.

Although virtual reality, or VR, has existed in some form for decades, it's mostly been utilized as a gimmick more than a viable first choice for media. Fortunately, the folks behind Meta VR Glasses seem to understand this. I got to see a clip from the recent concert doc "Billie Eilish — Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour (Live in 3D)" on the glasses, and the experience was like I was watching it on a movie theater screen. That is to say that the aspect ratio was exactly the same as its theatrical exhibition, and the 3D display was pitch perfect. Turning my head in any direction didn't move the "screen," but kept it fixed in front of me, as if it was a physical object in the space, which is a very smart design.

While the James Cameron documentary acted as a demo of how watching most films and shows on the glasses would go, the Meta employees next showed me what they're calling "Enhanced Cinema." Using a clip from "Avengers: Infinity War" in which Thor (Chris Hemsworth) constructs Stormbreaker, the presentation was almost exactly akin to the Cosm experience. This meant that the film was playing on a similar fixed "display" in front of me, while all around me (literally 360 degrees — I checked!) was the environment of the forge on Nidavellir. It's an effect that's totally immersive but not distracting, nor does it betray the original intent of the film itself. After being told that Meta has an exclusive license with the IMAX corporation to present movies filmed for that format on the glasses, I have no doubt that the device could brilliantly replicate those screens for home viewing, and that's incredibly exciting.

While the Meta VR Glasses are not intended to replace a smartphone or similar device, they do seem to do a lot of what those devices do, only bigger and better. From working on VR video games and multiple computer monitors at once to allowing you to watch sports games as they broadcast while seeing the view from courtside, the glasses seem almost too good to be true as a personal media device.

This is where the catches come in. For one thing, watching something with other people at the same time can only occur depending on the content. For another, though they're engineered to be used while stationary, the temptation for people to wear them in public while walking (or, god forbid, driving) exists, and it's quite troubling. Then there's the fact that the glasses seem designed to only work with whatever services and content Meta allows. This means that us physical media fans are SOL, and as with any all-digital service, the content available on the glasses could be subject to change (or disappear) at any time. That's a lot to ask for a device priced at $1,299.99 USD, which is about the same as a new iPhone.

Note: Following publication, a representative for Meta did inform us that the VR glasses will support playback devices that are compatible via a wired DisplayPort-over-USB-C connection, meaning that additional content (like physical media) that the consumer has control over may be viewable on the glasses.

Right now, Meta's killer app beyond the tech itself are its exclusive licenses, such as with IMAX and James Cameron's Lightstorm Entertainment. The only way it'll compete with devices already on the market is if it can consistently deliver the quality experiences I got to have with it while being as user friendly as possible. If the glasses prove they can be used at home and on the go as smoothly as an iPhone can now, then they could be a game changer. Until then, they're just a gimmick, albeit a really nice one.

#3554. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3552. 10 Years Ago Today: The Harry Potter Universe Expanded With A Star-Studded Spin-Off

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Harry Potter" is perhaps the defining franchise of the 2000s, but all good things must come to an end. That end originally came in 2011 with "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2" which had the biggest opening ever up to that point in cinema history. But creator J.K. Rowling and Warner Bros. weren't content to let the Wizarding World end there. Ten years ago, they expanded the universe with a star-studded spin-off.

Set decades before Harry Potter was even born, 2016's "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them," which opened 10 years ago today, brought the action to America and focused on entirely new characters within the Wizarding World. Specifically Newt Scamander, played by Oscar-winner Eddie Redmayne. Redmayne had an unexpected inspiration for his performance, namely film icon Buster Keaton. The movie itself was loosely based on an in-universe textbook mentioned in the main series, with Rowling eventually releasing a version of the book, though it didn't contain a narrative.

The resulting prequel/spin-off takes place in 1926 centered on magizoologist Newt Scamander as he arrives in New York during a worldwide tour to research and rescue magical creatures. A mysterious magical being begins causing chaos in NYC, which threatens to expose the wizarding world to the muggles of Earth.

Redmayne was far from the only big star to secure a role in the spin-off. The stacked cast also includes but is not limited to Katherine Waterston, Dan Fogler, Alison Sudol, Samantha Morton, Ezra Miller, and Colin Farrell. "Fantastic Beats" also cast Johnny Depp as Grindelwald in a surprise appearance. Arguably the most important casting decision the movie made, with the benefit of hindsight.

J.K. Rowling wrote the script for "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" personally, which wasn't the case with the other "Harry Potter" movies. David Yates, who helmed the final four "Harry Potter" movies, was recruited to tackle the spin-off as well, providing a sturdy hand.

The majority of the core cast were on the upswing. This movie was expected to be a big break for all of them. In many ways, it was. "Fantastic Beasts" was dubbed a worthy extension of the Wizarding World in many reviews, with audiences tending to agree. Even if it wasn't effusive praise, it was good enough.

The movie was released in November 2016 and did quite well for itself, pulling in $816 million at the global box office. That was more than enough to convince Warner Bros. to double down, with four "Fantastic Beasts" sequels announced before the first one even hit theaters. Everyone involved fully expected this to be the long-term future for the "Harry Potter" franchise. What's perhaps most surprising about that, especially in light of the first movie's success, is the fact that the words Harry Potter don't appear anywhere in the title. All the same, audiences found it.

The train had left the station and everyone involved had every reason to believe, on paper, that people would show up for the sequels en masse. After all, the first installment scored well enough with critics and was the eighth-biggest movie of 2016 overall. Unfortunately, the future had different plans.

Warner Bros. and director David Yates wasted no time, with the second "Fantastic Beasts" installment dated for November 2018. Much of the cast returned, with new additions entering the fold. But in no small part due to forces beyond the studio's control, "The Crimes of Grindelwald" doomed "Fantastic Beasts."

The sequel pulled in more than $650 million at the box office, but made a lot less domestically and had to rely on international audiences to bail it out. Then there's the Depp of it all. Controversy started swirling around the actor due to his public feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard, involving accusations of domestic abuse. Depp later dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise following a court case verdict. Mads Mikkelsen took over as Grindelwald in "The Secrets of Dumbledore," but the writing was on the wall.

The third installment made hardly more than $400 million globally, failing to break even theatrically. "The Secrets of Dumbledore" proved that the magic was gone, despite the appeal of Jude Law as a younger Albus Dumbledore in a lead role. The cast continued to be star-studded all along the way but, at a certain point, appealing casts only go so far. Especially in the 2020s when audiences are more content than ever to stay at home and stream something from the couch.

Controversy and middling results with diminishing returns eventually derailed "Fantastic Beasts." Ten years ago though, the spin-off arrived with a great deal of promise and a lot of potential. That potential just never proved out.

You can grab "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

There's a lot to unpack about this big move.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Word is out that Elon Musk has invested a significant amount of money in Skydance, making him part-owner of the newly merged studio alongside David Ellison. With headlines suggesting the company may sell DC Studios and make other changes, I'm most concerned and have my eye on what the plan is for Star Trek.

It's been a tough year for Star Trek fans, despite it being the 60th anniversary. The year was marked by news that there are no new shows on the horizon, and ended with the passing of Walter Koenig and, of course, the death of Patrick Stewart. As the year ends, I have mixed feelings about what the future holds and how these two men may impact it in 2027 and beyond. Let's talk about it.

Ellison had a history with Star Trek before becoming head of the studio that owns it. Skydance helped co-produce both Star Trek: Into Darkness and Beyond alongside Paramount when they were separate studios, and he was on the record as a card-carrying Trekkie.

The CEO quickly mentioned Star Trek upon taking over Paramount in its original merger, and got the ball rolling on a new film. Unfortunately, we've seen this song and dance before with Paramount, as the issue was never developing a new Trek movie, but rather getting far enough along that it actually screens in theaters.

Additionally, Star Trek has zero shows in active development at this time. With no new announcements about any progress on that front, it feels as though the game plan is to let the final seasons of Strange New Worlds and Starfleet Academy air in 2027, and then maybe announce a new direction for the franchise. That's just an optimistic guess, however, as we've gotten no confirmation that is the plan.

Which brings me to the main problem I've had with David Ellison thus far. He's stated that Star Trek has a big role in what he wants to do with the future of Skydance, but we aren't really seeing any evidence of that. Right now, it feels like a lesser priority, something on the back burner, if you will, and I'm worried about just how long that will be the case.

Elon Musk's entry into Star Trek puts another alleged Trekkie at the top of Skydance's ladder, which could propel moves into happening sooner rather than later. For those who don't know, Musk is actually a canon figure in the universe, having been directly mentioned by Gabriel Lorca as one of the great minds of humanity. Despite his various movie and film appearances, Musk has never appeared in Trek.

As A Star Trek Fan I'm Eternally Grateful For What Patrick Stewart Did For The Franchise

He's also preached about recreating Star Trek in real life via his SpaceX company, but has simultaneously butted heads with other fans in interpreting what the series is about. We saw that when Starfleet Academy came out, and he openly joked about the show having obese actors and people wearing eyeglasses.

Perhaps he was not privy to Gene Roddenberry's view that looks wouldn't matter in an idealized society. It doesn't seem to be the only message he missed, as Musk has openly criticized the franchise's embrace of diversity and inclusion, two major principles Roddenberry stressed from the beginning.

I feel as though Musk loves the part of Star Trek that is about space exploration, especially with it matching his eventual goal for humanity to expand and colonize other planets. It's imperative, however, for him to also understand the bit that the series is a morality play, and without that bit included, it ceases to be the franchise that's thrived for 60 years.

Now, it's entirely possible David Ellison and Elon Musk keep their hands out of Star Trek, and entrust someone else to do what they think will make it most successful. As it stands right now, I have my apprehensions about either being too hands-on with it, but maybe I'll be surprised a year from now.

Star Trek remains available to stream on Paramount+. I'm waiting for those final seasons of Starfleet Academy and Strange New Worlds, and hoping that movie goes into production by the end of next year.

Mick Joest is a Content Producer for CinemaBlend with his hand in an eclectic mix of television goodness. Star Trek is his main jam, but he also regularly reports on happenings in the world of Star Trek, WWE, Doctor Who, 90 Day Fiancé, Quantum Leap, and Big Brother. He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

#3550. Here's What We Know About Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026 Sales

Gone are the days when holiday sales had a firm beginning and end. These days, if you're not scouring the internet weeks before the actual date of the event, you will miss out on deals. Black Friday is no exception. Amazon released its official Black Friday and Cyber Monday plans for its sale, but there's plenty that's discounted already, many reaching or matching their lowest price ever.

Amazon is treating Black Friday and Cyber Monday like one long sale. The official sale kicks off at 12:01 a.m. PST on Nov. 19 and runs through Nov. 30.

Yes, you will need to be a Prime Member to shop the exclusive sales during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Prime membership starts at $14.99 per month. While only you can decide if buying a yearly Prime membership is worth it for you, remember you can always sign up and then cancel your Prime membership once the sale is over: Amazon offers a free 30-day trial, so you can shop during both Black Friday and Cyber Monday before canceling without being charged. #3549. Dolly Parton on Her Mother Avie Lee Parton’s Album, Mama Sings

Many people know of my mama, Avie Lee Owens Parton, from my song “Coat of Many Colors,” but my mama gave me a gift that was far more valuable than a colorful coat. She gave me the gift of music.

As far back as I can remember, Mama loved to sing—at church, at family get-togethers, and most of all to her children. Her love of music came naturally; she had inherited it from her parents, her grandparents, and all the way back to Wales, where her family, the Owens, came from. Most of all, she inherited her love of music from her father, the Rev. Jake Owens. Grandpa Owens was a singer, songwriter, musician, and music teacher, in addition to being a full time Pentecostal preacher. He and my grandma Rena raised eight children, and all of them took to music in one way or another.

So, it was a natural thing that Mama shared her love of music with her children. She especially loved the old mountain songs—ballads that reached all the way back to the British Isles, popular songs from the 1800s that mountain people had made their own and, of course, beloved hymns.

So, when my uncle Louis Owens, Porter Wagoner, and I opened Fireside Recording Studio in Nashville in 1973, both my uncle Louis and I knew we had to get Mama in the recording studio to capture her songs on tape. Working with just a guitarist and an autoharp player, Mama recorded her own versions of some of her favorite songs.

Dolly Parton, Carl Butler, Avie Lee Parton, Robert Lee Parton, and Pearl Butler.

The plan was to release an album, but for one reason or another, it never happened. Fortunately, my uncle Louis saved all the tapes, and when he passed away, his son Richie, who has always loved our family history and heritage, decided to clean them up and get them released.

Dolly Parton and her mother, Avie Lee Parton.

Many of them are well-known tunes, but you may know them under different titles. Like all mountain singers, Mama preferred to call songs by the name she’d learned them under, and we decided that that was the way we needed to present them to you.

If you’ve ever wondered where my music came from, this album tells the story, and I am so proud, happy, and honored to have shared this music and my mama’s voice with you.

#3548. Avengers: Doomsday's PG-13 Rating Explained

We are a month away from potentially the biggest box office weekend of 2026, with Dunesday set to blow Barbenheimer out of the water as both "Dune: Part Three" and "Avengers: Doomsday" make their way into theaters. These movies are aimed at similar audiences, yet they're vastly different when it comes to their tones and approaches to adapting popular characters for the big screen. Indeed, where Denis Villeneuve's cinematic takes on the "Dune" books have so far been somber and introspective, the road to "Doomsday" has been paved almost entirely with nostalgia.

To be sure, between Robert Downey Jr. returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (this time to play Doctor Doom), the latest Avengers roster featuring multiple beloved characters from the MCU's past, and several actors reprising their roles from 20th Century Fox's "X-Men" films, "Doomsday" has had no problem catching the attention and interest of virtually every kind of moviegoer out there. After all, where "Dune: Part Three" can afford to target older audiences given the mature themes of its source material, "Doomsday" is aimed at everyone with a pulse and a heartbeat.

Hence, it's no surprise to learn that the new "Avengers" movie is now officially rated PG-13, just like almost every other previous film entry in the MCU since 2008 (save for "Deadpool & Wolverine"). Per FilmRatings.com, the film earned this rating from the Motion Picture Association (MPA) based on its "violence/action, bloody images, and language."

Just in case it needs to be said, "Avengers: Doomsday" was never going to be rated anything other than PG-13. The MCU's movies, in general, tend to feature too much intense action for any of them to garner a mere PG rating, yet they also tend to avoid going overboard into full-blown adult territory. At the same time, the explanation for its rating suggests "Doomsday" will make good on its promise of being one of the darker installments in the franchise.

Keeping that in mind, Marvel Studios and Disney were never going to allow a movie as costly as this one to get slapped with an R rating either, lest it severely limit the number of people who can pay to see it in a theater. And yes, "Deadpool & Wolverine" managed to become a massive success with an R-rating, but that was a different situation. Since the first two "Deadpool" films had been R-rated, it might've actually hurt the movie financially if it had tried to take the larger "Deadpool" property in a more family-friendly direction.

That's not to suggest that "Doomsday" won't be sufficiently dark or violent, though. Just too long ago, in fact, Sam Raimi pushed the PG-13 rating as far as humanly possible with 2022's "Doctor Strange In the Multiverse of Madness," the most gruesome Marvel movie yet. As you may recall, that film was filled with incredibly brutal death scenes, legitimate jump scares, and upsetting imagery that's not suitable for younger audiences. On the other hand, we can probably safely assume "Doomsday" won't push the envelope that far, given everything that's riding on it.

You can see what "Avengers: Doomsday" has to offer for yourself when it opens in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3547. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3545. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3544. Avengers: The Kang Dynasty's Scrapped Doctor Doom Twist Explained By Marvel's Kevin Feige

As we march ever closer to "Avengers: Doomsday," it's easy to forget this movie was supposed to look very different. The original lead-in to "Avengers: Secret Wars" was supposed to be "Avengers: The Kang Dynasty," as directed by Destin Daniel Cretton (who had already helmed "Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings" for Marvel and would go on to direct "Spider-Man: Brand New Day").

Kang the Conqueror (Jonathan Majors), a time traveler who hails from the 31st century, appeared as the main villain of "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." A post-credits scene debuted the "Council of Kangs," or all of Kang's variants from a multiverse full of different timelines. But "Quantumania" earned unenthusiastic reviews upon its release in February 2023, and worse, Majors was arrested for assault the following month. (He was found guilty, and then fired by Marvel/Disney, in December 2023.)

Yeah, not exactly the launching pad you want for your next Thanos. Cue a pivot, and the announcement at San Diego Comic-Con 2024 that "Kang Dynasty" had been reworked into "Avengers: Doomsday," featuring Robert Downey Jr. returning to Marvel but as Doctor Doom, not Iron Man, as well as the return of "Infinity War" and "Endgame" directors Joe and Anthony Russo.

Now, this all seems like a "break glass in case of emergency" situation. But Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige, sitting down with Empire Magazine, now claims that even before "The Kang Dynasty" became "Doomsday," Kang was planned to be a red herring for Doom:

"People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan's issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that. [...] It probably would still have been called 'The Kang Dynasty,' but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie."

Kevin Feige, noting the "very delicate" situation with Jonathan Majors, told Empire that "[Marvel] didn't want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment." He acknowledged the changes to "The Kang Dynasty" started after the bad reception and underperformance of "Quantumania," noting:

"'Quantumania' was not received the way we would have liked. There are many elements of that that we're proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [The Kang Dynasty] even at that point."

Reading between the lines of Feige's claims, it would appear that once Majors was fired, the studio decided to push forward with Doom as the villain from the start instead of recasting Kang. But is this credible? I'll admit my first thought while reading this was, "Yeah, right!"

In his Empire interview, Feige appears to say the plans to bring in Doom to supplant Kang happened after the release of "Quantumania" but before Majors' arrest. "Quantumania" was released on February 17, 2023, and Majors was arrested on March 25, 2023. That seems like a pretty slim window to rework "The Kang Dynasty."

In November 2023, Variety reported that — at the annual Marvel Studios retreat held that past September — studio leadership was actively discussing how to move forward with Kang. ("Marvel is truly f***ed with the whole Kang angle," an insider was quoted as saying.) Apparently, the Marvel brain trust discussed replacing Kang with another villain, Doom specifically being named, as well as bringing back Avengers who died in "Endgame," like Robert Downey Jr. as Iron Man, to gin up excitement. As we now know, that's basically what Marvel did.

During a November 2023 appearance on the "Hot Mic" podcast, journalist Jeff Sneider claimed that Doom would appear in the then-upcoming "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" (which he did) as set up for him to show up in "Avengers: Secret Wars." However, Sneider said in that same interview that, "It'd be inaccurate to say [Doom is] the villain."

But Doom is the villain of Marvel Comics overall. The only reason the Marvel Cinematic Universe waited so long to use him is because 20th Century Fox held the film rights to his character. Once the Disney and Fox merger was completed in 2019, and Doom became available to Marvel Studios, Doom had to be high on any list of characters being considered for inclusion.

The "Secret Wars" comics — both the 1984 original and the 2015 pseudo-remake — also feature Doom as the main villain. In both, he attains godlike power and rules over a domain called Battleworld. If you're adapting "Secret Wars," the thought of using Doom has to cross your mind.

Kevin Feige's claim that Doom would take over "midway" through "The Kang Dynasty" also aligns with supposed leaked plot summaries for "Doomsday," which assert that Doom initially presents himself as an ally before revealing his true intentions. If that's accurate, it appears the movie still has the broad structure of "The Kang Dynasty," just with no Kang.

On the other hand, "Secret Wars" (especially the 2015 one) is a culmination of Doom's character. Rushing right into him becoming a God Emperor of Battleworld, without him being the villain in a "Fantastic Four" movie first? Yeah, that sounds like something that was "accelerated," per Feige.

"Avengers: Doomsday" releases on December 18, 2026.

I can't be the only one who's ever wondered what it would be like to spend a night in the mall.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses the ultimate winners of the reality competition series Win the Mall, now available with a Netflix subscription.

Somehow Netflix has become the place to go if you want to watch a reality TV competition set in an unexpected location. (Hey, Wonka’s The Golden Ticket, I’m looking at you.) I enjoyed and see more potential in Win the Mall in the future, the one thing that became immediately clear is that I would like to see more of the actual mall itself.

It’s a simple idea. I mean, who hasn’t thought about at least spending the night in a mall, going on a shopping spree, and having free rein of the food court before sleeping in one of the mattress store’s beds? Clearly, it’s not just me, or there wouldn’t be this 2026 TV schedule release. I just wish we could have seen even more of the mall!

When you move 10 teams of two contestants into a shopping mall to compete for a $1 million grand prize, it feels like you should have a plan to incorporate the mall as much as possible. Part shopping spree and part social strategy, players are dropped into a real mall, but the fake storefronts make it challenging to fully utilize the mall itself, leaving it all to feel a bit disconnected at times.

The shopping spree challenges are the most fun because they see the teams ripping through the stores to guess what things cost to get close to their given dollar amount. It best embraces the chaos and energy of a shopping mall, especially on Black Friday. Something felt perfectly fitting about book-ending the season with shopping sprees, to introduce us to the competitors in the beginning and to narrow it down to the ultimate winner at the end. But that left six episodes in between where I wish I could have seen more of the actual mall.

There are a lot of challenges that take place adjacent to the stores, but I wish they’d found a better way to incorporate them. There’s a Starbucks in play, but we never really see the inside of it. And there’s a KFC boasted about for its lounge, but they only briefly hang out there. I just feel like there could have been some inventive ways to incorporate some of the stores themselves instead of having so many challenges set in the center space.

Surprisingly, one of the highlights of Win the Mall is TikTok creator-turned-host Haley Baylee, who is truly delightful. She’s a likable host who can wear anything and look like she’s on a runway, but she also never takes herself too seriously, being goofy when she needs to be and taking on a more serious persona while tempting contestants with possible game advantages.

Whether there’s ever another season of Win the Mall or not, I hope that we get to see more of her in the future. If we do get more, I just hope they can find a way to be more inventive in showing off more of the mall or even some “mall employees.” I liked a lot of the rest of the setup, and the contestants who ultimately won, but one possible idea is to incorporate some sort of sidekick for Haley Baylee who could be more directly related to the mall itself and could work as a bridge between the setting and the contestants. Just spitballing here.

There are a lot of great Netflix reality TV shows these days to choose from, including Squid Game: The Challenge, based on their own scripted programming. And while it wasn’t perfect, Win the Mall was entertaining and creative enough that I’d definitely watch another season. Don't let this one be a one and done, Netflix.

#3542. Brandon Sanderson’s Mistborn TTRPG Solves the Biggest Problem With Licensed Games

The wildly ambitious campaign takes generations

The wildly ambitious campaign takes generations

Licensed tabletop role-playing games provide players with a new way to experience their favorite franchises like Star Wars, Star Trek, and the Lord of the Rings. But those adventures always come with a big question about how player characters are supposed to make their mark on stories that already have their own legendary heroes. Rather than erasing canon characters or turning them into quest-givers, the wildly ambitious Mistborn Legacy campaign for the Cosmere Roleplaying Game allows players to forge legends as powerful as any of Brandon Sanderson’s characters.

Sanderson has written seven Mistborn novels set between two distinct eras. The first trilogy exists in a bleak time when most of the world is uninhabitable. The immortal Lord Ruler crushes all dissent and brutally oppresses most people. The second series kicks off 300 years later at a time when the world has been restored and transformed into something resembling a blend of the Wild West and the Gilded Age. Mistborn Legacy spans both these eras as the PCs work to ensure the Lord Ruler can’t return.

Brotherwise Games’ designers worked closely with Sanderson and his longtime collaborator Dan Wells to devise a way for the players to really matter in the story of Mistborn. They take the historical view that the concentration of wealth and power is problematic in every era, whether that’s the nobles in Era One or the railroad barons and weapons manufacturers in Era Two. The players are always acting from a position of weakness as they try to uncover the machinations of powerful interests that could undo all of the progress the heroes of Mistborn sacrificed to make possible.

The campaign introduces the Eternity Spike, an artifact created through mass human sacrifice that could imbue someone with power that rivals the Lord Ruler. It cannot be destroyed and is actively pursued by a secret society. Era One strongly evokes the original trilogy, as players take on the role of a crew of thieves infiltrating high society and making allies of urchins and revolutionaries. There’s a whole scene where the players have to impress people at a secret masquerade ball and try to untangle a love triangle, but there are also tough fights against twisted monsters and killers trained to negate the players’ magical powers.

Era Two leans more into that series’ pulp adventure sensibilities. The Gilded Trio resemble Indiana Jones villains as they search for ancient secrets that can lead them to a lost magical artifact. Era One can get quite dark, and while Era Two has its own twisted villains, it’s a lighter adventure involving illegal street racing and spending time on a university campus.

The sections are connected by a legacy system, with hooks for the party at large and each individual character archetype. The characters become legends akin to Sanderson’s characters like Vin and Kelsier, so the game master takes notes on what they did at key moments as they inspire future fashion trends and build organizations that stand the test of time. The book is filled with “legacy moments” that create special conflicts or opportunities in Era One depending on whehter your character is a convict, urchin, or veteran. After completing the Era One adventure, players create new characters with connections to other players’ previous characters. For instance, the storyteller in Era Two is working on the convict’s biography while the rookie is inspired by the veteran’s heroism.

Both parts are meticulously detailed, packed with maps, character art, and subsystems for mini-games and downtime planning. There are also detailed handouts for everything from party invitations to newspaper articles. Getting a group together to play through a campaign of this scale requires commitment, but GMs and players are rewarded by an extremely rich world filled with plenty of ways to make a mark.

Mistborn Legacy is best run by someone familiar with Sanderson’s series, but there are so many character hooks that it would be easy for Cosmere novices to slip into the game world. Even if you’re not already invested in the story of Scadrial, it’s easy to empathize with heroes trying to fight oppression and ensure that the future is bright for everyone. Rather than making players feel like they’re walking in the shadows of the series’ protagonists, Mistborn Legacy lets them preserve what they built while forging their own legends.
