#3508. The Rings Of Power Season 3 References The Most Powerful Dragon In Lord Of The Rings History

Spoilers ahead for Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Rings of Power" Season 3.

As a "Lord of the Rings" prequel, "The Rings of Power" takes an interesting approach. Sure, when you think about it, the show doesn't always fit into he greater "Lord of the Rings" canon, and it sometimes introduces elements that threaten to change the larger franchise as we know it. At the same time, it has some pretty cool ideas, whether it's the creation of Mount Doom from Season 1 or Sauron (Charlie Vickers) meeting a Balrog (Simon Pegg) in Season 3. Overall, the series knows how to capitalize on the vastness of J. R. R. Tolkien's literary source material to imagine new concepts for a different medium.

But perhaps one of the most fascinating aspects of "The Rings of Power" is how its writers have been able to reference material from "The Silmarillion" — in particular, where it concerns the First Age of Middle-earth — despite Amazon not having the rights to adapt the book. Not only that, the show has alluded to plot points from that work on more than one occasion, be it Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) being jealous that he's unable to match the craft of the legendary Fëanor or the continuous allusions to Morgoth being Sauron's former boss.

"The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 5 even name-drops a First Age legend when Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) tells Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) exactly how he was captured so many centuries ago. As it turns out, he was taken in after Ancalagon the Black — the most powerful dragon in Middle-earth's history — set his entire legion ablaze, with Sauron astride. The only reason Celeborn survived was because he was kicked off his horse and into some water, shielding him from the inferno.

Ancalagon the Black has never appeared on-screen, but his legacy is legendary. In J.R.R. Tolkien's literature, dragons were specifically bred by Morgoth, first as terrestrial lizards, but later as winged monsters. Ancalagon was known as the Great Dragon of Morgoth, the largest winged dragon in the history of Middle-Earth. He is described by Tolkien as being "as tall as a mountain" and was the leader of the great host of winged dragons that Morgoth unleashed during the War of Wrath in the First Age. The great beast only serves one purpose in the larger Legendarium — to be Morgoth's ultimate weapon of war, one so terrible it nearly ruined the Valar.

Ancalagon is by far the largest dragon in fiction and is much, much larger than any of the dragons in George R.R. Martin's "Game of Thrones" stories, the massive Balerion the Dread included. But unlike Balerion, Ancalagon didn't really do much. Indeed, in Tolkien's canon, he basically appeared for about a day, driving back the Valar until Eärendil arrived with his flying ship and an army of eagles led by their king, Thorondor. Eärendil and the eagles then battled Ancalagon and the dragons for a day and night, only for Eärendil to eventually overthrow the great dragon and cast him into the volcanoes of Thangorodrim (where Morgoth's fortress lay).

The death of Ancalagon also marked the end of the War of Wrath in Middle-earth. And even though the race survived, as evidenced by the later existence of dragons like Smaug, they never reached the heights of the Great Dragon again. Anyway, there's something for you to keep in your back pocket as you continue making your way through "The Rings of Power" on Prime Video.

#3507. Steam Makes Strategy RPG Masterpiece Free For a Limited Time

Build a medieval dynasty, plot against rival nobles, and claim a kingdom without spending a cent this weekend

Steam is giving PC strategy fans another opportunity to try a major grand strategy game without spending a cent. This week's promotion is particularly appealing for players who enjoy medieval history, political intrigue, and building a dynasty from the ground up.

Crusader Kings 3 is temporarily free to play on Steam, giving everyone a chance to experience the acclaimed strategy game and see whether they can keep a medieval dynasty alive before committing to a purchase.

The free weekend runs until Monday, Nov. 23, at 10 a.m. PST. Players who enjoy the experience can also purchase the game at a 70% discount, bringing its usual $49.99 price down to $14.99. The sale runs until Nov. 30.

Released in September 2020, Crusader Kings 3 is a grand strategy game that lets players take control of a medieval noble family and guide its dynasty across generations. Rather than focusing exclusively on warfare, the game puts considerable emphasis on diplomacy, relationships, succession, and political maneuvering.

Players can choose from historical starting points, claim territories, arrange marriages, forge alliances, and expand their influence across a sprawling medieval map. Every character has individual traits, ambitions, and relationships, meaning a seemingly harmless family dispute can eventually turn into a succession crisis or an opportunity to seize a neighboring kingdom.

Death also isn't the end of a campaign, as players continue their family's legacy through successive heirs. That combination of emergent storytelling, political scheming, and grand strategy makes every playthrough potentially different.

The free weekend also arrives shortly after the release of Silk & Silver, the game's latest major expansion, and the accompanying 1.21 "Florin" free update on Nov. 17. It's a particularly good opportunity for newcomers to see what Paradox's long-running strategy series has to offer.

#3506. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3505. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Timeline Explained – When Does It Take Place?

Don't train for the Hunger Games if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" or the original set of "Hunger Games" films — spoilers ahead!

Suzanne Collins, the author of the "Hunger Games" books, doesn't reliably write new stories set within this expansive, totalitarian universe. 10 years after the final novel in her original trilogy, "Mockingjay," hit shelves, she decided to write "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," a prequel that brings us back to some of Panem's earliest days. Similarly, her 2025 book "Sunrise on the Reaping" looks at the 50th Hunger Games.

So, how does the "Hunger Games" timeline even work at this point? It's actually still pretty streamlined, even with Collins jumping around in said timeline across various books. With that in mind, let me walk you through it.

We'll return to "Ballad" and the original trilogy in a moment (all of which have blockbuster movie adaptations, obviously), but as for "Sunrise on the Reaping," the film version stars Joseph Zada as young Hunger Games victor Haymitch Abernathy and sits smack in the middle between "Ballad" and the very first "Hunger Games" book and movie. During the 50th Games (which, as the second "Quarter Quell" — meaning, an extra-evil edition of the Games held every 25 years — features 48 teenage tributes fighting to the death on TV instead of 24), Haymitch makes important alliances, defies the odds, and emerges as the winner. Decades later, he serves as a mentor to characters we meet in "The Hunger Games," making "Sunrise on the Reaping" an important bridge between "Ballad" and the other "Hunger Games" stories.

(A note: specific years are never mentioned in the franchise, so we just use iterations of the Games to organize its timeline.)

In 2020, Suzanne Collins released "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" (her first "Hunger Games" book in a decade), and it focused on the 10th Hunger Games and a young Coriolanus Snow, the man who grows up to be the oppressive president of the totalitarian dystopia known as Panem. In both the book and its film adaptation (where Coriolanus, or "Coryo," is played by Tom Blyth), we meet Coryo as his family faces poverty, total reputational ruin, and even eviction from their home in the Capitol. Desperate to claw his way back up the ladder (his family has a saying that "snow lands on top"), Coryo decides that the tribute he mentors must win the 10th Games, which are newly televised and which take place in a downtrodden, themeless arena (something that changes quite a bit as the Games continue).

Unfortunately for Coryo, his dean at the Capitol Academy, Casca Highbottom (Peter Dinklage), hated Coryo's deceased dad and gives him a tribute from the impoverished coal mining district, 12, assuming she can't possibly win. That, admittedly, backfires: Songstress Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler) from the musical Covey not only charms viewers watching the Games at home, but Coryo himself, and he helps her cheat and win the Games.

When Coryo's machinations are discovered, he's sent to become a Peacekeeper in District 12 ... and despite reuniting with Lucy Gray there, he keeps secrets that send her fleeing, and his descent into depravity truly begins. We do see Snow in "Sunrise on the Reaping" (as president and played by Ralph Fiennes in the movie adaptation), and appropriately, he warns Haymitch about girls from the Covey after learning about his Covey girlfriend and Lucy Gray's descendant, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak).

President Snow is still Panem's leader by the time we get to "The Hunger Games" and are introduced to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), the girl and boy chosen to represent District 12 in the 74th annual Hunger Games. Haymitch, portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original films, is their mentor, and he initially phones it in after years of mentoring young tributes only to watch them die on TV in variously horrifying ways. He does take a shine to Katniss, though, identifying with her stubborn nature and unwillingness to listen to figures of authority, and before long, the two are essentially working together to try and protect the genuinely kind and good-hearted Peeta.

When Katniss and Peeta are allowed to jointly win the 74th Games, Snow wants revenge after a teenage girl makes him look like a fool. As a result, the Third Quarter Quell, the 75th Games, only pulls existing victors back into the arena ... and Peeta volunteers when Haymitch's name is called, sending him and Katniss back into the arena just a year after their win. These Games end abruptly, however, when Katniss fires an arrow through the force field surrounding the arena. She and Haymitch then decamp to the rebellious District 13, while Peeta is captured.

Eventually, the rebellion succeeds, Snow is defeated, and Katniss, Peeta, and Haymitch live out the rest of their lives in District 12. Hence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" fits perfectly into the existing "Hunger Games" movie timeline (it marries "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and the stories that kicked off the Hunger Games franchise), and it's in theaters starting tonight.

#3504. ‘The Gilded Age’ Renewed for Fifth Season Following Ratings Boom

Fans of “The Gilded Age,” rejoice! There are still more luncheons to plan, more balls to savor, and more opera opening nights to fight over. Yes, the HBO original series has been renewed for a fifth season.

The move follows a surge in popularity that began with the show’s drama-filled third season, which saw Bertha (Carrie Coon) and George Russell’s (Morgan Spector) relationship strain, and has continued with the fourth season, which has dealt with their marriage troubles, the wedding of Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), and a visit from Grover Cleveland.

Clearly, it’s working. Viewership for Season 4 has grown week over week, HBO stated in a press release. Episode 3 hit a season high of 4.3 million U.S. cross-platform viewers and episodes are averaging 5.9 million viewers and growing. That outpaces the prior season by nearly 20 percent. Related Stories ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface ‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix’s Slight Sam Bankman-Fried Series Tells a Strange, Crooked Love Story

The turnaround is striking because “The Gilded Age” was very much on the bubble for most of its first two seasons. Bringing 19th-century high-society to life is expensive, and the show initially struggled to become a ratings powerhouse despite being co-created by Julian Fellowes of “Downton Abbey” fame. In interviews, the cast admitted that they often feared they would be canceled. But audiences have shown up in a big way, and Fellowes and his co-creator Sonja Warfield recently told IndieWire that they have more stories to tell beyond this season.

“We have a Season 5 in us if we’re allowed to do it,” Fellowes said. “But when you write a TV series, you have to finish every season so that it could be the end, because one day it will be.”

In its three eligible seasons, “The Gilded Age” has earned 15 total Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Drama Series and Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series, as well as a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

“The Gilded Age” cast includes Christine Baranski, Cynthia Nixon, Louisa Jacobson, Taissa Farmiga, Harry Richardson, Blake Ritson, Ben Ahlers, Ashlie Atkinson, Dylan Baker, Kelley Curran, Jordan Donica, Jessica Frances Dukes, Amy Forsyth, Jack Gilpin, Simon Jones, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Ben Lamb, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Debra Monk, Hattie Morahan, Donna Murphy, and Kristine Nielsen.

#3503. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3502. GTA 6 Gamble to Get Army Soldiers to Reenlist Actually Worked

Dozens of soldiers traded more years in the Army for 4 days off to play GTA 6

With Grand Theft Auto 6 finally launching, some fans are booking time off work, while others are making considerably bigger commitments to secure a few uninterrupted days in Vice City. According to reporting from Task & Purpose, 43 soldiers from the U.S. Army's 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion at Fort Stewart, Georgia, have signed up for a special reenlistment incentive offering a four-day weekend to play GTA 6 when it launched on Nov. 19.

The catch? They had to commit to another two to six years of military service to get the time off.

The unusual offer has already attracted dozens of volunteers, with some soldiers getting additional financial incentives alongside their extended weekend. Sgt. Jamire Smith, a combat engineer who reenlisted for another six years, told Task & Purpose that he was particularly excited about the game's campaign.

"I'm all campaign. I'm all about the heist," Smith said. "I think I have a good 24 hours to waste on it," he joked.

Smith was already considering leaving the Army before his unit helped convince him to stay. His reenlistment also came with a $60,000 bonus, as the Army wanted to retain his specialized skills operating heavy breaching vehicles.

The four-day GTA 6 weekend was the brainchild of Staff Sgt. Brittany Wolfer, a career counselor who wanted to find a more creative way to connect with soldiers considering reenlistment.

"There is always going to be a disconnect between your senior command and your lowest soldier," Wolfer told Task & Purpose. "So how do you bridge that gap to where that lower soldier still knows that their battalion commander or their senior leadership cares about them and sees what they're interested in."

With 43 soldiers now signed up, the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion has found a pretty unconventional way to make reenlistment more appealing. Rockstar Games might want to take notice, too. Wolfer told Task & Purpose she'd love to see the 3rd Infantry Division's bulldog mascot, Rocky, make an appearance in the game.

"Put Rocky in 'Grand Theft Auto.' Absolutely, that'd be, like, peak in my career, honestly," she said.

The incentive comes as GTA 6 fever reaches a new level, with Rockstar's long-awaited sequel earning a 99 Metascore on Metacritic and tying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the highest rating in the site's history. The game has also shattered streaming records, attracting more than 3.29 million concurrent viewers on Twitch alone as players and content creators get their first look at Vice City. With reviews praising its sprawling open world, impressive attention to detail, and emotionally driven story, it's safe to say those 43 soldiers have plenty to look forward to during their four-day weekend.

Rockstar’s magnum opus searches for love and catharsis in desperate times — and finds them

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Re-enlistment strategies and incentives are as old as military units, but this is a pretty unique cherry on top of the bigger more robust incentive.

I would imagine most were re-enlisting anyways due to the bonuses they usually come with.., but getting 4 days off on top of that is probably why they chose this time to re-enlist

#3501. Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break

I don’t think I was supposed to hear Anthony Ippolito when he exclaimed, “20 minutes?” right before this interview, as he was given the amount of time this interview would last. Though, it kind of hit me, if you’re not used to doing interviews — and there’s no way Ippolito can be at this young stage of his career — 20 minutes is a long time to make conversation with a total stranger. Especially, as he is quick to point out, after a barrage of quick, three-minute interviews.

Ippolito has been in films and television before — kind of famously now, he played Al Pacino in “The Offer” — but none of those were roles in which he’d have to do press. Let alone playing the lead role in a major motion picture in which everyone wants to talk to him. Oh, and that lead role is as … Sylvester Stallone. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards

In “I Play Rocky,” yes, Ippolito plays Stallone at the make or break point in Stallone’s career. Stallone had written “Rocky,” a very in-demand script. Not in demand was the idea of Stallone playing Rocky — as MGM offers more and more money to Stallone in an effort to get him to not play Rocky. (If you don’t know, Stallone stuck to his guns, played Rocky, and is now a very wealthy and famous actor.)

Directed by Peter Farrelly, Ippolito says he sent in multiple tapes trying to land this role — which does seem to be in the same spirit as the film itself. Though, Ippolito said, when he was actually going through the casting process, that’s not at all what he was thinking, even though it may seem that way now.

Ahead, he tells us (yes, over the course of 20 minutes) the Stallone movies he used to prep for playing Stallone, what is was like to talk to Stallone before filming, and why he loves Stallone and Dolly Parton together in “Rhinestone.” Also, if he had to play Stallone again in another movie, he does have another “I Play” installment in mind…

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You seem excited about this being 20 minutes?

It’s a little strange, I’ve been having three-minute increment conversations with somebody. So, yes, I am excited.

OK, so how many Stallone movies did you watch? Did you stick to that era? His voice kind of evolves by the late ‘80s.

Yeah, I really tried to stay focused on a period of time. I don’t know the exact number. More so, from the stuff I was looking at I was watching it over and over again, rewatching. With the exception of a few.

Well, “Rocky Balboa.” It’s one of the best movies of the franchise.

For people who haven’t seen that one in a while, it’s very sweet.

It really is. It really is. And he does some excellent work in it. And I think it’s really powerful that he was able to come back many years later, after the fifth one, and make this incredible movie.

From closer to the “Rocky” era, I kind of love him in “The Prisoner of Second Avenue.” Jack Lemmon thinks he stole his wallet…

It’s just scene after scene of Jack Lemmon chasing Stallone through Central Park trying to get his wallet back…

But then Jack Lemmon realizes he left his wallet at home and wound up being the one who mugged Stallone.

But he was mistaken for a mugger and this was part of his issue, right?

It’s funny watching it now, because it’s so obviously Sylvester Stallone. So it’s amusing the whole role is just him being chased.

I agree with you and I found that throughout a lot of the stuff I was unearthing throughout this process.

In that, if he hadn’t become famous, I’d still look at him and think, “what an interesting looking dude,” and wonder what happened to him.

Speaking of that, there were times during “I Play Rocky,” knowing full well what happens in real life, and I’m still like, “Maybe just take the money. That’s a lot.”

It’s really remarkable. Especially when you convert the amount from what it was then to what it would be now.

I know you made a video for your audition which involved an old punching bag and gloves. What were you saying in it?

Oh, well, there was certain dialogue I was coming up with, or thinking of coming up with. And I hadn’t had my hands on too much of the script at this point. So I was just trying to capture his physicality and his movement as a boxer. I was just really passionate about the project. I wanted to put myself out there in a way. And, thankfully, I was able to get my hands on the script a bit later on.

So are you doing lines from “Rocky”? Or just stuff you came up with on your own?

I ask because that’s a time when you haven’t gained the weight yet, so you’re not in the physical condition you are when filming. So I feel you had to really sell this dialogue? Which obviously worked.

Yeah, I mean … it was difficult to come up with that part of it. I had given myself inspiration with some parts of the original film, and some parts from what I felt would work for dialogue from what I was understanding of the story. And then once I was able to get the script, then I was able to just put scenes on tape. And then continuously send them stuff until they relented.

Oh, there was more than one? You just kept going?

Well, that’s the spirit of this movie. Did you feel that way when you were sending them in? “Well, that’s what Stallone did.”

Hm … maybe? You know, it seems that way kind of now?

Right. But at that time, I was just like, “I probably seem crazy to everyone who is on the other end of this.”

Yeah, but I wasn’t thinking about that part for some reason, I guess.

Which is probably good, if you were getting ahead of yourself it doesn’t work out the way it did?

I know you spoke to Stallone before filming. A year ago, he was saying he knew nothing about this movie. When and how did that change?

Peter Farrelly tells a funny story about that. He had actually met with Stallone prior to that and discussed his level of involvement. And they discussed how Stallone would kind of not be necessarily in the trenches with us, just for the sake of Peter not wanting people to feel like Stallone had his hand in it in a way that it was shaped…

And historically Stallone never does that. I say that sarcastically because I’m well aware he has a specific vision for any movie he’s involved in…

Right. Right. So, Stallone went back after that and told somebody he has no idea about it. And Peter was like, “What are you doing?” And Stallone said, “You told me to separate myself.” And Peter was like, “Not that far, man!” So, I guess that was just a bit of a communication breakdown.

So in Stallone’s mind, he was doing a favor by saying that?

I’m not sure, but I was able to speak with him about a month before we started shooting. And I’m very grateful he was willing to take the time

What was that like? Was he in good spirits or was he apprehensive?

He was in great spirits about it. I was nervous, as you could probably imagine.

Yeah, and not only that, I had done so much of my own research. So, up to that point, it was really built up as this really big thing in my head. So, I was just really, really excited to meet him and to listen to him. He was really, really generous and disarming and very willing to share what that period of time was like for him.

What did he tell you that you don’t know already?

Oh, man. Well, he discussed with me building the character of Rocky as a writer. That’s where it became really interesting to me. Because he had studied filmmaking and writing while being an usher. So, hearing his perspective and his kind of clinical breakdown of how he approaches a script and of a character? It was hugely informative in developing and my understanding of this side of him as a writer.

From that, what changed on how you approached playing him? How does that conversation inform what we see?

You just really understand that this thing is his baby. And it really makes more sense that these numbers going so high during these negotiations because the script is that good. And so well written. Yeah, he’s a terrific writer and I think he proved that to Chartoff and Winkler with “Paradise Alley,” first.

My only experience with him was at the afterparty for “The Family Stallone.” He shows up at this restaurant in Little Italy and it’s like the Red Sea parting. Everyone stopped talking and made room so he could walk by. When he got near me I said, “Hey, Sly,” which I immediately regretted. He stopped, looked at me, and gave me a little nod.

He then walked off and I thought, “You know, good enough.”

Are you glad that you said it now? I feel like I would be.

But you keep bringing up meeting Wim Wenders. I know you’re a fan of his, is there something maybe happening?

I got to meet him at the Zurich Film Festival.

I know you like his movies, are you going to work with him?

I just think he makes great films, he’s made great films and he was a really, really sweet man and we got to speak. That’s pretty much it.

I feel that way about so many. Well, Scorsese obviously. Richard Linklater, Derek Cianfrance, Tim Burton.

That’s an eclectic group. “Place Beyond the Pines” and “Beetlejuice” are very different movies.

Very different movies. Well, I like that, You can go in so many different directions. And I appreciate directors and filmmakers who are singular.

And that is kind of the thing about Stallone, too. Did you look at the movies Stallone directed?

Honestly, well, I know he directed all the “Rocky” movies other than the first and fifth ones. And I understand he directed more stuff past that as well. But I hadn’t specifically looked at stuff he directed for this.

How far back did you go back to watch with Peter Farrelly’s films? Did you go back to “Dumb & Dumber”?

I’ve seen so much of his stuff already. So there’s not one that jumped out at me, but also, obviously, “There’s Something About Mary.”

It really is. I think he really killed it with that one. I mean, he has such an incredible sensibility. And he’s always aware of something on set. If there’s a moment to be discovered, to make a meal out of it, he’ll find it.

I always think about, “Unless someone comes up with six-minute abs.”

On social media a lot of people are doing their own “I Play …,” then insert any other Stallone movie type posts. If you had to play him again, what movie would you want to do?

Like, “I Play Cobra,” would be interesting. I do love “Cobra.”

You know, I guess I’m not the right age for this, but “I Play Rocky Balboa” would be very interesting…

Well, it’s the first one I remember. I would have had to have seen the ones prior? To the point I’m in the theater for “Rocky Balboa.”

Well, not necessarily. The first one I saw was “Rocky III”…

Because it was the one on cable all the time. Then I was told, “Oh, you know, the first one is a lot different.”

Yeah, I was pretty young, but I do remember seeing “Rocky Balboa.” And I just think there’s something interesting about the fact that, similar to how he’s fighting the boxing commission at the time to let him fight, because they think that he can’t, or shouldn’t — I think he was having a similar dialogue with the studio at the time. About him making the movie in the first place.

It’s interesting, even at that point, they still didn’t think they could take a chance on him making a “Rocky” movie.

I guess, yeah. It’s strange, but history does repeat itself.

Ah, OK, it’s not streaming, so it’s a little harder to find. It’s just interesting this is only a few years after “Rocky” and now he’s on stage singing with Dolly Parton. It’s kind of fascination what that one decision did for him…

It’s very true. And I think Dolly Parton is spectacular in that.

How good is she in that? Right? I mean, she has such a warmth to her. I mean, yeah. She’s just incredible in the movie and it makes it so fun. The two of them! They are dynamic.

You could also make “I Play Nick Martinelli.”

So what are the lessons you personally took away from playing Stallone? I can’t help but think there are lessons here for actors starting out.

I agree. Well, he really overcame so much and he didn’t have too many people in his corner at the time. I mean, thankfully, he had Sasha who was there for him, who AnnaSophia Robb plays in the movie. And she’s so great in it. And as much as you want to see Stallone persevere, and be kind of a lone wolf through this? For actors there’s meaning in that, and there’s a lesson to be learned in that.

But there’s also a lesson to be found in Sasha. Because you need that person sometimes in your life. Or sometimes it’s good to be that person for people — to remind people to believe in themselves. Because, no matter what, Stallone overcame so much, but of course he doubted himself. And if you don’t have at least somebody who is there, willing to be that person to remind you to believe in yourself, it’s a tough road.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “I Play Rocky” in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.

#3500. Yellowjackets Season 4 Review: The Survival Thriller's Final Episodes Answer A Big Question

"What are we capable of when our darkest urges are given not only a voice, but also a stage on which to use it? And can you ever really go back once you've seen what's underneath?" asked Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson in the pitch deck for their thriller series "Yellowjackets," claiming this would be the central question driving their show. As "Yellowjackets" debuts its fourth and final season, its answer comes due.

Set in both the late 1990s and early 2020s, "Yellowjackets" follows the aftermath of a plane crash that was taking the Wiskayok, New Jersey Yellowjackets soccer team across the country to a national championship. The teenage survivors descend into a barbarity, cannibalism, and pagan ritual across 19 months stranded in the Canadian wilderness. In their present, their now middle-aged selves reckon with old wounds coming unsealed.

"Yellowjackets" returns from a third season that hit some stumbling blocks. The departure of Juliette Lewis in particular was a hard void to fill, even if the show is trying with the introduction of Hilary Swank as an adult counterpart to Yellowjacket Melissa (Jenna Burgess). But the season ended on a high note.

In the Season 3 finale, "Full Circle," Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) uses a salvaged satellite phone to call for rescue. With help's imminent arrival in the Wilderness, the Yellowjackets must scramble to tie up loose ends. In the present, Taissa (Tawny Cypress) and Misty (Christina Ricci), fed up with cleaning Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) messes, are planning to kill her — until Melissa puts the spotlight on the Yellowjackets again.

Paramount+ has only shared the first two (out of ten) episodes of "Yellowjackets" Season 4 for review. Going off that extremely limited view of the season, the ride is steady enough so far.

It's been a nail-biting wait for the return of "Yellowjackets," especially knowing since last October this would be the end of the show. I'll admit I've been counting down the weeks for Season 4, yet when I first received those screeners, I held off for several days. Suddenly the reality of the show ending, and the risk of it disappointing, became too real.

As previously confirmed by the creators, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 is the most structurally complex season yet. Now there are three parallel timelines, as we see play out in these first two episodes. The adult Yellowjackets are still in one story, but the teens are in two. Instead of depicting their rescue and readjustment in chronological order, Season 4 cuts back and forth between their last days in the wilderness and their first days back in Wiskoyak. Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown) is taking lead as the one keeping the other Yellowjackets on script — she does grow up to be a lawyer and politician, after all.

Knowing "Yellowjackets" was originally planned for five seasons, it's tempting to consider if this new structure is a way to cram the remainder of the 1990s timeline into one densely-packed season. Indeed, we see very little of the Wilderness timeline in these first two episodes, which will frustrate some since that's still the most exciting storyline. It's got the running clock, as the Yellowjackets have to get their stories and evidence straight without knowing exactly when help is arriving, and the biggest mysteries, since we know that a few more of the Yellowjackets are going to die in the time gap.

"Yellowjackets" Season 3 previously skipped months ahead of Season 2's cliffhanger ending. Watching the Season 4 premiere, with the Yellowjackets recuperating in a hospital, you might think the show has done so again. After all, Season 3 ended with Nat calling for help, so it's not a huge jump. Plus, is there any more story to tell in the Wilderness? Indeed there is, because the last minutes cut back and forth to violence still unseen. But is it wise to fall back on the "keep the audience waiting" trick in your last season?

Opening on the immediate post-rescue timeline, though, delivers on a promise the show has made since the beginning. Since we've known from the jump that some of the team makes it home, the show invites you to imagine what will happen when that moment arrives. How will they adjust to seeing their old parents and peers again, who have no idea what their daughters and friends faced for 19 months? The Season 4 premiere finally introduces many of the characters' parents, and sets up a season exploring the Yellowjackets' home lives, like what made them into the people they were before the Wilderness.

How does the 1990s timeline bridge to the 2020s one? How do the Yellowjackets assimilate to suburban mundanity? How will they handle the unwanted public spotlight that flattens them into sainted heroes but also piles on the salacious theories of what they did to survive? How do they cover up any and all investigations into their crimes that still remain buried as of 2022? "Yellowjackets" Season 4 is on track to deliver all those answers and, so far, they appear promising.

As for the 2020s timeline, the premiere picks up with Melissa, catching up to where she went after running off in Season 3 Episode 9 "How The Story Ends." The show still hasn't quite overcome what a narrative patch her introduction was back in Season 3. Now, though, she is at least giving the present day timeline a villain and conflict uniting the other Yellowjackets, something the show has struggled with after Season 1.

The adult timeline of "Yellowjackets" is often best when the leads are together. In Season 4, they're sharing a united front early on instead of converging mid-season. Let's also just say that how Melissa re-inserts herself into her old friends' lives fits the absurdist black comedy the show excels at, and it's looking like it could be an impetus for the Yellowjackets to finally earn a public reckoning.

Conversely, the teen timeline looks like it might be splitting the girls up as they slot back into their old, separate lives without the Wilderness binding them together. But the teen timeline actors, who've always held the show up through peaks and valleys, remain as strong as ever.

Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) brief reign as the Wilderness' cannibal Antler Queen is over, and she's not happy about it. She says very little as her anger stews; she's cowed and quiet, but not regretful. Episode 2 focuses mostly on Shauna, and the very beginning of how she's going to force herself into a box of domestic tranquility for two decades — a box that her middle-aged self is breaking out of.  Shauna's mask is off again and it's scary, and also incredible how Melanie Lynskey makes her sweet, high-pitched voice sound as cold and sharp as an icicle.

The show's usual MVPs remain Sophie Thatcher in the teen timeline — Natalie is the one Yellowjacket not returning to a happy home — and Christina Ricci in the adult timeline. Misty's manically planning to stage Shauna's suicide brings out her unhinged comic relief side; no one can do a wide-eyed, violent smile like Ricci.

Yet, dialogue is a mixed bag. There's plenty of clever and cutting lines, but a bit too much hand-holding exposition recaps, as well. The killer soundtrack of "Yellowjackets," though, remains on point, bringing out '90s favorites like Nirvana and Depeche Mode for montage sequences. The most striking needle drop is in Episode 2, when Shauna is walking alone at night (a genuinely eerie shot) to Portishead's "Wandering Star."

Blunt yet clever visual storytelling is on the menu in these episodes, too. Take Lottie (Courtney Eaton) sitting in a hospital exam room where the wall is painted with a forest full of Disney-like animals, a reminder of her abandoned Wilderness home. Continuing on from a dream sequence in Season 3 Episode 8's "A Normal Boring Life," Season 4 Episode 2 uses a grocery store as the ultimate setting of modern normality (the contrast, of course, is that the Yellowjackets had to fight and scavenge for their food in the Wilderness).

Shauna is surrounded by seemingly innocuous reminders of her last 19 months as the group's butcher (in more ways than one), like sliced deli meat or a dead deer (crowned with antlers) being sliced up as roadkill. If this season can stick the landing, the legacy of "Yellowjackets" should be stronger than Shauna's as the Antler Queen.

"Yellowjackets" Season 4 premieres on Paramount+ on Friday, November 20, 2026.

#3499. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3498. Buffy The Vampire Slayer’s New Franchise-Changing Story Confirms Official Release Date

Buffy the Vampire Slayer is returning soon with a franchise-changing story.

The franchise was previously expected to return in the near future via Hulu's Buffy the Vampire Slayer: New Sunnydale series, with Sarah Michelle Gellar reprising her titular role and serving as an executive producer. Academy Award winner Chloé Zhao directed a pilot episode based on a script written by Nora and Lilla Zuckerman and featuring Ryan Kiera Armstrong as a new Slayer. However, Hulu chose not to move forward with the series.

Now, a new novel called Buffy the Vampire by Taylor Hartley will be released on July 20, 2027. The story revolves around the game-changing premise of Buffy Summers becoming a vampire via a spell discovered by her friend and increasingly powerful witch, Willow Rosenberg. The heroic protagonist does this in order to fix a mysterious crack that has formed in the Hellmouth, and the spell makes her the first to have the blood of a human, Slayer, and demon all at once.

The spell proves difficult to reverse, though, with Buffy's soul beginning to slip as she contends with the return of threats like Spike and Drusilla. Hartley previously clarified that the story is set during the early part of season 3, with Buffy, Willow, and Cordelia Chase serving as the point-of-view characters. Other fan favorites confirmed to return alongside Spike and Drusilla are Rupert Giles and Daniel "Oz" Osbourne.

With Random House, which is owned by Disney, as the publisher, and given the premise, Hartley previously described the book on Instagram as "an official, OG Scooby Gang Buffy book," in addition to being "a feminist romp and a love letter to the series that quite literally saved me in more ways than one." "Bangel vs. Spuffy" will also be present given Spike's return and Buffy worrying about Angel turning evil again.

Click here to pre-order Buffy the Vampire.

While the franchise has had no shortage of new stories released via publishing, including a Buffy the Vampire Slayer comics series from Dynamite Entertainment coming in 2027, having the character actually become the demon she usually hunts is a very different and exciting approach. Since it is set within the existing canon, readers familiar with the show know that Willow's spell won't be permanent, but it is still a deeply original and compelling premise.

Much of the focus will remain on the Slayer, but other Buffy characters are also poised to play a significant part in the story, especially with chapters being told through the perspectives of Willow and Cordelia. If the book was set later in the show's timeline, having Cordelia be a point-of-view character would be less feasible given her move to the Angel spinoff series and the city of Los Angeles after season 3.

The cancellation of Hulu's Buffy the Vampire Slayer sequel series remains a massive disappointment for the fandom. Just as Zhao expressed her longtime enthusiasm for the original show, though, Hartley has also made it clear that she is a major fan as well, which contributed to her being able to write an official novel set within the beloved franchise. Between the novels and comics, with there being an ongoing Angel one as well, there will be many new stories via publishing in 2027.

Buffy the Vampire will be released on July 20, 2027.

#3496. Valve Warns of a Possible Steam Machine Price Hike

The 2TB model will be especially impacted by the ongoing PC components shortage

Video game hardware manufacturers have been impacted by the computer component crisis, with Nintendo, PlayStation, and Xbox all raising the prices of their consoles this year. PC gaming giant Valve has increased the cost of its Steam Deck, and its PC-but-looks-like-a-console Steam Machine ended up being more expensive than Valve originally intended. Now, Valve has warned that its Steam Machine might get a price hike while opening up purchases for the cheapest model.

In an update posted on Thursday, Valve said it has fulfilled all reservations for the 512 GB Steam Machine model, which costs $1,049, and has now opened it up for purchase to anyone while supplies last. Nice! "However, we are continuing to encounter supply constraints for hardware components, which impacts our ability to source parts." Ah, nuts. Once the 512 GB model is sold out, Valve will mark it as out of stock instead of opening up a new waitlist.

According to Valve, there are more customers on the 2 TB model ($1,349) waitlist than its current production can meet. "Even when we are able to build more it will be at smaller quantities than we planned," Valve said. There are more people on the 2 TB model waitlist than units made, so Valve is closing the waitlist. Those on the waitlist can purchase the 512 GB model, but they will be removed from the 2 TB model waitlist.

But here's the real kicker: Because PC parts continue to increase in price "at unprecedented levels," Valve is unsure how many Steam Machines it will be able to make, and unsure of how much they will be priced at when they're available. "The 2 TB model in particular will be especially constrained." Valve says it will share more information in January.

For now, PC gamers contemplating purchasing a Steam Machine will have to wonder if they should pull the trigger now on the 512 GB model (especially before scalpers gobble them all up), take their chances on the 2 TB model waitlist, or hope for good news come January.

#3495. Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles

40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics. No, not the “Heat” directed by Michael Mann that starred Robert De Niro and Al Pacino and would go on to become a revered classic — that came nine years later. The “Heat” that played in Europe in 1986 starred Burt Reynolds, was directed by multiple journeyman helmers, and was almost immediately forgotten only months after it limped into U.S. theaters in March of 1987.

American reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong. “Heat,” in which Reynolds plays an aging mercenary held prisoner by a crippling gambling addiction, is not only one of Reynolds’ most interesting films but one of his most personal, and a top-tier entry in the canon of the subgenre that is “Burt Noir.” Related Stories Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors

From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath. Reynolds was one of the premier talk show guests (and occasional guest hosts) of the 1970s and early 1980s, a guy who could always be counted on to tell a funny, self-deprecating anecdote that made the audience feel like a part of his inner circle.

But Reynolds always gave the sense that there was a chip on his shoulder — that he was mad about not being taken seriously enough, or being taken too seriously, or losing out on the best parts to his friend and competitor Clint Eastwood and other stars. (Never mind the fact that Reynolds lost out on most of his potentially successful roles — “Terms of Endearment,” “Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman” — because he turned them down, not because anyone took them from him.)

Early on, Eastwood let his controlled rage be a defining trait of his star persona; Reynolds generally tried, and failed, to cloak his under chuckling humility. Many of Reynolds’ best performances exploit this tension, from John Boorman’s “Deliverance,” in which Reynolds’ male bonding fishing expedition descends into a horror, to Paul Thomas Anderson’s “Boogie Nights,” in which the actor’s initially nurturing father figure turns dark and violent when tested.

Reynolds’ memoir, “But Enough About Me,” offers a fascinating glimpse into the contradiction between his healthy self-regard (hilariously exhibited in passages in which he disparages two of the best directors he ever worked with, Anderson and Peter Bogdanovich) and his persistent self-loathing (demonstrated in his candid appraisals of his many terrible personal and professional decisions). The latter informs an ongoing, if intermittent, cycle of Reynolds movies of which “Heat” is a key example: movies I define as “Burt Noir,” in which the actor plays supremely confident men of action tormented by regret and the knowledge that they’ve failed to live up to their potential.

The first, and possibly best, example of Burt Noir is the 1975 cop drama “Hustle,” in which Reynolds plays a Los Angeles detective surrounded by moral decay and corruption. Reynolds and director Robert Aldrich got to make “Hustle” after their commercial success with “The Longest Yard,” and they immediately squandered whatever mainstream goodwill that comedy had bought them with a film so grim and pessimistic it made James Ellroy look like Fred Rogers.

In “Hustle,” Reynolds is surrounded by evil both banal and terrifying, and he meets almost all of it with a weary resignation — aside from one desperate, possibly pointless act, he doesn’t even try to fight the men to whom he knows he is morally, intellectually, and physically superior. The movie reeks with sadness in spite of being marketed as a muscular action movie — though it is a muscular action movie, as is a later and more commercially successful Burt Noir, “Sharky’s Machine.”

That movie, in which Reynolds plays a cop who falls for the prostitute he’s got under surveillance, further explores the sense of moral outrage that marked “Hustle” and Reynolds’ directorial debut, “Gator,” and it gives Reynolds another of his tortured heroes who alternates between spurts of violent action and long passages of almost complete impotence — a combination that reaches its apotheosis in “Heat.”

A clue to what Reynolds is up to in terms of deconstructing his persona comes in the opening of “Heat,” a 12-minute prologue that doesn’t have much to do with the rest of the film other than breaking down Reynolds’ heroic image for audience members who still see him as a conventional leading man. Reynolds’ Nick Escalante tries to pick up a woman in a bar in the ugliest, aggressive way possible, and it’s confusing for the audience — why has the guy who was such a sweet charmer to Sally Field, Goldie Hawn, Jill Clayburgh, and Julie Andrews in earlier movies turned into such a misogynistic pig?

Even more confusing is what follows, when the meek twerp the woman is dating shows up and beats the hell out of Reynolds in the parking lot. We learn, later on, that the whole thing was a set-up — the guy hired Nick to fake everything so he could look like a hero in front of his girlfriend. But in the audience’s mind, the seed has already been planted; subconsciously we can never quite see this guy as a straightforward hero, and that’s the way Reynolds and screenwriter William Goldman want it.

The film progresses as a kind of hangout movie familiar to anyone who loves Quentin Tarantino’s “Jackie Brown” or “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”; there’s a relatively solid genre movie structure running underneath everything, but Goldman takes plenty of time for character-developing digressions that give the whole movie a rich sense of melancholy texture.

Escalante’s tale of attempted moral redemption in the form of his efforts to help the victim of a sadistic young gangster avenge her beating moves from sharp wit (in the form of the best dialogue Goldman ever wrote — which is saying something when you’re talking about the guy who wrote “Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid”) and contemplative scenes of self-examination to shocking bursts of expertly choreographed violence and wistful romance.

It’s all given added layers of irony and resonance by the Las Vegas setting, which seems to mock Escalante’s dreams of hitting it big and escaping to a peaceful retirement in Italy, and Goldman’s choice to set the movie at Christmas, which only mocks Escalante more cruelly. Although “Heat” is one of Goldman’s least well known films (a movie that is easily forgotten amidst the more honored “All the President’s Men,” “Marathon Man,” and “Misery”), it’s one of his most beautifully written, with badinage as snappy as it is revealing and a weaving plot whose emotional effects really sneak up on you.

So why were American critics so dismissive? As is so often the case, they mostly seemed to be reviewing the chaotic circumstances of the production more than the movie that actually resulted from them. “Heat” was a famously troubled movie, whose misfortunes made their way into the press long before the film actually hit American screens. Its beginnings were auspicious: Goldman, one of the most respected writers in the business, was adapting his own novel (with a clause in his contract that said he couldn’t be rewritten), and Robert Altman was set to direct.

Then, only days before shooting, Altman quit the project after his favored cinematographer, Canadian cameraman Pierre Mignot, was denied an H-1 Visa to work in America. Altman claimed that over the course of eight pictures he had developed a style and way of working with Mignot that he didn’t want to abandon, and certainly didn’t want to have to reinvent in a matter of days with another director of photography. Whether or not this is the whole story is anybody’s guess — it was reported that the real reason Altman left had to do with creative differences between him and producer Elliott Kastner, and that Mignot merely gave him the excuse he was looking for to walk.

Goldman suggested Reynolds, who had helmed “Sharky’s Machine” and other fine pictures, take over directing himself, but Burt said he wanted to focus solely on his performance. Thus began a game of directorial musical chairs that would be widely reported and which gave “Heat” the patina of a disaster in the making. Reliable craftsman Dick Richards came on first, only to leave the production after getting into a fistfight with Reynolds on the set. In spite of lawsuits flying back and forth, Richards returned to the set, only to leave again when he fell off a camera crane and ended up in the hospital.

On the days when Richards was out second-unit director and stunt coordinator Stan Barrett took on directing duties, and some of the most electrifying moments in “Heat” can be attributed to him. Barrett had worked as Reynolds’ stunt double for more than 20 years and had a great sense of how to capitalize on the actor’s physicality and image, and the set pieces he directed for “Heat” — like a hotel room fight between Reynolds and some thugs — are beautifully staged and filled with brutally effective and original instances of sudden and shocking violence.

DGA rules at the time prohibited Barrett from taking over the reins for more than five days, since the guild forbade any preexisting member of a troupe from replacing the director — a rule, ironically, that was created when Reynolds’ friend Clint Eastwood fired director Philip Kaufman from “The Outlaw Josey Wales” and replaced him with himself. With only eight days of filming left on “Heat,” television stalwart Jerry Jameson (who had directed Reynolds years earlier on “Dan August”) stepped in and finished the picture.

The experience doesn’t seem to have been a happy one for many of the principals involved, especially Richards, who gave interviews begging people not to blame him for what he saw as the film’s failures. A DGA arbitration determined that Richards was responsible for 40% of the film — more than any of the other directors on the project — and thus should have the credit. Not wanting his name on the movie, Richards eschewed his usual credit for “Directed by R.M. Richards” and tried to wash his hands of the entire debacle as soon as he could.

With the movie’s own director badmouthing the film in the press, “Heat” never really stood a chance. Yet the movie that exists doesn’t show signs of any of the production’s dysfunction, aside from a slightly abrupt and abbreviated finale (one of several that was shot). In the end, Goldman and Reynolds, more than any director, are the true auteurs of “Heat,” and the consistency of their conception of Nick Escalante as an honorable, self-destructive, romantic, tortured, possibly doomed hero gives “Heat” a lingering emotional resonance and power that still works 40 years later.

Burt would continue his forays into Burt Noir both in film (“Malone,” “Rent-A-Cop,” “Physical Evidence”) and television (“B.L. Stryker,” “Hard Time”), but he never played this kind of character better than he did in “Heat.” The movie was remade, incidentally, in 2015 by “Con Air” director Simon West as “Wild Card.” That version didn’t connect with critics or audiences either, in spite of Goldman once again writing the screenplay. At this point it’s fair to assume that “Heat” is just a doomed project, which is a shame — since it also happens to represent one of Goldman’s finest artistic moments.
