#3494. Focker-In-Law Could Be A Rare Theatrical Comedy Box Office Hit Over Thanksgiving

It's no secret to anyone who even sort of pays attention to box office happenings that comedy hasn't exactly been booming in recent years. The 2020s have been especially unkind to theatrical comedy, as it's been tough sledding when it comes to comedy for comedy's sake. But "Focker-In-Law" looks to be the rare out-and-out comedy hit when it arrives over Thanksgiving.

Directed by John Hamburg, the fourth entry in the "Meet the Parents" franchise is currently expected to pull in as much as $56 million across the Thanksgiving holiday frame, per Box Office Theory. Mind you, the movie comes out on Wednesday to get in on the holiday, meaning it will have a full five-day Wednesday to Sunday stretch. So, that $56 million figure isn't a standard weekend figure. Meanwhile, the holiday's other big release, the Hailee Steinfeld-led Disney animated flick "Hexed," is targeting a softer opening in the $30 million range.

If all goes well for Universal Pictures, then, "Focker-In-Law" may take the number one spot ... that is, unless Lionsgate has anything to say about it. Indeed, the studio's "Hunger Games" film "Sunrise on the Reaping" is shaping up to be a massive hit, pulling in at least $100 million domestically this upcoming weekend. As such, assuming it's not too front-loaded, it could compete with the Focker family for the crown during its second frame.

Ben Stiller's "Meet the Parents" buried Sylvester Stallone's "Get Carter" at the box office back in 2000, eventually pulling in $330 million worldwide on a $55 million budget. "Meet the Fockers" was an even bigger success, earning over $500 million on an $80 million budget. The problem? By the time "Little Fockers" came along in 2010, the franchise was running out of gas. Against a $100 million budget, it made $310 million.

To be clear, $310 million is nothing to sneeze at. Nevertheless, "Focker-In-Law," has to pay stars Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner, Owen Wilson, Ariana Grande, and (to a lesser degree) Skyler Gisondo, meaning it's likely its budget is once again in the $100 million range.

Even so, with an over/under $50 million debut over a typically robust holiday weekend, that's a damn good start. "Moana 2" smashed box office records leading to the biggest Thanksgiving ever in 2024, for example. This year won't be as big, but families go to the movies around the holidays. And when we consider that this franchise has generally performed well overseas, international audiences should turn up as well. (Notably, Paramount is handling overseas distribution.)

Comedy could use a win, too. Earlier this year, two very different comedies in "One Night Only" and "Super Troopers 3" both flopped at the box office on the same weekend. As such, the only true, blue comedy success story of 2026 is "Scary Movie" ($231 million worldwide). Fittingly, that was another revival of an early 2000s-born franchise that's long been dormant. The difference is that we're talking about something more family-friendly with "Fock-In-Law," so that helps.

Moreover, most recent comedy hits have been rom-coms like "Ticket to Paradise" ($168 million), "The Lost City" ($192 million), and "Anyone But You" ($220 million). "Focker-In-Law," by comparison, is much more comedy-forward. However, it does have a central romantic element, which should only further aid its cause.

Basically, this one has a good shot at attracting audiences eager to catch up with characters they haven't seen in a while, with or without critics on its side. We'll see how everything pans out.

"Focker-In-Law" hits theaters on November 25, 2026.

#3492. Why The Odyssey's Blu-ray Has No Deleted Scenes

Once Christopher Nolan movies have had their run on the biggest screens possible, their home-video release is often just as exciting for fans, letting them pore over every detail and moment and explore all the behind-the-scenes features. However, longtime Nolan fans already know the one thing most digital/physical movie releases have that you won't find in The Odyssey's new home release.

Because Nolan's films often push the envelope with the latest cameras, practical effects, and groundbreaking filming techniques, the behind-the-scenes featurettes and technical breakdowns are major draws once they finally get a digital/physical release. However, one feature notably missing from The Odyssey (and almost every other Nolan film) is deleted scenes.

Having recently spoken about The Odyssey's lack of deleted scenes directly, here are some comments from Christopher Nolan himself about his process, lack of interest in deleted scenes, and the true advantage of being a writer-director.

While promoting The Odyssey's digital and physical release in various interviews and a Q&A with Universal Pictures, Christopher Nolan confirmed that he's not a believer in deleted scenes, often a traditional feature found on most home video releases:

"I don't really deal in deleted scenes. I kind of never have. If you know my work on Blu-ray as it's come out over the years and DVD before that, I think we've only ever put two deleted scenes on Insomnia. I think it's the only film we ever had them."

During this same Q&A, Nolan went on to explain that his typical process as a writer-director helps him avoid filming large amounts of material that ultimately won't make it off the cutting-room floor, confirming that most of his deleted scenes were only ever pages "crumbled up in my wastebasket that you won't ever see."

Despite the lack of deleted scenes, Nolan confirmed that The Odyssey's release on DVD, Blu-ray, and 4K UHD still has plenty of great extras, praising the behind-the-scenes material assembled for the release and confirming he's happy with the film's overall transfer.

Ultimately, Christopher Nolan's explanation makes perfect sense when considering how intentional and demanding his productions reportedly are. Likewise, it's clear that Nolan has leveraged his dual role as writer and director to his films' full advantage, ensuring deleted scenes are never shot in the first place. He can address potential problems and narrative excesses well in advance during the scripting process, rather than wasting time and money on set.

Although that has been Christopher Nolan's approach for his movies for years, it's especially understandable with a production as big and challenging as The Odyssey, with so many practical locations, effects, huge action sequences, hundreds of extras, and one of the most ambitious scopes of all time.

Because of that impressive level of intention and efficiency, this also means that there won't ever be a director's cut of The Odyssey, as confirmed by Nolan himself in the same Q&A:

“I don’t really believe in director’s cuts. I want to stand by the film that goes out. As a writer-director, I try to do a lot of that weeding out. There aren’t many scenes that were shot. On a film like this, to spend a day shooting something on top of a mountain or in the rain or on a boat or whatever that isn’t gonna be in the film, I would really rather not do that. And so I wanna stand behind the cuts of the films that are put out there.”

While that may seem disappointing in a world where director's cuts and theatrical re-releases with new footage added are happening more and more (see Spider-Man: Brand New Day's newly announced re-release)...it's really not. It simply means the original theatrical cut is exactly what Christopher Nolan envisioned and always wanted The Odyssey to be, with nothing left out or left on the cutting room floor to begin with, which is pretty dang impressive all things considered.

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is now available to purchase digitally and on 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray.

#3491. Why Lenore Dove Baird From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

In 2025, "Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins released one of the most long-awaited stories in the entire franchise — the backstory of District 12 victor Haymitch Abernathy, "Sunrise on the Reaping." A film adaptation titled "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" immediately took shape, and after Joseph Zada was cast as a young version of Haymitch — before he's an aging, depressed, drink-swilling lout portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the four original films — the rest of the cast began to round out.

Immediately after I read the book, I wondered who might be cast as Lenore Dove Baird, the beautiful and wild girlfriend Haymitch is forced to leave behind in District 12 when he's essentially chosen to participate in the Games by mistake. I was then extremely pleased when Whitney Peak was cast in this important part, who's not only Haymitch's love interest but a vital link to the other prequel "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" ... in that Lenore Dove is distantly related to that film and novel's heroine Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler).

So where have you seen Peak before she took on the role of Lenore Dove? I should say that, in general, Peak's star is still on the rise, but there's a reason she earned this role; not only is she extremely talented, but she's appeared in some pretty high-profile projects in recent years. From a major HBO reboot (that did fail, by no fault of Peak's) to some independent films, here's where you've seen Whitney Peak, who plays Lenore Dove in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," before.

After small roles in films like "Molly's Game" and TV shows like "The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina," Whitney Peak booked her first lead role courtesy of the "Gossip Girl" reboot that aired on HBO Max from 2021 to 2023.

As a huge fan of the ridiculous campfest that is the original "Gossip Girl" — which was adapted, very loosely, from a novel series written by Cecily von Ziegesar and ran on The CW from 2007 to 2012 — I was excited for this reboot, but sadly, it was a largely toothless and lackluster impersonation of the original. Still, Peak was very good! She plays Zoya Lott, a newcomer to the high-status New York City preparatory school who finds out that her late birth mother had another daughter. After Zoya and her half-sister, the wealthy and popular Julien Calloway (Jordan Alexander), make plans to meet up, they end up attending Constance Billard together ... but Zoya, who doesn't come from extreme privilege, struggles to fit in with Julien and her high society friends.

Again, this version of "Gossip Girl" is entirely too concerned with social justice crusades, whereas in the original show, the 20-somethings did insane stuff like sell each other for hotels. (Social justice is ... just not the point of a show like "Gossip Girl!") It was ultimately canceled after its Season 2 finale aired, leaving the story unfinished ... but it also freed Peak up for bigger and better opportunities.

In terms of her big-screen work, Whitney Peak has appeared in a solid mix of independent project and a few bigger movies — aside from "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." In 2022, Peak showed up in the supporting role of Becca in the legacy sequel "Hocus Pocus 2," and I already mentioned that she was in "Molly's Game," which marked her film debut.

Elsewhere, Peak led films like the independent horror movie "Eye for an Eye," directed by Colin Tilley and adapted from Elisa Victoria's book "Mr. Sandman" — in that, Peak plays a young woman grieving the tragic loss of her parents who finds herself newly traumatized by a shocking, violent incident in her new home in Florida. Peak also appeared in the action thriller "Trap House" alongside Sophia Lillis, Inde Navarrette, Jack Champion, and Bobby Cannavale, as well as Tommy Wirkola's survival film "Thrash" with Phoebe Dynevor and Djimon Hounsou.

You can see Peak as Lenore Dove Baird in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters now.

#3490. Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition

Finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about. First-time feature filmmaker Brydie O’Connor’s Sundance-winning documentary “Barbara Forever” is a hypnotic archival collage that retraces the life, work, and death of Barbara Hammer.

The documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing. (Kristen Stewart also jumped on board as an executive producer.) It’s not hard to see why. “Barbara Forever” is an archival documentary that unfolds in the shape and style of its subject, an experimental filmmaker who put together some of the first publicly projected lesbian erotica actually made by a lesbian. Voiceover by the filmmaker spans her early career in the Bay Area (and halcyon days as an out lesbian), her 1992 feature debut “Nitrate Kisses,” and the final years of a cancer battle that ended in 2019. Related Stories Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break

Now New York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met. “I read about Barbara and studied Barbara before I even saw her films,” O’Connor told IndieWire. She reached out to Hammer to “buy her DVDs because they weren’t showing anywhere in D.C. And she wrote back to me. At first, she was a little bit hard on me. She was like, ‘I see you’re writing from an edu.edu address. I just want to make sure that you’re actually a student because if you’re faculty, it would be much, much more expensive.’ [Laughs] And I said, ‘I promise, Barbara, I’m a student. I just can’t wait to see your movies.’ And she sent me her DVDs. So yeah, I think that initial impulse to explore her work was really about … ‘Why don’t more people know about Barbara and her work?'”

Hammer had degrees in psychology and literature before encountering “Meshes of the Afternoon” director Maya Deren’s films (which also influenced David Lynch) at San Francisco State in the 1970s. They lit the fuse for making her own movies. Circa that time, she’d been living in Santa Rosa and married to a man. She came out as a lesbian — busting through that closet, really, with abandon — and took off with her Super 8 camera to start making lesbian films. Growing up in Kansas, O’Connor, in her early 30s, resonated with Hammer’s early biography, and Hammer’s early lust for self-reinvention.

“She was not really tentative about anything. She picked up a camera in her late 20s as she was getting a divorce from a man when she realized that she was a lesbian and she made her film,” O’Connor said. “She learned by doing. And I was so inspired because, at the time, I was studying American studies and history in school. I had no background in the arts really, except for enjoying consuming them. And I really thought I would be a film critic or a writer… [Barbara Hammer] was not afraid to fail creatively. And she tried so many different ideas, of course, throughout her entire career in making over 85 films, but especially in that first decade of her career.”

Post-college and in New York, O’Connor, who’s spent “a decade in the Hammer world, and my entire adult consciousness,” would see Hammer at the Metrograph in Lower Manhattan. “I definitely was ‘the girl who wrote her thesis on Barbara,’ probably one of many, and I was day-playing in the film industry,” O’Connor said. “I would occasionally go up to Yale, where her formal archive is held, to continue doing independent research. I was looking at her love letters and her photographs… I wrote to her in January of 2019 when I was about to make my first short film. I said, ‘Hi, Barbara.’ I didn’t know how sick she was at the time. I was like, ‘I’m making my first film. Can I take you to coffee? Do you have any advice for me?’ And she wrote back to me and said, ‘I’m at the very, very end of my life, but best of luck with everything in your career.'”

Hammer died in March 2019, which is when O’Connor contacted the filmmaker’s partner, the human rights advocate Florrie Burke. “Florrie was the love of her life. They were together for 31 years,” O’Connor said. Their meeting culminated in O’Connor’s 2022 short film “Love, Barbara,” which she expanded into the feature that hit theaters this year. In a 2026 Oscar documentary race heavy on genocide and social issues — or a three-hour A24 movie that’s shaken up the entire form — “Barbara Forever” is life-affirming, lovely, yet still-important counter-programming.

The organic archival rhythm of “Barbara Forever” eschews talking heads altogether, instead conversing with what Hammer’s work looked and felt like. One of the film’s most charming snippets finds Hammer showing one of her (SFW!) films to a classroom of small schoolchildren. They end up having an unexpected appreciation for the experimental film clip’s non-narrative sensibilities.

O’Connor collaborated with Burke on sifting through 35 hours of audio recordings to stitch together a narration unfolding entirely in Hammer’s own words. “Florrie was so happy with [the short], but she always reminded me there’s so much more to Barbara than just our relationship,” O’Connor said. “Barbara’s this huge personality. She’s so charismatic and charming and really both thoughtful, but also very savvy. She wanted to be recognized. She wanted to be known for her work and her efforts, and she was uncompromising in what she made and how she shared her work. So it just made sense that she would be the narrator of the film.”

The Sundance-winning editing, too, proved a challenge, as O’Connor and her filmmaking team pored over more than 400 hours of visual material — from Hammer’s films, to outtakes, B-sides, home videos, and more. “I really wanted to convey with this film: Why did Barbara turn the camera on herself and her life and her lovers and her body as a method of alternative history making? What did she see in the value of that approach and then making experimental cinema out of it and demanding the value of that within culture?”

That Hammer’s work wasn’t more canonized during her life — an effort O’Connor has made partly her own, especially as a new digital restoration of “Nitrate Kisses” is making the rounds — isn’t only because of how confrontational she was about gender and her own sexuality. “Nitrate Kisses” is, after all, an experimental movie about lesbian repression dating back to the early 20th century. Is it also that autofiction and individualism, now a dominant mode of contemporary artistic expression, were also marginalized at that point within her particular corner of the art world?

“She was both an experimental filmmaker and avant-garde artist and a lesbian filmmaker. And she says, and this was something she said all throughout her life and career, that she didn’t fit neatly into either category where she could just build an audience within that space,” O’Connor said. “She really was uncompromising about being both and working at the intersection of both and having both audiences… The experimental film world didn’t necessarily want to see lesbian work, didn’t necessarily want to see the nude woman’s body on screen. And lesbians, there was not so much representation, especially in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, increasingly so, but her work was experimental and thought-provoking, and she felt like a lot of her queer audiences wanted more realistic depictions of queerness.”

O’Connor, who received a 2026 Creative Capital to not only finish her work on “Barbara Forever” but also continue making docs, said, “The industry is hard, but that certainly won’t stop me from making nonfiction films. I’m just excited to pivot to my next project.”

“Barbara Forever” is now available to stream on PVOD platforms.

#3489. Controversial GTA 6 Easter Egg Will Annoy Millions of Gamers

A physical game joins NFT jokes as relics of the past included in GTA 6

Grand Theft Auto 6 is now out everywhere, and players are discovering just how much this game is filled to the brim with an overwhelming amount of things to do. In the game’s opening hours, you’ll land a place on the water, steal a car from a police impound, get into a car chase, and more. There are a million little things to do, like playing video games inside GTA 6 itself.

Early in the game, Cal, a friend of co-protagonist Jason, spends an afternoon gaming with his buddy. Ironically, he does something that IRL players can’t do with GTA 6 itself: bring a physical game disc with him.

As GTA 6’s nearly 20 million players (at the time of this writing) know, GTA 6 is digital-only. “Physical” copies simply contain a digital download code in a box. As such, you can’t bring your copy of GTA 6 to a friend’s house to show them the game like you could with previous GTA games, or like how Cal introduces Jason to Tenebrae Lux, a very artsy game that spoofs Jonathan Blow’s The Witness. (Jason’s not impressed; he’d rather go kill zombies.)

The two then have a party-filled night together that ends with them drunkenly fighting over who gets to sleep in the bed, which then cuts to the both of them sharing the bed in their undies. It’s a surprisingly wholesome sequence that includes Jason opening up about the strains in his relationship with Lucia on the eve of her getting released from prison. The moments of genuine friendship between Cal and Jason contrast well to the rest of GTA 6, which is all about, ya know, stealing drugs from rednecks, evading death-by-gator, running away from cops, and all other kinds of wild shenanigans.

Trading games, bringing a game disc to a hang sesh with the boys, introducing a new game to a friend by popping your copy into their console — for years, sharing games was easy because they were all on discs or other physical formats. When I reviewed the Gears of War remaster last year (with a digital copy), it reminded me how I first played the original game by trading my copy of Assassin’s Creed with a friend for his copy of Gears. Fast-forward to this year, and I’m playing Pokémon Pokopia by borrowing my partner’s copy. (OK, maybe I stole it from her Switch 2 case, who can say.)

PlayStation once famously demonstrated how to share used games in a 2013 video intended as a dig toward the always-online Xbox One. That joke has aged like milk in the wake of Sony’s announcement that it will cease manufacturing physical discs for PlayStation games in January 2028. Sony’s news hit just a short time after Rockstar Games announced its own digital-only plans for GTA 6 back in June.

Sony’s move prompted a wave of angry commenters spamming every PlayStation promotional video and blog post with disdain ever since. Some PlayStation owners tried to wrangle together a “no disc, no buy” blackout campaign where they wouldn’t use PSN, make purchases at the PlayStation Store, or basically engage with their PlayStation console in any way. That blackout had no effect on Sony. In fact, Sony’s digital game sales have continued to grow since the announcement.

The outrage over the decline of physical games clearly hasn’t had an impact on Rockstar’s GTA 6 either. It broke preorder records, despite there being no real need to preorder a copy — they’re all digital, so Sony and Microsoft won’t be running out. This isn’t 2009, when you had to preorder a physical copy of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 to make sure you could pwn some newbz day one. (And snag a sleek poster in the process.)

Though we can’t say with certainty yet, it seems likely GTA 6 will end up as 2026’s top-selling game, in spite of the uproar around its lack of a disc version. Yet none of the eleventy billion people who buy it will be able to share it with their buds in the way that Cal shared a disc version of Tenebrae Lux with Jason.

Rockstar’s magnum opus searches for love and catharsis in desperate times — and finds them

#3486. The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Review: Fincher And Tarantino's Mean-Spirited Hollywood Sequel

There was a time in my life when a movie made by David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino would be the biggest cinematic event ever. Not to get all film bro on you, but Fincher and Tarantino were very important filmmakers to me in my youth. That's not to say they aren't still important to me now ... but the luster has faded a bit. Fincher has spent the last few years making movies specifically for Netflix, and while those films — "Mank" and "The Killer" — have their charms, they pale in comparison to his previous work, so much so that I'd say the last great movie was "Gone Girl" in 2014 (for what it's worth, Fincher's exclusivity with Netflix is now over).

As for Tarantino, while he tends to make everyone's eyes roll when he gives a new hot take-laden interview, I still think he has the juice. However, the "Pulp Fiction" auteur has decided that he will only direct 10 movies and then hang up his filmmaking spurs. Because of this, Tarantino seems hesitant to direct a movie again, since that hypothetical movie would be his last. He came close to making "The Movie Critic" only to drop the idea entirely, and now he's working on directing his first stage play, "The Popinjay Cavalier."

But his previous film, "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," might just be his best. It's certainly near and dear to my heart, as I find it inherently rewatchable. It's a funny, sad, surprisingly sweet hang-out movie that doubles as a slice of alternate Hollywood history. Tarantino has now returned to the world of "Hollywood" with his new script, but again, since he doesn't want to direct his tenth and final movie just yet, he's handed the project over to Fincher.

All of this is a long-winded way of saying that everything about "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" should, in theory, appeal to me, a movie nerd who still considers Fincher and Tarantino to be among the greats. But Fincher's not-so-stellar Netflix output coupled with Tarantino's weird insistence on not directing the movie himself muted my enthusiasm a bit, as have some lackluster trailers. On top of all that, Fincher and Tarantino have vastly different movie making styles. Would a union between the pair even work? I'm pleased to say the answer is "Yes." Sort of. While I was cautious about "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," it eventually won me over. But it's not quite the movie I think anyone is expecting, and that's going to catch a few folks off guard.

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" introduced us to washed-up actor Rick Dalton, played by Leonardo DiCaprio, and his trusty stunt man sidekick Cliff Booth, played by Brad Pitt. Pitt turned in a funny, scene-stealing performance that landed him an Oscar, but Cliff seemed destined to be a supporting player in Rick's life. "Cliff Booth" turns him into a leading man, and I'm not entirely sure that's a good idea. Because without Rick Dalton by his side, what is Cliff Booth? I think the case can be made that Cliff Booth is a very charming psychopath. He's certainly not against brutally murdering people, and while he's highly capable and smooth as silk, there doesn't seem to be a whole lot going on in Cliff Booth's head. Rick and his internal struggles were part of what gave "Hollywood" its heart. Without him around, "Cliff Booth" ends up frequently feeling cold and cruel.

Pitt's Cliff became so lovable and likable in the first movie that I can't help but think Tarantino, always one to subvert expectations, is deliberately hammering home the point that for all his charms, Cliff is not exactly a good guy. He's a cypher; an idealized version of machismo — a men's pulp magazine hero brought to life. He lives fast and hard, likes drugs and booze, constantly risks life and limb, flirts with every woman he encounters, can kick everyone's butt, and still finds time to chill out and watch TV with his dear old dad. And yes, he occasionally murders people. Is "Cliff Booth" an attempt by Tarantino, or maybe Fincher, to remind us that this guy isn't nearly as cool as he seems?

In "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," it's 1977, and Cliff's movie stunt days seem to behind him, especially since Rick Dalton has moved to Australia, where he's currently starring on a popular Aussie TV show. Cliff keeps busy, though, working an assortment of odd jobs. He runs the projector at the New Beverly Cinema, he works as a bartender making all sorts of elaborate margaritas, he participates in a demolition derby, and he even occasionally appears in an X-rated movie or two.

On the side, however, Cliff also works as a fixer for some of his old Hollywood friends. If they get into a jam that they can't go to the cops about, Cliff is willing to step in and work something out — for a price. And sometimes that results in a body count.

Cliff has become a legend due to his fight with Bruce Lee and the time he killed those damn hippies who broke into Rick's home (it's also worth noting that in "Hollywood," people suspected Cliff of murdering his wife, although that incident isn't mentioned here). At the end of the day, Cliff comes home to the apartment he shares with his dad Gus (Peter Weller) to watch old movies and TV. Weller's Gus is the warmest part of this surprisingly cold movie, and the banter between Cliff and his father is laid-back and believable in a way that made me wish the entire movie was just the two of them shooting the breeze.

"Cliff Booth" is in no hurry, but eventually a shaggy Hollywood crime thriller plot emerges. The logistics of what's going on are hilariously convoluted, but Cliff is hired by manic actor Charlie Peters (Scott Caan, looking eerily like his late father in nearly every frame) to help get him out of some trouble. Cliff doesn't exactly like Charlie, but he does like Charlie's wife Toni (Carla Gugino), whom he had a love affair with over a decade ago. And Cliff really likes Charlie's agent, amazonian goddess Karen Crosby, played Elizabeth Debicki.

The flirty relationship between Cliff and Karen is meant to be sweet and romantic, but while Pitt and Debicki are both quite good in their respective roles (Debicki is particularly funny, bugging her eyes out at all the ludicrous things that happen), they don't have much chemistry. There's the glimmer of something interesting in how Cliff reveals he's a masochist who gets off on the idea of Karen slapping him around, but this angle is ultimately treated as little more than a throwaway gag.

While "Cliff Booth" has the same hang-out movie vibes as "Hollywood," there are bursts of brutal violence that left me uncomfortable. Tarantino is no stranger to violence, and the big finale of "Hollywood" is drenched in blood. But here is where the styles of Fincher and Tarantino seem to clash the most. Tarantino's violence is almost always hyper-stylized and over-the-top. Influenced by countless splatter flicks and kung-fu movies, Tarantino shoots his violence in ways that are so ludicrously graphic that they become funny in a twisted sort of way.

Fincher, however, has a more realistic approach, which results in a handful of brutal scenes — most notably when the film's villains, a pair of gangsters from the Philippines (played by Matt Groove and JB Tadena) butcher an entire family during a home invasion. This moment has no bearing on Cliff's story, and seems to only exist to show us how bad these bad guys are. Which is fine, in theory, but Fincher stages it in such a cruel, unpleasant way that when he tries to lighten the mood in the following scenes, it rings hollow.

There's a conversation worth having here about movie violence, I suppose. Which is the more questionable approach: depicting these moments in an unrealistic over-the-top fashion, or making them as real (and therefore upsetting) as possible? Again, I can't help but think that Tarantino is intentionally trying to flip the script and deliver something harsher after the good vibes of "Hollywood." The '60s are over, and here we're at the tail-end of the '70s, nearing the '80s. It makes sense for the vibes to be drastically different. But intentional or not, this contrast between Fincher and Tarantino makes "Cliff Booth" more mean-spirited than expected.

Midway through the film, Tarantino's script gives Karen a meaty monologue about movies. Before becoming an agent, Karen was a budding film critic, and in her professional opinion, movies should entertain above all else. While she thinks movies can be artistic, she doesn't think of them as art. It's 1977, and the movie everyone is talking about is "Star Wars," which Karen thinks proves her point: audiences don't want a fancy cinematic meal, they want movie fast food. Even "The Godfather" is little more than pulp in her estimation.

I don't think a lifelong movie nerd like Tarantino actually believes this (and I don't think Fincher does, either), but this little speech must be here for a reason. Are we meant to just sit back and enjoy the ride of "Cliff Booth" and not think too much about what's unfolding here? Or is the film itself trying to prove Karen's theory wrong? For all it's moments of comedy, there's a cold darkness lurking beneath "Cliff Booth" that keeps it from being fully entertaining. It's as if Fincher and Tarantino don't quite have a grasp on the material.

Regardless, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is Fincher's best movie in years — since "Gone Girl," really. While I do think he and Tarantino don't quite mix as well as we'd all hoped, the material has energized the filmmaker to craft a great-looking movie with several standout set pieces (I particularly liked a montage, told entirely via press photographs, showing Karen attending the premiere of "Looking for Mr. Goodbar").

Still, I can't help but wish Tarantino had just gone ahead and directed this himself. If he had, I think the tonal clashes might've been smoothed out considerably. "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" felt like something of a masterpiece to me when I first saw it, and the film's hefty runtime was a blessing rather than a curse — I wanted to spend as much time in this world with these characters as possible.

But that world is nowhere to be found in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Tarantino clearly didn't want to tread the same ground all over again when he banged out this script, and there's nothing wrong with that. But if everything is so different this time around, why would we want to check back in with Cliff at all, then? Especially without Rick by his side? "Cliff Booth" builds towards a memorable, brutal, action-packed climax before just sort of giving up and rolling credits. It's as if, in the end, everyone involved realized that old "Hollywood" magic was finally gone.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" will be released exclusively in IMAX on November 25, 2026 for a two-week engagement before streaming on Netflix December 23, 2026.

#3485. Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel

This year’s TIFF and Venice were quieter in terms of breakout sales, especially when compared to last year’s splash for “Obsession,” and several awards contenders were scooped up before they even premiered at the festival. But other smaller buyers have emerged in recent weeks to release some of the more critically acclaimed titles that didn’t land major sales ahead of time.

The festivals are long done, but we’re still tracking every sale that happens, so check back frequently.

Distributor: MagnoliaDirector: Kris ReyFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: Not unlike Jordan Firstman going from comedian to unexpected leading man and festival circuit darling, Caleb Hearon earned some praise for his leading man turn in “Trash Mountain,” a dark comedy he wrote and starred in along with Zooey Deschanel that grapples with grief and growing up. Kris Rey directed the film that premiered at TIFF and was produced by “Jurassic World” filmmaker Colin Trevorrow. The film also stars Jacki Weaver, Jaboukie Young-White, and Kyle Marvin and was co-written by Ruby Castor. Curiously, Lilly Wachowski was at one point attached to direct the film before Rey came aboard. Magnolia now is planning a theatrical release in 2027. Related Stories ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ Comes to VHS in Special Pan-and-Scan Edition from Mutant ‘Epic Zombie Christmas,’ Family Comedy About Senior Citizens and Teenagers Making a Horror Film, Begins Production

Distributor: Kino LorberDirector: Maiken BairdFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: This documentary about Palestinian-American author and intellectual Edward Said earned strong reaction in its premiere at TIFF and festivals like NYFF and IDFA, in part because though he’s been dead for over 20 years, his writing and his views have been far more relevant in a post-October 7 landscape. IndieWire’s review out of TIFF praised the construction of the documentary and how it manages to be decades-spanning and comprehensive in a manageable running time. And Anne Thompson spoke with the filmmakers about the challenges of making the documentary and the fear that it being about Palestine would pose barriers to a distributor stepping up to buy it. Thankfully, Kino Lorber did just that, and it will be planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

Distributor: Black BearDirector: Nahnatchka KhanFestival: TIFF MarketBuzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Distributor: 1-2 SpecialDirector: Jacqueline LentzouFestival: Venice OrizzontiBuzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Sony PicturesDirector: Roshan SethiFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic MonsterDirector: Joshua GiulianoFestival: TIFF Midnight MadnessBuzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

Distributor: HBO Documentary FilmsDirector: Rebecca HunttFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

Distributor: Roadside Attractions and VerticalDirector: Lauren Miller RogenFestival: TIFF Gala PresentationBuzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

Distributor: Focus FeaturesDirector: Simon StoneFestival: Telluride and TIFFBuzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

Distributor: NetflixDirector: Danny BoyleFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.

#3484. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Ending Explained: How Haymitch Wins The Hunger Games & What Happens To His Family

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.The newest addition to Suzanne Collin's nearly 20-year-old, smash-hit Hunger Games franchise, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, has finally arrived in theaters, and while any Hunger Games movie is going to leave audiences devastated, this ending truly packs a punch. The new movie, like the novel, centers on Haymitch Abernathy, the mentor of Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark from the original Hunger Games trilogy, and that automatically meant that audiences would know Haymitch made it out of the arena alive. However, his path to victory was far from straightforward.

After all, Haymitch didn't just fight in any Games; he fought during the 50th anniversary year, what is called the Second Quarter Quell, which saw double the number of tributes—two boys and two girls from each district, totaling 48 children. With that alone, the bloodshed for Sunrise on the Reaping was going to be significantly higher, as were the tragedies and the deaths. Sadly, for Haymitch, the horrors didn't stop there, as cruelty followed him all the way home, back to District 12.

Hunger Games fans who read the book may feel that they already know how this story ends, and while reviews of Sunrise on the Reaping have already made it clear that the story, in many ways, remains loyal to the book, not everything about this ending—from character deaths to how Haymitch responds to these many losses and more—remains exactly the same. Here's everything you need to know about how the brand-new movie, Sunrise on the Reaping, ends.

Initially, like Katniss, Haymitch is an unlikely hero and relatively resistant to the idea of truly becoming a rebel against the Capitol; he doesn't see himself that way, it seems, even as he clearly hates everything that the Capitol stands for and what they do to the people of Panem living in the districts and forced to fight in the Games. However, especially after connecting with Beetee and formulating a plan, Haymitch agrees to use his time in the arena as a way to, hopefully, ruin the Games—even if it means his death, which he assumes is certain.

In the end, though, Haymitch doesn't die. Rather, he becomes the last man standing, almost accidentally. Like in the books, in the movie, Haymitch is determined to bring an end to the Hunger Games, or at the very least show President Snow that the districts are no longer willing to play his games. However, the numbers of the remaining districts dwindle, ultimately leaving just a few tributes fighting to the death. That includes, towards the end, Haymitch, Maysilee Donner, Wellie (one of the Newcomers and therefore an ally to Haymitch), and the lingering career named Silka.

Similar to the book, Maysilee is devastatingly attacked by vicious birds, eventually dying as a result of their assault on her. Likewise, despite Haymitch hoping for Wellie's survival and even, potentially, victory, Wellie is ultimately killed by Silka. Notably, there is a change from the book, as in the novel, Silka gruesomely cuts off Wellie's head, whereas in the movie she kills her without thrat horrific decaptiation.

In the end, though, it's Haymitch against Silka, and while certain details are different, such as where Silka is struck by the hammer, her fate is the same. Ultimately, Haymitch uses the force field built into the arena to his advantage, watching as Silka sends her axe flying, only for the axe to rebound from the force field, striking and killing Silka. This leaves Haymitch as the winner, although he still tries, in the end, to destroy the arena rather than survive. Sadly, for Haymitch, his plans are foiled, and he becomes the victor.

Although Haymitch is the victor of the 50th annual Hunger Games, his troubles are far from over once he leaves the arena. On the contrary, President Snow ultimately decides to punish Haymitch in the most horrific ways following his win in the arena. Once Haymitch returns home in the movie, he is immediately greeted by the caskets of his four former allies and other District 12 tributes, Maysilee, Louella, and Wyatt. That's very far from the worst thing that Haymitch witnesses after his return home, though.

First, Haymitch loses his only surviving relatives, both his Ma and his little brother, Sid, in a house fire. Very obviously, though, this house fire isn't an actual accident. Rather, Snow has orchestrated this house fire, determined to to kill both Sid and Haymitch's Ma as a form of cruel punishment for his rebellious behavior. Still, though, the cruelty is not over, as Snow is also dead set on killing the only person remaining who Haymitch cares about: his girlfriend, Lenore Dove.

A Covey, just like Snow's former love interest Lucy Gray, Lenore Dove is Haymitch's last remaining loved one. Brutally, Snow sets up a horrifying scenario, in which Haymitch unwittingly feeds Lenore Dove poisoned gumdrops. Try as he might, once he realizes they are poisoned, Haymitch is unable to save Lenore Dove, and she dies right in front of him, leaving him well and truly alone.

Amidst all the devastation is the return of fan-favorite characters Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark, who appear in the epilogue of the movie, set not only after the events of Sunrise on the Reaping but also after the events of the original Hunger Games books/movies. In this scene, Katniss and Peeta are clearly established as Haymitch's true family in his older age, and while there is very little in terms of the story at this point in the movie, seeing them is enough.

Based on what is shown, Peeta, Katniss, and Haymitch have finally found true peace, living out their days in District 12 without fear of the Hunger Games, the Capitol, or war. It's a heartwarming conclusion, and however brief, it really is nice to see Katniss and Peeta again and get confirmation that, long after the books and movies, this trio remains a happy, finally safe family.

As mentioned, the epilogue of Sunrise on the Reaping is set many years after the original Hunger Games movies and books. It's not clear precisely how long afterwards this epilogue takes place, nor is it all that important. What's really being shown here is simply that Katniss, Peeta, and Haymitch do eventually find some well-deserved peace. In terms of the story prior to the epilogue, though, the story is set more than two decades before the original Hunger Games book/movie.

Specifically, Sunrise on the Reaping takes place during the Second Quarter Quell, 24 years before Katniss's first Hunger Games. However, the end of the movie does showcase several skips in time, depicting Haymitch witnessing reapings and then returning home with caskets again and again. It's a compelling, meaningful sequence, but in addition to it demonstrating the suffering that Haymitch continued to experience for years, it does show a small passage of time within the movie.

Understandably, the question on many fans' minds is whether Sunrise on the Reaping will truly be the end for Hunger Games movies and books. It was honestly shocking that Collins eventually continued beyond The Mockingjay, but with both Sunrise on the Reaping and The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes coming out, it seems like Collins is open to additional stories. Even so, it seems safe to assume that Sunrise on the Reaping is the true end. Never say never, but for one, all previously written books (and therefore movies) focus on the District 12 victors.

With Haymitch, those stories have come to an end. What's more, the conclusion of Sunrise on the Reaping is geared towards establishing that the Hunger Games are now truly over. It would be more than a little surprising if Collins now decided to revisit other stories. Granted, there are those who want Finnick's story or a story set before the Hunger Games began, and that's not off the table, certainly, but for now, it seems most likely that Sunrise on the Reaping is the true end of this fan-favorite franchise.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3483. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Soundbars From Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3482. 10 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics About Cavemen and Their Early Innovations

Gary Larson’s comic strip The Far Side broke the mold of traditional newspaper comics by not having a recurring cast of characters. Peanuts had Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Linus and the rest of the gang. Garfield had Garfield, Odie, Jon, and some others. Calvin and Hobbes had Calvin, Hobbes, and Calvin’s parents. But The Far Side introduced new characters and scenarios every single day.

However, there were several different types of characters Larson returned to again and again, like cows, dinosaurs, scientists, and others. One of the most comedically lucrative subjects Larson brought back repeatedly were cavemen, who he often portrayed as prehistoric idiots tangling with dinosaurs and other primitive beasts. Larson returned to cavemen so often that he had a variety of different running jokes reserved just for them. Many of his cavemen comics were about the discovery of fire, while he also had a whole series of others about the invention of the wheel. My personal favorite Far Side cavemen gags, though, were the ones which depicted them with early inventions and innovations, like the first game of checkers or the earliest means of transportation. The joke for these was always that they were stupid and wouldn’t work, but they just never stopped being funny.

Here are the 10 best Far Side cavemen comics featuring early inventions.

First up is this utterly useless invention, the Swiss Army Rock, which I’m sure predates Switzerland by thousands of years. The Swiss Army knife, of course, is a handy multitool with a bunch of great, useful stuff inside. What about a small rock containing three other, smaller rocks? Totally pointless — and priceless.

This is one of those Far Side comics that is so brilliant on its own that it requires no caption to explain the joke. The idea that the first symphony was a single note is so stupid and funny, especially since the cavemen have fairly modern-looking instruments to play the music.

Gary Larson’s depiction of early peer pressure feels like an insane twist on the D.A.R.E. messaging from the 1980s and 1990s. Will that innocent caveman be able to stand up against the influences of his ne’er-do-well peers? Honestly, this needs more than a single panel. We need an entire after-school special about this.

I love the idea that checkers developed from a game which merely had two squares. Larson was so brilliant at taking everything down to its most absurd conclusion and this is a great example of that.

This is another great example of Larson’s absurdist humor. Does it make any sense that the first microscopes would be gigantic? Not really, but it sure is a funny visual.

My favorite detail in this comic strip is just how long the trail is behind the cavemen. Not only is that one caveman’s head in the dirt, but he's been pushed for miles at this point.

Necessity is the mother of invention, and this comic strip plays with the idea that the caveman built a car first, then invented the wheel to go with it. It’s one of those Far Side comics that is both remarkably dumb and remarkably smart all at once.

This comic strip was published more than three years after the previous one, but it sure feels like they go together. Gary Larson did a whole lot of wheel-oriented caveman jokes and this is maybe the best. Just imagine what happens to the caveman riding the wheel once it begins going downhill. It will obviously be very unpleasant (if it doesn't immediately kill him).

Even millions of years ago, plumbers were exactly the same as they are today. I do wonder what he’s going to use that wrench for.

The all-time funniest caveman gag about early inventions has got to be the one with the caption “Early piñatas.” With a stick and a blindfold, piñatas are already a pretty dangerous activity, but fill the piñata full of rocks and they make for a disaster, especially if you win.

#3480. Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media Hires Former Netflix Exec Tendo Nagenda as President

Tendo Nagenda, a former executive on Netflix’s film team, has been tapped as president of Proximity Media, the production company founded by Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler, and Sev Ohanian, the founders announced Thursday.

Nagenda spent four years at Netflix under film chief Scott Stuber, exiting in 2022, and in that time he shepherded films like Spike Lee’s “Da 5 Bloods,” “The Old Guard,” “Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom,” “The Harder They Fall,” and “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery.”

Nagenda will oversee all aspects of creative development and production at Proximity, including its film, TV, and non-fiction divisions, and will report directly to the founders. The heads of Film, Television and Nonfiction will all report directly to Nagenda, and he’ll work alongside marketing and operations lead Terra Potts and music lead Ludwig Göransson. He starts on November 30. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition

“Tendo has spent his career working alongside talented filmmakers, championing original ideas, and helping make projects that resonate with audiences around the world,” said Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler and Ohanian in a joint statement. “As Proximity continues to grow across film, television, and nonfiction, we’re excited to have his creative instincts and experience helping guide this next chapter. He shares our belief in the power of storytelling to connect people, challenge perspectives and create meaningful impact, and we’re thrilled to welcome him to the team.”

“I’m honored and excited to join Ryan, Zinzi, Sev, and the entire Proximity team,” said Nagenda. “Their commitment to ambitious, meaningful storytelling reflects everything I’ve always believed in, and I look forward to building on what they’ve created, collaborating with extraordinary filmmakers and creators, and bringing compelling new stories to audiences around the world.”

Since leaving Netflix in 2022, Nagenda launched 10 by Ten Entertainment, which produced and released Jeymes Samuel’s “The Book of Clarence” in 2024. Prior to working at Netflix, he had a long track record at Disney and oversaw films on the live-action slate, including “Beauty and the Beast,” “Cinderella,” “Saving Mr. Banks,” “Mulan,” “A Wrinkle in Time,” and “Queen of Katwe.”

Proximity Media had a banner year last year with the release of “Sinners,” which grossed $365 million worldwide. Some of its other features have included “Judas and the Black Messiah,” “Space Jam: A New Legacy,” and “Creed III.” It’s now working on a reboot of “The X-Files” for Hulu starring Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel. Proximity recently entered into a multiyear TV deal with Netflix for scripted and unscripted projects. And it also has produced some nonfiction work including Nat Geo’s hit “Hurricane Katrina: Race Against Time,” as well as other titles like “Stephen Curry: Underrated,” “Homeroom,” and “Anthem.”

Nagenda is a graduate of Claremont McKenna College and a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and Producers United. He also serves on the Social Services Committee of the Motion Picture & Television Fund and the board of the UCLA Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

#3479. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3478. Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’

Director Brian Duffield is a cinephile who watches a lot of movies, but when the time came to direct his adventure film “Whalefall” he was dismayed to realize he couldn’t think of a single film he could look to as a model. “It was a nightmare for that reason,” Duffield told IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “It also the joy of it, having a room full of amazingly gifted artists all starting from this place of real befuddlement.”

In the movie, Austin Abrams plays a scuba diver who gets swallowed by a sperm whale and has only an hour of oxygen to keep him alive while he tries to escape; it’s a premise that posed multiple challenges for Duffield and his team, starting with the question of how exactly to build the stomach that Abrams would be trapped inside for the majority of the film — and how to shoot those scenes. Related Stories Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media Hires Former Netflix Exec Tendo Nagenda as President Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel

“It wasn’t normal coverage,” Duffield said. “Even a shot of Austin just sitting in the stomach required months of preparation and planning — every shot of him in the stomach is, by its nature, a stunt.” The ultimate effect onscreen is terrifying, but on set Duffield says the stomach scenes looked more than a little ridiculous. “The set looked crazy.  From the outside it’s this black weird bag, and then it’s on a gimbal so it’s moving, and it’s full of water.”

To give the impression of the stomach chewing, Duffield’s crew found an old-school, practical solution. “When the stomach chews, it compresses,” Duffield said. “The way we did that is we just had burly men jump onto it. Austin’s inside, and there’s a guy with a camera, and I can’t fit in the stomach so I’m just watching these New Zealanders leap and compress, then I’m hearing Austin scream.” Although Duffield planned his shots meticulously, he often found that the stomach had a mind of its own and required swift adaptation from the crew.

“There’s water in the stomach, and we would drain it every night,” Duffield said. “The material that the stomach was made of would change shape overnight, and we’d come back to resume a scene, and our set would be a different set — we’d fill it with water, and it would all lay different.” Doors also contracted due to humidity and other conditions. “By the end of the shoot, there were so many jagged doors that we’d cut for cameras.”

Ultimately, all of Duffield’s storyboards “went out the window” because the stomach kept changing shape, and Abrams couldn’t roll in the planned directions. “The stomach was kind of directing the movie,” Duffield said. “Austin and I had to sync up and figure out how, with this new environment every day, to get the shots that tell the story as cleanly as possible.” That was no easy task, especially since the set’s very nature made it hard to acclimate the audience geographically.

“It sounds ridiculous, but we had so many conversations about trying to get an audience to see that ‘that sphincter leads to the throat,’ or ‘that sphincter leads to the second stomach,'” Duffield said, adding that he constantly had to think about how one shot would connect to another to let the audience know where Abrams was inside the whale. “Austin’s moving around the whole time, and the stomach goes in every direction. Bit by bit, shot by shot, every shot is its own unique challenge.”

Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron worked with Duffield and the camera team to come up with visual cues that could help the audience follow Abrams’ journey through the whale, but the task was further complicated by the fact that the audience was sharing his point of view — and for long portions of the story, Abrams’ character was supposed to be confused. “Austin’s character doesn’t have a lot of information about what is happening to him,” Duffield said. “You want the audience to have the same information as him, but not get so lost and confused that they’re out of the movie.”

Duffield knew that striking that balance would be tricky throughout production and editing. “It’s hard to have a character in a situation he doesn’t know anything about and then have an audience get invested,” Duffield said, adding that the usual test screening questions were useless here. “It’s the classic test screening thing: ‘Is there anything that’s confusing to you?'” Luckily, Duffield worked with master editor Pietro Scalia, who worked with the director to find the most straightforward way to connect the audience to the material.

“We eventually concluded, just focus on Austin,” Duffield said. “Austin is dynamite, and he’s carrying you, and the more you’re in lockstep with Austin, you’re going to be okay.” The key, Duffield felt, was to preserve the illusion of reality at every possible moment. “ When we were editing and sound designing, it was just like, ‘How do we keep trying to make it feel real?’ I’m a very pro-CG guy, but even if there’s some stitching from a stuntman or a digital double to Austin, Austin’s in every shot of the scene. I think some of the things that people think is a digital double are not a digital double — it’s Austin just getting yanked around and fighting for his life.”

Though Duffield is sure Abrams wouldn’t want to return for a sequel, he said his lead actor was as up for the physical demands of the role as the department heads were for the mental and logistical challenges — challenges unlike any they had ever faced. “Nothing any of us had done before applied to this project,” Duffield said, adding that nothing they learned would apply to future projects given the singular nature of “Whalefall.” “It was really challenging, but I was looking for that kind of filmmaking challenge. It was the hardest shoot I’ll probably ever have, but everyone was also giddy about it.”
