#3477. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3476. Spider-Man: Brand New Day's Cut Daredevil Crossover Revealed In Official Photo Ahead Of Re-Release

"Spider-Man: Brand New Day" broke box office records, cementing Spidey as a reliable draw at a time when most other superhero movies aren't bringing in the crowds like the used to. Now, Marvel Studios and Sony Pictures have decided to re-release the movie for the holiday season, complete with previously unseen footage that will reintroduce a cut Daredevil crossover. We just got a sneak peek at that same crossover via a picture posted to Claire Temple actor Rosario Dawson's Instagram.

Temple originally appeared in Netflix's "Daredevil" series before becoming a mainstay in that small-screen universe. The nurse not only tended to Charlie Cox's Daredevil but also his fellow Defenders: Krysten Ritter's Jessica Jones, Mike Colter's Luke Cage, and Finn Jones' Iron Fist. (Temple didn't appear in Jon Bernthal's "The Punisher" series.) Alas, the Netflix series were all canceled by early 2019. Since then, Cox's Matt Murdock has returned in the Disney+ show "Daredevil: Born Again," in addition to making a brief cameo in 2021's "Spider-Man: No Way Home."

Originally, "Brand New Day" also featured a crossover with the erstwhile Netflix "Daredevil" series. Sadly, a scene that featured Temple was removed from the final cut prior to its debut in July 2026. Now, however, that scene has been reinstated for the extended cut, awkwardly titled "Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day," which hits theaters on December 4, 2026.

Per The Hollywood Reporter, "Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day" features 10 minutes of extra footage, most of which remains a mystery. One thing we do know, however, is that Rosario Dawson's Claire Temple cameo has been reinstated.

The actor took to Instagram to post a photo from the scene in question, which shows Temple standing alongside Tom Holland's Spider-Man inside a hospital room. This clearly takes place at the end of the movie, following Spidey's tumultuous final showdown with Sadie Sink's Jean Grey. Beyond that, however, Dawson didn't reveal much about what happens in the footage. "So excited to enjoy this record-breaking movie on the big screen," she wrote in her caption."[...] with an extended cut of new scenes and surprises... Ahhhh!"

Dawson previously revealed how she felt about being cut from "Brand New Day," saying that she had a BTS post ready to go about her time on-set that she ultimately had to scrap. Clearly, the actor was disappointed, which isn't surprising considering "Brand New Day" absolutely ruled the box office. Still, as she said at the time (via Variety) "Because everybody's in it, it still means that my character is somewhere in that same universe, and I really love that. So, I hope I get to be Claire again." Now, with her footage being added back into the movie for the re-release, she has even more reason to be hopeful.

With Rosario Dawson's Claire Temple appearing in the "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" re-release, the question becomes whether she'll show up again as the Marvel Cinematic Universe enters its next phase. As of now, "Daredevil: Born Again" has been canceled at Disney+, which means the upcoming third season will be its last. Thus far, Claire Temple hasn't appeared in the revival series, but there have been a few oblique references to a friendly nurse. Whether she'll show up in "Born Again" Season 3 remains unclear, but it wouldn't be surprising if she did.

With the show having been axed, however, Temple's MCU future remains even more uncertain. Perhaps if we get a fifth Tom Holland Spidey outing, she might come back. But such a film is also yet to be confirmed. "Brand New Day" producer Amy Pascal has one rule for making another movie, which essentially amounts to focusing on one film at a time. Still, with "Brand New Day" becoming nothing short of a phenomenon, it seems almost certain Sony Pictures and Marvel Studios will want to get Holland back for another outing ASAP.

Indeed, "Brand New Day" has made $2.5 billion at the global box office, and the re-release will likely bring in a decent bit of extra profit. Hence, with "Born Again" ending after its next season, a "Brand New Day" sequel seems like the most likely venue for a Temple return. For now, though, we'll have to await further news.

#3474. 53 Years Later, The Greatest Closing Line In Sci-Fi History Is Still The Best Book Quote Of The 1970s

Redrick Schuhart's final words offer a remarkably simple wish

The canon of science-fiction literature is home to countless unforgettable endings, from 1984’s short but devastating retrospective ("He loved Big Brother") to The Three-Body Problem’s defiant reminder that humanity cannot be so easily wiped out. The best sci-fi endings don't offer comfortable closure. Instead, they reframe everything that came before. In their closing lines, great sci-fi novelists leave readers suspended in the aftermath, forced to stew in the terrifying logic of cold technology, the fragility of human nature, and the vast expanse of space.

Every once in a while, I come across a line that feels bigger than the book that birthed it. Of course, there are classics with years of literary study behind them that speak volumes on the nature of society, technology, or the world writ large. But few are quite as elegant or as profoundly humanistic as the final moments of Arkady and Boris Strugatsky’s Roadside Picnic. The 1972 novel offers a very different kind of sci-fi ending than its myriad predecessors and successors.

A grounded masterpiece of Soviet-era speculative fiction, Roadside Picnic explores a vision of first contact where humanity isn't a partner or an enemy, but an afterthought. The extraterrestrial life forms briefly touch down across six isolated sectors on Earth, linger without acknowledging human life, and vanish as abruptly as they arrived. What they abandon isn't a message or a technology transfer, but cosmic litter: lethal spatial anomalies, defying physics, filled with inexplicable artifacts. In the wake of their departure, these quarantine areas — called "Zones" — become dangerous frontiers where cold state science and desperate black-market "Stalkers" risk death just to sift through the trash of an alien passerby who didn't even notice us.

In its closing moments, the story shifts from a gritty sci-fi noir into a devastating existential tragedy. Redrick Schuhart, a Stalker who enters the Zone illegally to find and sell loot, reaches the legendary Golden Sphere (a wish-granting alien artifact), but only after knowingly sacrificing a naive young companion to clear a lethal anomaly. When Redrick finally sits before the Sphere, traumatized and hollowed out by a lifetime of violence, he suffers a complete psychological collapse. Realizing he is incapable of formulating a single selfless thought of his own, he falls to the ground in tears and simply echoes the dead boy's final words back to the machine.

“Happiness for everybody, free, and no one will go away unsatisfied!”

That desperate act of surrender delivers one of speculative fiction's most haunting final lines. Antonina W. Bouis’ 1977 translation renders it with a focus on transactional satisfaction, but a 2012 translation by Olena Bormashenko restores the original Russian text’s all-caps formatting to convey an internal, soul-tearing scream: “HAPPINESS, FREE, FOR EVERYONE, AND LET NO ONE BE FORGOTTEN!”

The differences between the two translations reveal distinct emotional shades of Redrick's breakdown. Bouis’ choice of "unsatisfied" leans into the black-market pragmatism fitting for a character who spent his life dealing in illicit contraband. Bormashenko’s rendering ("let no one be forgotten") stays closer to the literal root of the Russian word “obizhennym” — meaning to be wronged, slighted, or left out in the cold. Whether framed as a tired plea or a frantic shout, both versions converge on the same tragic core: a broken man using a godlike power to beg for the basic human grace he was never able to afford.

The ending resonates because Roadside Picnic has spent every prior page rendering genuine happiness unthinkable. Redrick does not stand before the Golden Sphere as an enlightened hero. He’s presented more as an exhausted, morally compromised thief at wit’s end. After spending years exploiting the Zone in a world driven by mutual self-interest, he finally confronts a force capable of giving him anything he could possibly imagine. Yet the words that remain are not born of greed, vengeance, or self-preservation. They’re meant for everyone.

This radical turn toward universal grace is especially striking when set against the world Arkady and Boris Strugatsky inhabited. Written at the height of the Cold War, Roadside Picnic emerged from a Soviet Union locked in fierce ideological division, an era when the future felt less like a promise than an existential threat. Such an atmosphere of suspicion and control defined the novel’s fraught publication history. First serialized in the Soviet magazine Avrora in 1972, the text spent years fighting through state censors, meaning the 1977 English translation was bound to a heavily altered Soviet edition. It wasn't until Olena Bormashenko’s 2012 translation that Western readers were finally given the text as the authors originally intended.

Yet for all the battles fought over the manuscript’s moral framing, the Strugatskys refused to offer either state censors or readers an easy catharsis. Nor does Redrick’s desperate plea make the conclusion comfortably optimistic. The novel offers no proof that the alien Sphere actually works, or that it even possesses the capacity to care; the Zone remains as cold and unknowable as ever. What matters is that, in his final shattered moment, Redrick reaches for an idea far larger than his own wretched circumstances.

Refusing to soften the story is precisely what gives the wish its weight. Roadside Picnic is utterly devoid of sentimentality — the aliens never acknowledge us, the Zone remains a cold wasteland, and Redrick reaches the Sphere only by stepping over the body of a boy he sacrificed. His prayer does not erase a lifetime of exploitation; if anything, it throws all that human ugliness into stark relief. Where other sci-fi giants reach for the grandly cosmic, from Arthur C. Clarke transcending physical existence to William Gibson leaving digital ghosts in the matrix, the Strugatskys close their story with something smaller and infinitely harder: a man who has known only brutal self-preservation finally wishing that no one else has to live in the same conditions.

Viewed through this lens, the subtle divergence between translations only deepens the moment's emotional resonance. Whether rendered as "no one will go away unsatisfied" or "let no one be forgotten," both versions circle the same impossible mandate that no single human life is disposable, and no one should be asked to sit in the cold so another can thrive. For a novel about humanity picking through the cosmic trash of an indifferent universe, it is a staggering final note. More than half a century later, Redrick’s desperate, stolen prayer remains one of the greatest closing sentiments science fiction has ever given us.

#3473. GTA 6: Should You Choose Saved Cash Or Say Nothing In "Buck Me"

"Buck Me" is one of the shortest missions in Grand Theft Auto 6, but unlike plenty of more robust ones, it does present Jason with an intimidating choice. With his financial future — and Lucia's — potentially on the line, making the right decision can seem like an objective of the utmost importance.

GTA 6 doesn't offer much time to choose, as the prompt to select between saying nothing or mentioning Jason's saved cash comes and goes on a quick timer. If you've paused the game in search of an answer, though, here's everything you need to know about the choice.

After Jason picks up Lucia from prison and spends his first night with her, he'll get a new mission to take care of the next day, courtesy of Donnie. "Clean Up After Donnie" will take Jason north to locate a missing package, and as he heads up that way, Lucia might go ahead and ask him to join her at the bank when it's convenient for him.

Finish Donnie's objective, as this will ultimately take Jason back in the direction of the bank anyway. After wrapping that up, head to the nearby bank, go inside, and talk to the teller. She'll direct Jason to the manager, and once those two begin to converse, Lucia will appear.

When speaking to the bank manager, it quickly becomes clear that Jason and Lucia aren't in a great position to set up a bank account or take out any loans. Jason does have one asset, however: his saved cash, which he keeps under a floorboard in his bedroom.

When asked about the potential to deposit money, the option to mention Jason's saved cash is on a timer. You can also actively choose to say nothing, but if you wait too long to mention the cash, Jason will do this by default.

Faced with the timed choice, you should choose Saved Cash. The first chapter of GTA 6 features plenty of opportunities to impress Lucia by giving Jason a responsible attitude, and this is one of them. Choosing Saved Cash will immediately boost their relationship, while choosing to say nothing will do the opposite.

You can check out a full profile of ScreenRant's guides for GTA 6 here.

Unfortunately, the relationship perk is the only active effect of this choice. Due to their credit scores, Jason and Lucia are ultimately unable to open a bank account at this time, even if the cash is mentioned. Regardless of which selection is made, they'll be pushed to use the BuckMe app, which Jason can deposit money into via ATMs and use for various payments. Money can also be transferred from the standard BuckMe account into a Family Savings profile, providing a more long-term savings goal.

If you do make the mistake of choosing to say nothing (or you simply run out of time), it's not the end of the world. Grand Theft Auto 6 features plenty of opportunities to improve the relationship between Jason and Lucia. This is a particularly easy one to take advantage of, but making up the deficit shouldn't be much of a challenge.

#3471. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping's Katniss And Peeta Scene Explained

This article contains discussions of addiction.

Don't go to the old reaping site with your buddies and reminisce if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Spoilers ahead!

We've known, for quite some time now, that Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson's Peeta Mellark would return in the highly anticipated big-screen prequel "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." If you've read the book, you know that they come back for an epilogue, and in late October 2026 — just about a month before the film's release — Lawrence opened up about the experience and confirmed that Woody Harrelson, who plays the older version of "Sunrise's" protagonist Haymitch Abernathy in the original Hunger Games films, is also part of the scene. So ... what happens?

There are some differences between the epilogue in the book and the film adaptation helmed by Francis Lawrence, but the gist is the same — and I'll return to those differences later on. After we see how Haymitch wins his games and how the Capitol punishes him for attempting to destroy the 50th Games arena — Haymitch attempts to blow up a water tank and essentially drown the machine, but safeguards stop his plan from going through, and his family and loved ones are killed upon his return to District 12 — we see Harrelson's Haymitch approach an ivy-covered structure that's the old site of the annual reaping that chose one boy and one girl to compete in the deadly Games. He's joined by Katniss and Peeta, who wish him a happy birthday; it's a major plot point in "Sunrise" that reaping day always falls on Haymitch's birthdays. They thank him for everything, and Haymitch says "Nevermore" before departing.

Putting the prequel "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" aside — because none of the characters I'm talking about were alive during that story — it makes complete sense for Katniss and Peeta to show up to close out Haymitch's standalone movie. The three are, for all intents and purposes during the original Hunger Games timeline, a package deal. We see, at the end of "Sunrise on the Reaping," that Haymitch arrives home in District 12 and sees the coffins of his fellow tributes, and we also see a montage of Joseph Zada's younger take on the character overseeing the delivery of coffins that are clearly tributes he was forced to mentor as a former victor.

By the time we get to the 74th Games, Haymitch is constantly drunk and imbibes to survive, telling his tributes his only advice is that they stay alive. When he and Katniss click, though, he starts to wonder if these tributes have what it takes ... and thanks to a plot conceived by him and Peeta that presents Katniss and Peeta as star-crossed lovers forced to compete, they get to jointly win the Games.

That next year, only previous victors can be reaped, and Katniss and Peeta go back in to fight, though Haymitch hatches a plan with other rebels to break them out of the arena. Though Peeta is kidnapped, tortured, and brainwashed by the Capitol, they eventually rescue him and take down the Capitol, ultimately returning to District 12 to live out the rest of their days together.

In "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," this ending for Haymitch, Katniss, and Peeta feels hopeful and optimistic. Suzanne Collins, the author of the franchise, takes a darker approach in the literary epilogues for both "Mockingjay" and "Sunrise on the Reaping." In "Mockingjay," Katniss notes that both she and Peeta have post-traumatic stress disorder and still suffer greatly, experiencing night terrors and other symptoms. In the book version of "Sunrise," Haymitch speaks directly to the reader about how he didn't even want to care about his two tributes initially because he felt too broken, but he was worn down. "I didn't want to let them in, her and Peeta, but the walls of a person's heart are not impregnable, not if they have ever known love," he muses before mourning his one true love, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak in the film), who was poisoned by Capitol forces when Haymitch initially returned to District 12 as a victor.

Beyond that, Haymitch is blunt about the way that chronic drinking has affected his body. "I'm not sure I'll be here in the old therebefore much longer. My liver's wrecked and I only dry out when the train's late," he says. "I drink differently these days, though, less to forget, more out of habit. When my time comes, it comes, but I've no idea when that will be." Still, Haymitch gets a relatively happy ending with Katniss and Peeta.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters.

#3470. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

#3469. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3468. Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons

When you hire a 20-year-old director to adapt his own viral YouTube series into a major Hollywood film, you’re not going to end up with a traditional movie. That’s part of what made Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” such a massive critical and commercial success for A24. Audiences were eager to embrace Parsons as a major new filmmaking voice — and his crew members were just as excited for the chance to work with him.

During IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “Backrooms” VFX Supervisor Edward Douglas broke down the unique workflow that he developed with Parsons during pre-production. He explained that Parsons was used to making his own effects in Blender, so the team started communicating with him using the popular VFX software. Related Stories Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’

“The first conversation I had with Kane Parsons was ‘How do you like to work?’ And we embraced his process,” Douglas said. “Because his way of communicating with the entire crew was first, through Blender. He built 100,000 square feet of sets in Blender and passed it off to the production designer. And it immediately crashed his computer. But that let us start breaking down everything.”

Despite costing less than $10 million, “Backrooms” contained a significant number of VFX shots. Douglas explained that the process became a unique mix of traditional effects work by seasoned pros and found-footage-style shots that Parsons did himself.

“It was an indie budget film, but it had over ten minutes of full CG,” Douglas said. “Some of it was traditional, and some of it was Backrooms found footage exploration. That ended up being a hybrid VFX process. We had very traditional sequences when we were working with VFX Blenders. And then we had more of our Kane Parsons DIY pipeline for scenes that he would really be touching himself. And we set it up so that Kane could actually log into the VFX Blender servers and tweak things, set up shots. Because that was his way. He could say, ‘Here are the notes,’ or Can I show you?’ And we’d want to create a way for him to show us. Because he is, at his heart, a VFX artist.”

#3467. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3466. The MCU’s Doctor Doom Setup Officially Makes More Sense Than The Infinity Saga’s Thanos Story

Marvel Studios has spent years teaching audiences to look at the Marvel Cinematic Universe's bigger picture, showing how "it's all connected" through various pieces of connective tissue between projects, key character appearances, and major post-credits scenes. This was best exemplified by the Infinity Saga and the years of build-up to Thanos and the Infinity Stones, starting from his first appearance at the end of 2012's Avengers to his full debut in 2018's Avengers: Infinity War.

That said, it can certainly be argued that the set-up for Doctor Doom leading up to Avengers: Doomsday has made a lot more sense compared to how the Mad Titan was gradually introduced in the MCU. Although Thanos was introduced and made small appearances six years before his full debut in Infinity War, it was actually pretty messy overall, with more than a few pivots for his character along the way.

Keeping that in mind, let's compare the MCU's set-up for Thanos in the MCU's Infinity Saga to the more recent pieces of set-up for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom ahead of Avengers: Doomsday, the beginning of the end for the current Multiverse Saga.

At the very beginning, Thanos the Mad Titan first appeared in the mid-credits scene of 2012's Avengers, revealed to be the cosmic benefactor behind Loki's Chitauri armies, and gave the God of Mischief the mind-controlling scepter (later revealed to be the Mind Stone).

Receiving just a brief close-up of Thanos' face, the Mad Titan turns and smiles when he hears reports of Loki's failure from his servant, who told his master that "to challenge the humans is to court death." At the time, this was clearly a tease referencing Thanos' attempts to court Lady Death in the comics, the living embodiment of death itself. However, no such romance was featured for the Mad Titan in Infinity War or Endgame.

Likewise, Thanos' first appearance looked very different compared to his full debut in Infinity War, and the same goes for his appearances in Guardians of the Galaxy and Avengers: Age of Ultron, as the Mad Titan had multiple visual design changes leading up to Infinity War. While technology improved over time, so did Marvel Studios' understanding of what they actually wanted their biggest villain to look and feel like in the MCU compared to the comics.

2014's Guardians of the Galaxy gave Thanos a speaking role with Josh Brolin's casting, remaining a distant benefactor supporting Ronan in the hopes of obtaining the Power Stone. However, both his characterization and appearance weren't quite there yet, with Thanos acting more like the two-dimensional cosmic conqueror seen on the page than the more somber, determined, and self-perceived savior of all existence as he's come to be depicted in Infinity War and Endgame.

The same goes for 2015's Avengers: Age of Ultron, which saw Thanos at the very end taking an empty Infinity Gauntlet and declaring, "Fine, I'll do it myself." While it was an exciting tease for a more direct role in the next Avengers movies, he still didn't have the final visual appearance seen in Infinity War. Likewise, taking the gauntlet made very little sense, with Infinity War confirming Thanos forced Eitri the dwarf to forge the gauntlet on Nidavellir, just before the movie's events.

Ultimately, it wasn't until Avengers: Infinity War itself that audiences received a true understanding of what Thanos actually looked like, as well as his true intentions for the Infinity Stones themselves. It had nothing to do with courting Death like in the comics, but instead a twisted philosophy about universal balance and saving half of all existence from annihilation.

Looking at all the MCU's Thanos build-up together, it's pretty easy to argue that Doctor Doom's setup in the MCU's Multiverse Saga has been much more straightforward by comparison (and there's a pretty big reason why).

The MCU's setup for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom has admittedly been compressed into a much shorter period due to various creative pivots behind the scenes for Avengers 5. However, the trade-off seems to be that the setup makes a lot more sense leading up to Avengers: Doomsday, with Doom now having the same number of appearances before his full MCU debut as Thanos himself.

Doctor Doom's first MCU appearance came in the mid-credits scene of 2025's Fantastic Four: First Steps, which jumped four years ahead to reveal the masked villain approaching Reed Richards and Sue Storm's powerful young son, Franklin.

Secondly, the Avengers: Endgame: Encore theatrical release added several new post-credits scenes to the fourth Avengers movie to better connect to Doomsday. This included a scene featuring Bruce Banner locked away in a secure facility following the events of Spider-Man: Brand New Day (where Banner lost control for the first time in years). However, Doom appears before Banner, telling him that he's come to collect him before triggering Banner's transformation into the Hulk and presumably taking him to another reality in the multiverse.

Additionally, Encore also featured a scene of Doctor Doom forging his mask, echoing Iron Man and Endgame's original audio at the end of the credits, clearly teasing some sort of multiversal connection between Victor von Doom and Tony Stark.

Last but not least, VisionQuest's finale featured a post-credits scene revisiting Wanda Maximoff's sacrifice and apparent death at Mount Wundagore, as seen in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. Now, it's been revealed that Doom revived Wanda, lifting the rubble and telling the Scarlet Witch to awaken before claiming that "her power would be his", effectively establishing a pattern between all three appearances with Doctor Doom collecting beings of great power, no doubt connected to his goals for the multiverse.

Doctor Doom has approached Franklin Richards, collected Bruce Banner's Hulk, and has revived the Scarlet Witch, most likely in an effort to claim all of their respective powers in some fashion. While Marvel Studios hasn't explained the full scope of his plan just yet ahead of Doomsday, the implication from trailers has been that he intends to "save" the multiverse no matter the cost, and he may even attempt to remake it in his own image given what we know about Doctor Doom's Secret Wars role in the comics.

At any rate, the actual storytelling in these Doom appearances before Avengers: Doomsday certainly feels more focused and intentional compared to Thanos' in the Infinity Saga, which is no doubt the result of Marvel's most rushed timetable. Nevertheless, the end product is still setup for a major MCU villain that's a lot more cohesive.

Avengers: Doomsday releases in theaters on December 18th from Marvel Studios.

Avengers: Doomsday is the fifth Avengers film and kicks off Phase 6 of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. A stacked cast of heroes both new and old to the MCU — including members of the X-Men — will face off against Victor von Doom, revealed at San Diego Comic-Con in 2024 to be played by a returning Robert Downey Jr.

#3465. Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation

Film is always a collaborative medium, but one of the special things about animation is that you can craft incredibly nuanced performances with people who never get to meet. Voice acting in animation is a discipline in its own right — as legends like Mel Blanc and Eric Bauza show — where actors impart a kind of electric energy that carries through into the art style of what they’re voicing. So is voice directing. And the secret to both is in providing foundations for animators to build something bigger.

“Wildwood” director Travis Knight did a lot of the directing of his voice cast in lockdown Zooms, and hodge-podge recording setups, where it can be hard to remember that you’re developing something that needs to spiritually connect to the animation, whether existing animatics already exist or not. There isn’t the same kind of immersiveness for actors that live-action sets, costumes, and the basic pleasure of getting to read lines against other actors all provide. They have to build it from scratch. Related Stories Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie

“It asks something very different of an actor, which is challenging because an actor can bring so much to performance before they even utter a word,” Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “So when you cast these things, it’s really interesting because sometimes the things we love about actors are not their voice; it’s everything else. So we will always listen, we’ll take clips from actors’ other films and their interviews, and we’ll put them against a design of a character.”

Hearing a voice against a design can be revelatory, Knight believes, because it can teach a director and an animation team about who a character really is, whether a performer is really going to work or not, even before they step into the booth. It’s also an important way to help sort the whole of an ensemble so that actors occupy different aural frequencies and accents, and don’t sound too similar. You want to really be able to feel the difference between Carey Mulligan’s powerfully sinister Alexandra and Angela Bassett’s regal General.

And then, once the voice cast is in the booth, it’s also on the director and the team to help each voice actor sketch out all the different permutations of emotion the animators will then use as inspiration, and as tools.

“You’ll get the scene 30, 40, 50 different ways,” Knight said. “It takes forever. But, in the end, if you can do it properly, it feels like these characters are living in the same scene at the same time. And then it comes down to the animator to try to figure out how they can match the beauty of the vocal performance with the physical performance.”

That’s the normal process for feature animation: finding compelling voices, matching them with a design that feels spiritually connected to that voice, covering the performance many different ways, and then assembling a template for animators to build off of. And it’s the director, really, who has to hold in their head the many ways that the disparate parts will all come together.

“An animator is an actor, but they’re just acting through their hands and through a puppet, and it’s two actors collaborating to create a complete performance. But oftentimes it happens across space, across time. And when it comes together in a harmonious way, it’s really beautiful because this thing seems like it’s completely alive,” Knight said.

But sometimes, voice actors’ performances do get to be alive together. That was a key creative choice that director Leah Nelson made for “Tangles” — it’s hard to argue with the logic of putting Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and Bryan Cranston all in a room together to act out an earnest family drama, even if there’s a bit of mic bleed.

“I’m so glad we [put them together]. And it wasn’t that hard. It took a little bit of scheduling Tetris to get it done, but it was so worthwhile,” Nelson told IndieWire. “Abbi does a ton of voice work, and often they’re alone and not even able to have someone to read against them. Sometimes they’re just doing the lines and sort of jumping around. And what I ultimately wanted was to have this really naturalistic dialogue.”

“Tangles” boasts naturalism when it comes to sound, from bespoke foley to overlapping banter that isn’t meant to be precisely understood but to convey the chaos of one’s own (infuriating, loving) family. So Nelson and her team embraced the ways actors can build on each other, and even on improv, in recording the dialogue.

“A lot of humor came out of giving them time to not only play with the dialogue but to play with each other. But also, those really intimate and difficult moments of the film, they could look in each other’s eyes and work through those moments. That was important to me, and it was important to them as well. So it was an experience we all went through together.”

The one downside of treating recording sessions more like the rehearsals for a play is the risk of wrecking takes. “We spent a lot of time at the table trying to hold [our reactions] in or like, ‘Don’t sneeze! Nobody move!’” Nelson joked. “But I didn’t want it to sound like there was so much suturing; the mastery of the dialogue editing to make it all sound naturalistic, so we also did a lot of work to make that happen. But what we had to work with felt very naturalistic to begin with.”

The ultimate example of naturalistic voice acting, however, might be on display in “Wildwood.” Knight’s own son was a newborn while the team was laying down track for the film, which made him the perfect actor for the role of kidnapped Baby Mac.

“I essentially chased him around the house with a digital recorder. Sometimes with my iPhone. I was just trying to coax things out of him, make him laugh and giggle and verbalize. And the thing about babies is that they’re constantly trying to make sense of the world,” Knight said. “They’re always babbling and trying to make shapes with their mouths. So we have a lot of that babbling in the movie, and it helped make it feel naturalistic.”

It speaks to the wide-ranging power of voice acting in animation: you can get to naturalism through a grounded collaboration between actors, an actor in complete isolation, or hitting “record” on an iPhone while you’re changing a diaper.

“Wildwood” is now in theaters. “Tangles” releases in theaters on January 15, 2027.

#3464. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3463. Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear

Bill Hader‘s first film as a director has found its distribution partner. Black Bear has acquired North American distribution rights to “They Know,” Hader’s upcoming psychological horror film that he co-stars in with Linda Cardellini. The growing distributor, which just released “Wicker” nationwide, acquired the rights from financier MRC in what was described as a competitive situation.

Per an official synopsis, “They Know” follows a divorced dad who becomes increasingly suspicious and paranoid that his ex-wife’s new mysterious partner is exerting a strange, unsettling influence on their children.

“Bill Hader is a singular talent both in front of and behind the camera, and he has delivered a film in ‘They Know’ unlike anything we’ve ever seen,” Black Bear president of production & operations Michael Heimler said in a statement. “’They Know’ is authentic, original, and bold filmmaking at the highest level, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with Bill and re-team with our great friends at MRC, who consistently deliver boundary-pushing films that help define their genre.” Related Stories Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons

Hader co-wrote “They Know” with Duffy Boudreau and produced alongside Bob Graf, with Alyssa Donovan co-producing.

Hader is a three-time Primetime Emmy winner for his work on “South Park” and “Barry.” He co-created the HBO comedy “Barry” with Alec Berg and began directing episodes in Season 2, gradually working his way up to directing the entirety of Season 4. He has long been open about his cinematic influences and his desire to transition into feature filmmaking after the show ended.

Hader recently shared some more details about directing his first feature while speaking at IndieWire’s Los Angeles Future of Filmmaking Summit. He explained that “They Know” emerged after he and longtime friend and writing partner Boudreau both went through divorces and discussed their biggest fears about ways the process could have gone awry.

“We’re both divorced. We were talking about how lucky we were that we were on, like, we had really good terms with our ex-wives, and we have kids with them,” Hader said. “We started talking about the worst case scenarios of, ‘Oh, my god, this person is going through this and this person is going through that.’ And then this idea came up.”

Black Bear has yet to announce a release date for “They Know.”

#3462. 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

#3461. 8 Most Suspenseful Thriller Movies of All Time, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

There’s no single definition of a great thriller. However, what most of them have in common is a sense of tension. Now, the way this tension is created can vary dramatically from film to film. Some thrillers build suspense through psychological mind games, while others rely on shocking twists that completely reframe the narrative in a single moment. A memorable thriller doesn’t just surprise the audience, though — it traps them, makes them question everything, and refuses to play by any rules.

When a film leaves the viewers desperate to know what happens next, that’s when it’s doing something right. Over the years, filmmakers have approached countless ways to build this tension, but only a few have truly mastered it. This is a list of eight such suspenseful thrillers that know exactly when to tighten the noose.

Anatomy of a Fall is an intense, entertaining take on the courtroom drama. The film, directed by Justine Triet, opens with a man being found dead outside his remote chalet in the French Alps. His wife, Sandra Voyter (Sandra Hüller), insists it was an accident or possibly suicide. However, as the investigation unfolds, small inconsistencies lead to the case escalating into a courtroom trial where every detail of the couple’s marriage is called into question. Their visually impaired son, Daniel (Milo Machado-Graner), is the only real witness to the events surrounding his father’s death, which complicates things even more. Anatomy of a Fall is structured like an intricate puzzle where every new piece of information complicates the situation.

However, the procedural format never takes away from the gravity of Sandra and her husband’s fractured relationship. Hüller delivers an extraordinary performance, and her character’s emotional ambiguity is what fuels the narrative. This results in a story that isn’t merely about solving a crime. Instead, Anatomy of a Fall dissects the fragile dynamics of marriage, resentment, and grief. By the time the trial concludes, the audience is left with a lingering sense of doubt. The film builds suspense through uncertainty instead of relying on traditional twists or grand reveals. This layered, human approach is what makes it such a compelling thriller.

David Fincher’s The Game is the perfect example of a well-executed thriller. The film stars Michael Douglas as a wealthy but emotionally detached investment banker, Nicholas Van Orton, living in San Francisco, who receives an unusual gift from his estranged brother Conrad (Sean Penn) on his 48th birthday. The gift in question is an invitation to participate in an elaborate entertainment experience, known as a “game,” run by a mysterious company called Consumer Recreation Services. At first, Nicholas assumes it’s just a harmless distraction. However, things take a turn when strange things start happening in his everyday life. As the game intensifies, Nicholas finds TV broadcasts speaking directly to him, people start following him, his business reputation is threatened, and his money starts vanishing.

The film then becomes a masterclass in paranoia and unpredictability, where the protagonist stops trusting anyone and is constantly questioning his reality. What’s genuinely heartbreaking is when he learns that his alliance with a waitress named Christine (Deborah Kara Unger) might also be a part of the game. However, this kind of shock is exactly why The Game is such an effective thriller. Fincher creates a destabilizing experience for both Nicholas and the audience, which makes every twist feel unsettling but plausible at the same time. This growing sense of tension makes the final reveal land with absolute perfection, solidifying The Game as one of the most suspenseful thrillers of all time.

No list of suspense thrillers would ever be complete without this Alfred Hitchcock masterpiece. Rear Window has to be one of the director’s most influential works and proves just why he was known as the “Master of Suspense.” The film follows photojournalist L.B. “Jeff” Jefferies (James Stewart), who is stuck in his Greenwich Village apartment with a broken leg after a dangerous assignment. To kill time, Jeff begins watching his neighbors across the courtyard through his rear window. However, his harmless curiosity turns into something far more dangerous when one of them begins to stand out for all the wrong reasons. Lars Thorwald (Raymond Burr) is a traveling salesman who lives with his wife, who is often sick. Jeff notices him making several late-night trips carrying a suitcase, soon after which his wife mysteriously disappears.

The more Jeff watches, the more convinced he is that Thornwald has murdered her with the help of his girlfriend Lisa Fremont (Grace Kelly) and nurse Stella (Thelma Ritter). That kicks off an investigation based entirely on observation. Jeff can’t leave his wheelchair, so he relies on binoculars and instincts to piece together what really happened. Hitchcock places the audience in the same position as Jeff and restricts them to his confined perspective. This brilliant setup heightens every little movement and conversation and makes the viewers feel like active participants in this baffling mystery. Rear Window remains just as gripping decades later and proves that a great thriller doesn’t need to rely on spectacle to leave an impact.

Zodiac is another Fincher thriller that remains the benchmark for the genre. The film turns one of America’s most infamous unsolved crimes into a cinematic experience that stays with the audience long after the credits roll. The story follows the real-life manhunt for the Zodiac Killer, who terrorized the San Francisco Bay Area in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The film unfolds through the perspectives of three men whose lives become consumed by the case: political cartoonist Robert Graysmith (Jake Gyllenhaal), crime reporter Paul Avery (Robert Downey Jr.), and homicide inspector Dave Toschi (Mark Ruffalo). Graysmith, in particular, becomes increasingly fascinated by the killer’s cryptic letters to the police and newspapers and begins an investigation of his own to decode them.

However, this curiosity slowly turns into an obsession and pushes Graysmith into a web of complicated clues that seem to lead nowhere. The film explores how the case takes a toll on everyone involved and attempts to center the story on the painful process of investigation itself. Zodiac isn’t really interested in finding who the killer is and deliberately avoids the usual beats a crime thriller would typically follow. The tension here comes from watching these people chase lead after lead, only to end up with nothing. That lingering uncertainty makes the climax all the more shocking. Zodiac mirrors the frustration that defined the real mystery of the killer and perfectly captures the psychological toll of it all.

Hitchcock’s Psycho is just one of those films that never get old. In fact, it remains a defining moment in the evolution of modern horror and thriller storytelling. The story begins with Marion Crane (Janet Leigh) impulsively stealing $40,000 from her employer and going on the run in hopes of starting a new life with her boyfriend. During her drive, she runs into a terrible storm and decides to pull over at the quiet roadside Bates Motel. The establishment is run by the polite but socially awkward Norman Bates (Anthony Perkins), who lives in a giant Victorian house overlooking the property with his overbearing mother. The story plays out like a traditional crime drama centered on Marion before Hitchcock subverts all expectations, and the audience witnesses her shocking murder in the now-iconic shower scene.

As Marion’s sister Lila (Vera Miles) and boyfriend Sam Loomis (John Gavin) begin searching for her, the investigation slowly leads them back to the eerie motel and the secrets hidden inside Norman’s house. The narrative unfolds slowly, and the audience gradually uncovers that the motel owner is far more complicated and terrifying than he initially seems. Perkins’s performance definitely deserves a mention here because his portrayal of Norman is the heart of the film. That’s exactly what makes the final reveal and Norman’s eventual descent into madness land so perfectly. Looking back, the brilliance of Psycho lies in how carefully the director builds up to that one moment, and it is the reason why the film has stood the test of time.

The Silence of the Lambs is undisputedly one of the greatest psychological thrillers ever made. The film follows FBI trainee Clarice Starling (Jodie Foster), who is tasked with helping track down a brutal serial killer known as Buffalo Bill (Ted Levine). Now, to understand the mind of a killer, Clarice is sent to interview imprisoned psychiatrist and cannibalistic murderer Dr. Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins). The catch is that Lecter only agrees to offer clues about Buffalo Bill if Clarice reveals deeply personal details about her own past to him. This uneasy dynamic is the center of the story as Clarice pieces together fragments of information about Buffalo Bill’s disturbing motives while navigating her strange relationship with Lecter.

Their conversations feel like a cat-and-mouse game where Lecter is constantly trying to manipulate and analyze Clarice’s fears. On the other hand, Buffalo Bill continues abducting women, which raises the stakes of the investigation and pushes the FBI trainee to rely on Lecter’s transactional guidance. The film builds suspense by focusing on its characters and their psychology. The horror is rooted in the conversations between Clarice and Lecter rather than momentary shocks. The Silence of the Lambs is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates the art of a slow burn.

Shutter Island marked a turning point for modern era psychological thrillers. The film, adapted from Dennis Lehane’s 2003 novel of the same name, is set on an eerie, remote island that houses a psychiatric hospital for the criminally insane. The story follows U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his partner Chuck Aule (Mark Ruffalo) as they arrive on the island to investigate the disappearance of Rachel Solando, a patient who drowned her three children and somehow vanished from her locked hospital ward. Things only get stranger from there; when Teddy begins questioning doctors and patients, he realizes that everyone at the hospital is hiding something. Meanwhile, Teddy starts experiencing disturbing migraines, flashbacks, and extremely vivid dreams about his late wife, who died in a tragic fire.

All of this leads him to believe that something sinister is happening on the island, and he is entangled in rumors of secret experiments and impossible conspiracies. However, every conversation and clue pushes him further into a state of confusion. After a while, both Teddy and the audience begin to question what is real and what might just be an illusion. The film slowly builds up to what is easily one of the most memorable plot twists Hollywood has ever seen — one that completely recontextualizes the entire story. Ultimately, Shutter Island revolves around a man who is gradually confronting the darkest corners of his own mind. It’s a psychological puzzle that gets better with every rewatch and never loses its thrill.

Seven might just be one of the darkest thrillers Fincher has ever delivered. The film is unsettling from the get-go, and it refuses to offer the audience or its characters any respite. The story follows veteran detective William Somerset (Morgan Freeman) and his new partner David Mills (Brad Pitt) as they chase a serial killer whose crimes are inspired by the seven deadly sins. Things kick off with a disturbing murder scene where an obese man has been forced to eat until he dies, a crime that represents gluttony. When another victim is discovered with the words “greed” marked at the crime scene, Somerset realizes this is the work of an extremely methodical killer operating with a twisted moral compass.

What makes Seven such a compelling movie is the interesting dynamic between the thoughtful and patient Somerset and the younger, much more impulsive Mills, who grows increasingly frustrated as the killer keeps getting away. The film’s final act is what cements Seven as an unforgettable experience as the antagonist (Kevin Spacey) reveals that he committed the sin of envy and delivers that now-infamous Box to Mills. Seven ends on a devastating note that leaves everyone shaken because, despite everything, the killer’s plan works exactly as he intended. This bleak storytelling and relentless sense of dread make Seven a masterclass in suspense.
