#3460. Battlestar Galactica Cerberus & Prometheus Collection Officially Announced

It was on 17 September 1978 that Battlestar Galactica premiered for the first time, following the theatrical release of its pilot movie earlier that year. However, over the past 48 years, the beloved sci-fi franchise has been the subject of many renewals and sequels, including 1980's Galactica 1980, and more recently, the prequel series, Caprica, which aired in 2010.

Set in a distant part of the universe where human civilization has colonized a group of planets known as the Twelve Colonies, the story follows their migration from their ancestral homeworld of Kobol, and their ongoing war with the Cylons, a cybernetic race who wishes to exterminate the human race.

With so many sequels, prequels, and even a reimagined television series, it is no wonder why the sci-fi franchise is still as popular as it is today, and those who were a fan of the original series, will be pleased to learn that they can get their hands on both the Cerberus and the Prometheus.

It was during 1978's Battlestar Galactica that viewers were told of twelve battlestars, despite only eight ever being mentioned on screen. It was during this time that three more battlestars - Solaria, Cerberus and Prometheus - were waiting in the wings, with plans to add them to the Colonial fleet over time.

Now, two out of three of these battlestars will now be released courtesy of Master Replicas: the Cerberus and Prometheus. As for the Cerberus, it is available as part of a limited-edition, with only 500 being made. The same can be said for Battlestar Galactica (Classic) Prometheus Limited Edition. Coming in at the same price and length, it is also available for purchase now and will make an excellent addition to your collectible shelf.

It is clear to see that both replicas feature a staggering amount of detail, and manage to capture the battlestars in all of their canon glory. If you are not sure which one to purchase, it is safe to say that they look pretty similar, so if you are only able to get one, you need not worry about missing out on the other. Thanks to an accompanying stand, they will no doubt be a talking piece once displayed in your homes, and better yet, they will not break the bank to purchase.

So, if you are feeling nostalgic for the original Battlestar Galactica television series, and want a way to showcase your love, look no further than these stunning new releases which aim to highlight the beloved science-fiction franchise in all its glory. So, Cerberus or Prometheus?

#3458. I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

#3457. How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

#3456. GTA 6 launch day LIVE — latest news, first impressions and the best Black Friday deals to upgrade your experience

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s officially Grand Theft Auto VI launch day. It really does feel surreal to say GTA 6 is a game you can play right now. It’s been a long road, but Vice City is now open to visitors.

To celebrate GTA 6’s historic launch, Tom’s Guide is bringing you live coverage of launch day, with the latest news, our first impressions as we start playing the game for ourselves, and, because it’s Black Friday shopping season, there are also plenty of great gaming deals that can upgrade your experience, letting you experience GTA 6 at its absolute best.

I know you’d probably rather be playing the game right now, but if you can’t get to a console just yet, stick around for all the latest updates and best deals on GTA 6 launch day.

The wait is over, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Millions of gamers are taking their first steps in Vice City, and to celebrate, we're talking all things GTA 6 today in this live blog. I'll have news, first impressions from across the Tom's Guide team, some interactive polls (I want to hear your early thoughts, too), and plenty of early Black Friday deals so you can upgrade your gaming setup for the hours of play ahead.

I stayed up past my bedtime last time to play GTA 6 as soon as it unlocked at midnight. I've only played roughly 90 minutes of the game, but I'm already overwhelmed, and seriously impressed. Graphically the game is stunning, but it's the rich detail of the world that has grabbed me out of the gate. Vice City is a place I just want to wander. I didn't even complete any mission beyond the prologue, I just walked the streets, taking in the sounds and signs of this overwhelming location.

If for some reason you haven't already bought GTA 6, I bet you feeling the FOMO right about now. There's still time to join the party over in Vice City ahead of the weekend. You can either purchase the game digitally on the Xbox and PlayStation Store, or you can grab a "code in box" edition, which comes with a nifty poster (pictured above). I'm far too early to make a definitive judgement on GTA 6, but so far it's blowing me away.

Playing GTA 6 into the early hours of today reminded me how useful a second controller can be. My first DualSense ran out of battery just 30 mins into my session, but because I had a spare fully charged one, I could swap over. No need to pause playing or to play with a wired connection. If you need a spare DualSense, or just a shiny new one, PS5 DualSense controllers are $54 at Amazon (down from $74).

I won’t lie — I’m biased as a GTA fan. This is more than a game. It’s a chance to look back at how far you’ve come over 13 years.

But one thing remains the same across both. That feeling of escaping to another living world that nobody but Rockstar can capture. I played four hours when it launched at midnight (currently on my third cup of coffee to keep going), and I’m truly floored by the scope of GTA VI.

Setting aside the fact it’s a beautiful-looking game with a stellar soundtrack and a Leonida that feels truly alive, the biggest thing that’s stood out to me so far is what I’ll call the “Red Dead-ification” of GTA.

I spoke to my boss about doing some day-to-day menial tasks and DIY in-game — such as fixing my roof at 2 am — and the reaction was “...why?” It’s a good question, and the answer is the same as Red Dead Redemption 2. As much as the world feels alive, you feel like a part of it with your own personal stories and supporting cast of people you actually care about.

A skeptic’s take would be to say Rockstar’s made an “adulting” educational game for millennials. But in reality, these small elements are significant in really making you emotionally invested in the characters, their personalities and their stories.

It's been over 24 hours since GTA 6 reviews went live, and it still holds a near-perfect 99 score on Metacritic. After 150 reviews, it's the current highest-reviewed video game on the platform. Some other titles have the same score, but not with this many reviews accounted for. It's remarkable that Rockstar Games actually delivered on the extremely high levels of hype! Based on my limited playtime, it deserves the 99, too.

As noted, I'm only 90 minutes into GTA 6 — sadly couldn't stay up too late last night — but I want to hear how much time you've spend in Vice City already. Is anybody already at the 10 hour mark? Or do you just have a couple of hours in GTA 6 so far?

#3453. December 15 Is Officially A Dark Day For PlayStation Plus

A number of games are scheduled to leave the PlayStation Plus Extra and Premium Game Catalog next month, and the list includes a sizable action RPG alongside several smaller, more unusual adventures. You can still finish these games before December 15 arrives, but once it does, you’ll have to either stop playing or purchase these games to continue playing. So, this is your cue to run through them before the deadline.

The names appearing on the current PlayStation Store’s “Last Chance to Play” list are:

There is an important regional catch, though. The list was first spotted on Japanese and Asian storefronts, and not every title is marked for removal in every region. Dark Rose Valkyrie is flagged as absent from some regional lists, while Root Letter and Jake Hunter: Prism of Eyes are listed for select regions only. To confirm what’s leaving your store in particular, make sure to check the Last Chance to Play section on your console.

Coming to the games, the biggest loss for players who enjoy action RPGs is arguably Granblue Fantasy: Relink. Available on both the PS4 and PS5, Cygames’ creation sends players through the Sky Realm, where they build a party of four and fight using characters with different weapons, skills and combat styles. It can be played solo or with up to three other players online, and its quest list gives those who enjoy its combat plenty to work through. Somerville is another unique experience for the PS4 and PS5 that you don’t want to miss. The sci-fi adventure follows a family separated during an alien invasion, with players exploring the aftermath, solving environmental puzzles and trying to find their way through a strange, hostile landscape.

The rest of the games are PS4 releases, but can be played on the PS5 as well. Fade to Silence is a survival RPG set in a frozen, post-apocalyptic world. Gathering supplies, building a refuge and surviving blizzards are central to the experience, so it’s a more demanding pick than Granblue Fantasy: Relink or Somerville. Dark Rose Valkyrie is a Japanese RPG set in an alternate version of 1929, where a virus turns people into monsters called Chimeras. Root Letter is all about a mystery visual novel built around the disappearance of a former pen pal and the letters she left behind. And lastly, Jake Hunter: Prism of Eyes brings a detective adventure featuring 14 scenarios, including new cases and stories that previously appeared on mobile.

Game Catalog titles do not work like the monthly games that are claimed through PlayStation Plus. Downloading a game from Extra or Premium does not mean you keep access after it leaves the catalog. For the subscription, access ends when a title is removed from the collection, although purchasing it later can restore access to its save data, provided you don’t delete that data. There’s no need to panic-buy anything, but it’s worth checking your regional list for the last chance event and deciding what you actually want to finish. If you have any of these games in mind and own a valid Plus subscription, make sure you finish them before December 15.

#3452. MagSafe Monday: MOFT’s Trackable Field Wallet holds eight cards, cash, and supports Find My

The one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it shows up in the Find My app.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

MOFT has been making the origami-style folding wallet for many years, and this model works like any other Find My accessory. So that means you get left-behind alerts when you leave without it, and the ability to make it trackable through Apple’s network if it’s across town instead of under the couch. It also works with Google’s Find Hub on Android, which matters if you’ve got a mixed household of devices.

The wallet is powered by a built-in battery rather than a watch-style battery, and MOFT says a charge lasts about six months. You charge it by placing the wallet on a Qi charger for about an hour and a half, which, in practice, means dropping it on a MagSafe dock twice a year. That’s a better setup than an AirTag in a wallet as well.

The wallet holds up to eight cards, or closer to four to six if you also use the hidden compartment for cash. A pull tab in the wallet brings your everyday cards out in one motion, while your driver’s license and cash stay tucked inside of it. It’s made from MOFT’s vegan leather and at 14 mm thick, it’s slimmer than a traditional wallet but noticeably thicker than Apple’s card-only wallet, which is the price you are going to pay to hold up this much stuff.

The stand is the usual MOFT origami fold-out, and it works in portrait and landscape for FaceTime or watching a video on the plane. You can buy it without the stand if you’d rather have the thinner version. It comes in Jet Black, Misty Cove, Terracotta, and Peony.

Two things to know going in. There’s no RFID blocking in this version (MOFT has a non-Find My Snap Field Wallet if you want that). MOFT also warns that the magnets can affect magnetic-stripe cards, so avoid putting a hotel key in it.

I’ve spent the past month on a Pelican accessory beat, using wallets designed for outdoor use. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is the other end of that accessory spectrum: more cards, a stand, and Find My built in. If Find My is the reason you’ve stuck with Apple’s wallet, this is a really nice option that holds a bunch and is trackable.

The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from MOFT.

#3450. Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the company discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a new service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google launched the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

But perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the company hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

#3448. Four Things You Can Do With Google Maps' New 'Ask Maps' Feature

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

#3445. Zelda: A Link To The Past HD-2D Remake Leaves Gamers Stunned

Launching back in 1991 for the SNES, The Legend of Zelda: Link to the Past marked the third installment in the beloved Nintendo franchise, and, to this day, it is still remembered fondly despite being more of an underrated entry.

Serving as something of a prequel to the first two Zelda titles, A Link to the Past takes on the role of Link once more as he attempts to defeat Demon King Ganon and save Hyrule once more. However, what makes A Link to the Past as important as it is, is it was the first installment to introduce the Master Sword, which, to this day, is one of the most iconic weapons in video game history.

Over the years, The Legend of Zelda: Link to the Past has received multiple ports and re-releases and, in 2013, a sequel titled A Link Between Worlds also continued the story. However, in recent times, fans have caught wind of a fan-favorite project that aims to create an HD-2D remake of the hit 1991 title.

It was over on r/decomps that a trailer for this unofficial remake was shared, and it is clear to see that The Legend of Zelda: Link to the Past has never looked better, and as one user correctly put it, "Bro, I can’t keep up with these amazing projects. I was just about to start playing the dual-screen mod and now this?"

Shared by user JoggingThruThe6 who is the brains behind this project, they reveal that they have been working on it for the past few days and "tossed" together the trailer to highlight a few things. They continued, "I've been primarily testing and playing on my AYN Thor (I've built an enhanced version of the dual-screen UI)—but I wanted to record sound easily for some scenes and my Mac build chugged with the lighting in the intro... It's been a smooth 60 on my Thor."

Not only that, but the creator shared a list of features that players can expect with the HD-2D remake, including: dynamic lighting and weather effects, a day and night cycle, NPC schedules, an enhanced introduction scene, AI improvements, especially for the guards, seamless overworld and interiors, an improved UI, and sound replacements.

Additionally, JoggingThruThe6 has revealed that they are looking for collaborators to help with the project, so if you want to lend a hand in the creation of this stunning, albeit unofficial, HD-2D remake of The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, make sure to head over to Reddit and share your interest.

#3444. 'Yellowjackets' Season 3 Recap: What To Remember Before the Horror Thriller's Final Season

Few shows have been as unhinged as Showtime's Yellowjackets. Ever since its premiere in 2021, the series has attracted a large following thanks to its thrilling premise, intriguing storylines set in two different timelines, and endlessly fascinating characters. There are shockingly gruesome scenes (yep, there's cannibalism) and themes like the brutality of girlhood and the long-lasting effects of trauma — but no matter where the story has ventured, it's consistently entertaining to watch. Yellowjackets is returning for its fourth and final season on November 20, so here's a refresher on what went down in Season 3.

When Season 3 kicks off, the Yellowjackets girls' soccer team have actually found a surprising sense of contentment in the wilderness. They've set up new living conditions after the cabin burned down, and they've officially survived the harsh winter. But the cracks in the society the girls have built start to appear. While Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) has been in charge of the girls as Antler Queen, Shauna (Sophie Nélisse) still believes that she's the group's rightful leader.

Ultimately, the group decides that Coach Ben (Steven Krueger) should be killed because of his potential involvement in the destruction of the cabin. They begin to torture Ben until Natalie puts him out of his misery, adding one more death to the team's tally. This is viewed as a traitorous act, and Natalie is dethroned as Antler Queen, with Shauna stepping in as her replacement. We also learn that the Pit Girl we first witnessed at the very beginning of the series is actually Mari (Alexa Barajas), who unluckily drew the Queen of Hearts card from the deck, and becomes a target for the group to hunt.

The Yellowjackets Season 3 finale features every storyline firing on all cylinders. In the present-day timeline, the mystery of Lottie's (Simone Kessell) death is solved, with the show confirming that Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) daughter Callie (Sarah Desjardins) accidentally pushed her down the stairs during an argument. In another twist of fate, Van (Lauren Ambrose) doesn't die from cancer, as fans expected, but is stabbed to death by Melissa (Hilary Swank), who had tried to escape the group's collective past but finds herself drawn back in by her shared connection with her former teammates. Taissa (Tawny Cypress) is devastated by losing Van, and fully descends into madness — cutting out Van's heart, eating it, and burying her love in the wilderness. Shauna also seems to be embracing the unraveling of her life after her family deserts her, while Tai and Misty (Christina Ricci) team up to figure out what to do about Shauna next.

Back in the wilderness, the girls decide on a celebratory feast, intent on gobbling up poor Coach Ben. In the middle of the madness, some researchers stumble across the team, witnessing their cannibalism in the process. Lottie (Courtney Eaton), in the midst of a psychotic episode, murders one of them with an axe. Scientist Hannah (Ashley Sutton) sees an opportunity to survive by teaming up with the girls, and kills her wilderness guide, Kodiak (Joel McHale). Amidst the chaos, the group becomes divided on whether they actually want to be rescued. Van (Liv Hewson) wants to leave the wilderness behind and successfully repairs the scientists' satellite phone, which Natalie climbs to a mountaintop with to send out an SOS that will likely lead to the team's rescue in the final season.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

There are still so many questions that Season 4 of Yellowjackets needs to explore. We don't know exactly how the team will be rescued, or how they will be able to fold back into normal society. In the present day, will Shauna successfully win back her family's trust, and what will happen now that Tai and Misty have agreed to team up against her? There has already been so much death for these characters, and it's likely there will be even more bloodshed before the series concludes. However the story ends, Yellowjackets will remain one of the wildest and darkly satisfying shows ever made.

Yellowjackets Season 4 premieres November 20 on Paramount+.

#3443. 10 Shows Like 'Youth' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

#3441. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#3440. Apple’s leadership overhaul continues with new Apple Pay and Wallet chief

Bloomberg reports that Apple lifer Corey Fugman will replace Jennifer Bailey as the head of the Apple Pay and Wallet division. Here are the details.

A few months ago, Bloomberg reported that Jennifer Bailey, Apple’s head of Apple Pay and Wallet, who had led Apple Pay since its launch in 2014, would retire in October.

At the time, Apple’s services boss Eddy Cue said internally that the company would announce its succession plan before her transition at the end of October, and that she would “continue to be available to support the transition in an advisory role.”

October came and went without any public announcement on that front. Today, however, Bloomberg reported that Apple has tapped Corey Fugman, “a 26-year company veteran as the new head of its payment service and digital wallet unit.”

According to his LinkedIn profile, Fugman joined Apple in September 2000 as Merchandising Manager for Apple Retail and has held several leadership positions since then, including overseeing Apple Card and Apple Cash from 2019 to 2021.

Most recently, he served as Senior Director of Apple Pay and Wallet, a position he has held since November 2021.

With the new job, Fugman inherits a crucial tap-to-pay business, which is estimated to generate billions of dollars a year. It handles tens of billions of transactions annually across more than 90 markets, with Apple taking a percentage.

The division also includes the Apple Card, which is transitioning from a partnership with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to JPMorgan Chase & Co. Fugman has been highly involved with the shift to Chase, which is still ongoing, the people said.

The report notes that Fugman will report to Cue, and reaffirms that Bailey “will remain a consultant in the coming months,” echoing Cue’s earlier comments about her role in the transition.

Finally, Bloomberg adds that while Apple has undergone several leadership changes in recent months, including John Ternus replacing Tim Cook as CEO, Cue’s responsibilities have expanded considerably.

In addition to overseeing services such as Apple TV, Apple Music, Maps, and iCloud, Cue has recently taken charge of the App Store and Health following Jeff Williams’ departure as Chief Operating Officer and Phil Schiller’s decision to step down from overseeing the App Store.

#3438. HBO's 26-Episode R-Rated Thriller Series Has One Of Its Best Casts

Although one famous HBO thriller has arguably the best TV cast of the 2020s, this ironically hurt the show’s reception in its later years. From classic sitcoms like Seinfeld to dark psychological thrillers like True Detective, every TV show lives and dies based on the strength of its casting. Even shows that are seemingly driven by action rather than character need great casting to succeed.

One need only look at the critical acclaim and audience love heaped on Prime Video’s action thriller Reacher, compared to the muted reception of Tom Cruise’s earlier movie adaptation Jack Reacher, to see this principle in action. Cruise is a massive A-list and was even more famous and bankable back in 2012, but the comparatively little-known Alan Ritchson was a much better fit for the role of Reacher. As such, the lower-budget, less explosive series earned a much better reception.

However, as surprising as it might sound, a great cast can also sometimes prove to be a problem for some shows. Prime Video’s Patricia Cornwell adaptation Scarpetta assembled an astounding cast including Nicole Kidman, Rosy McEwen, Simon Baker, Bobby Cannavale, Ariana DeBose, and even Jamie Lee Curtis, but the show had no idea what to do with all these A-list names. Similarly, True Detective season 2’s starry cast left the series with no clear main character, and no narrative thrust as a result. Then, there is the tragic case of HBO’s R-rated three-season thriller Euphoria.

It has only been seven years since Euphoria debuted in 2019. However, the show’s immeasurable impact on the pop culture zeitgeist makes it difficult to introduce the series in 2026. Technically a high school character drama, Euphoria presented an absurdly heightened, debauched world of sex, drugs, and violence that made Gossip Girl’s worst excesses look like Cocomelon.

The show also assembled a cast that included Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney, Jacob Elordi, Maude Apatow, Hunter Schafer, Colman Domingo. Austin Abrams, and many, many more. However, this rundown might be a little misleading. Technically, Sweeney had appeared in HBO’s Sharp Objects and Hulu’s adaptation of Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale before Euphoria.

However, she was nowhere near the A-list mainstream fame that hits like Anyone But You and The Housemaid later afforded her. Similarly, Elordi was years away from Wuthering Heights, Frankenstein, or even Saltburn. Schafer’s roles in The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes and Blade Runner 2099 were still years ahead of her, as was Abrams’ one-two punch of Resident Evil and Weapons.

Of the show’s massive, starry cast, it was mainly Zendaya and Domingo who were already established stars, and even they were both nowhere near as big as they later became after the show’s success. At this stage, Zendaya had Spider-Man: Homecoming and The Greatest Showman under her belt, but the Dune movies, The Odyssey, and three more Spider-Man sequels awaited.

Domingo had an astounding history of consistent work on the small and big screen, but his blockbuster roles were all ahead of him. This is important to note since it explains why, rather than helping the HBO show gain more attention, the astounding cast also unintentionally helped derail Euphoria’s season 3 story and the show’s legacy more broadly.

To be clear, the bizarre ending of Euphoria was an unforced error, as there are countless better ways that the show could have ended. However, the fact that the entire main cast were busy with bigger, better projects meant the final season was repeatedly delayed and pushed off, which, in turn, prompted a big in-universe time jump to justify their new ages and life stages. This meant that Euphoria season 3 looked and felt nothing like its predecessors, exacerbating the existing cultural consensus that the HBO show had become a parody of its old self.

#3437. ‘Dune’ Director Officially Reveals Why He Cast Robert Pattinson as the New Bond

Many worries about the future of the James Bond franchise, following its $1 billion acquisition by Amazon, were calmed when it was confirmed who would be directing the next movie. The brilliant Denis Villeneuve was officially announced as the Bond director, and he will work alongside writer Steven Knight, best known for creating the Peaky Blinders franchise. Villeneuve's track record of producing high-quality, ambitious, big-screen favorites is arguably unrivaled in the modern era, so there is no doubt that the franchise is in safe hands.

But Villeneuve would not be able to get started on the Bond film in earnest until his latest big project had been completed. Dune: Part Three, the final installment in the director's adaptation of the Frank Herbert novels, will make its debut on December 18, as audiences watch in awe as Paul Atreides' (Timothée Chalamet) empire is threatened by the evil Scytale. This terrifying villain is played by Robert Pattinson, who just so happens to be the new James Bond.

Pattinson called the casting "the honour of a lifetime," with the British Royal Family even wishing him well, posting "Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond" to their social media. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin," Villeneuve also wrote in a statement celebrating the announcement of his Bond, but exactly why was Pattinson picked? There's no shortage of discussion online, but the director himself has now answered these questions in an interview with GQ.

"At the end of the day, the truth is, no matter who I choose, some people will be excited and others will be disappointed," Villeneuve admitted in the interview. The likes of Callum Turner and Jack Lowden were considered the frontrunners, and many have expressed their frustration that neither was picked. But Turner and Lowden must've lacked the perfect style and substance Villeneuve was searching for. "The first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer, because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin," he continued. "I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It’s not everybody who has that." He expanded on his criteria:

"I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that when he comes into the room, everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma and someone that has a lot of sensuality as well and that people are attracted to… someone who has dark humor, someone that has pleasure in being in deep shit, someone who is not afraid to put his hand in the mud. I need someone that is strong, muscular, someone that is a force. And someone, of course, who has a deep intelligence in the eyes, someone that is always ahead of us."

Pattinson's Bond is expected to begin filming in 2027. For more Bond stories, stay tuned to Collider.

#3436. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it."

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

However, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

#3435. New iPhone Duo orders now deliver a month earlier than before

Interested in getting an iPhone Duo before Christmas? You might be in luck, as Apple’s online store delivery estimates just got pulled forward by a full month, with December delivery now expected.

Apple seems to be finding success in ramping up its iPhone Duo production.

Within minutes of iPhone Duo pre-orders opening on October 16, delivery estimates quickly slipped into November, then December, and after about a half hour of orders, the earliest you could get an iPhone Duo was late January.

Apple did deliver some Duo units earlier than the initial estimates. But the late January timeframe remained in place for all new iPhone Duo orders until now.

But as spotted by Max Weinbach, new iPhone Duo orders from Apple just got bumped up by about a month. Now, delivery estimates are showing December 16-23 for customers in the US and elsewhere.

New Duo orders seemed to have been pulled forward ~a month They must be scaling manufacturing quickly pic.twitter.com/VFkCmCoRLF

This is a great indicator that Apple has been able to accelerate production. It’s also likely that there was a slowdown in orders due to the late January estimate putting off prospective buyers, thus making it easier for the company to catch up on backorders.

While we still don’t know sales numbers, the iPhone Duo by all appearances has been a hit already. And with iOS 27.3 adding a face unlock feature soon, one of the biggest critiques reviewers had is largely being mitigated.

#3433. Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

If you're switching from Apple Music or Spotify to Tidal, you probably want to bring your playlists with you. Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz. They both have a free tier, but they only transfers a few hundred songs gratis. My playlists are way bigger than that. The easy solution is to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when your tracks are transferred, but that didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music and Spotify to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee. Here's how it works:

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection."

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

#3432. Apple expands Apple Intelligence beta testing in China to iPads and Macs

Following the arrival of Apple Intelligence on iPhones in China with iOS 27.3 beta 1, Apple is now expanding support to iPads and Macs ahead of the public release of its 27.3 updates. Here are the details.

Apple’s road to releasing Apple Intelligence in China has been a particularly eventful one.

After a significant amount of regulatory back-and-forth, the company confirmed in late October that Apple Intelligence would make its way to iPhones as of iOS 27.3, beginning with the first beta of the system, released in early November.

Just a few days later, Reuters reported that Apple had cleared another regulatory hurdle in the country by registering Apple Intelligence for use on tablets and laptops.

Today, Apple released the second developer betas of iPadOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3, both of which now include Apple Intelligence support in China, as spotted by MacRumors.

As with the initial iPhone rollout in the first iOS 27.3 beta, Apple Intelligence on iPads and Macs in China does not include Siri AI or the other next-generation AI features announced at WWDC 2026.

Instead, users get access to earlier capabilities such as Writing Tools, Genmoji, Live Translation, and notification summaries, with Alibaba’s Qwen model powering certain features.

You can learn more about the Apple Intelligence features set to be available in China at launch here.
