#3431. Unbelievable Is Netflix's 8-Part True Crime Thriller With 98% On Rotten Tomatoes

Netflix's acclaimed 8-part true crime thriller follows two detectives pursuing a serial attacker while a young survivor struggles to be believed. Released back in 2019, this limited series remains one of the most critically acclaimed Netflix shows ever produced, delivering top-tier performances with masterful storytelling that brings a shocking true crime story to life with great execution and impact. Starring Kaitlyn Dever, Toni Collette, and Merritt Wever in some of their career-best roles, this is one of the best weekend binges on Netflix.

Unbelievable is one of the best limited series on any streaming platform released over the last seven years, as evidenced by its near-perfect 98% Rotten Tomatoes score and 4 Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Limited Series, Writing, and Casting. The 8-episode crime thriller is an ideal weekend binge with a total runtime of 6 hours and 25 minutes that can be viewed from start to finish in just a few sittings. Unbelievable delivers a masterclass in police detective work through an assault case investigation, making it a rewarding watch.

Similar to Netflix's celebrated miniseries Adolescence, Unbelievable can be a tough series to watch but is worth every single minute. Dever stars as Marie Adler, a young woman who reported being sexually assaulted by an intruder in her home in Lynnwood, Washington. Despite her claims to law enforcement, police discounted her allegations by discrediting her account as inconsistent and convinced her to withdraw her report, slapping her with a false police report charge. Marie faced public backlash from these events, which resulted in her losing trust in others even though her report was entirely true. Marie not only experienced trauma from the assault, but psychological trauma as well.

The most appalling aspect of Marie Adler's true crime case is that the justice system penalized her for reporting a legitimate crime, which represents systemic institutional corruption inflicted by those meant to protect the public. Following further investigation in 2015, seven years after the initial incident, Adler was eventually awarded a $150,000 settlement by the city of Lynnwood, Washington.

A third-party investigation determined that Marie was coerced by law enforcement personnel into saying that she lied about the assault in her report. Two Colorado-based detectives discovered a connection between Marie's report and Marc Patrick O'Leary, a serial rapist, who was later convicted on multiple assault charges. Netflix's Unbelievable powerfully chronicles this chain of events through Marie's psychological lens.

Collette and Wever portray two of the key Colorado detectives who investigated O'Leary and eventually provided justice for Marie. Collette plays Detective Grace Rasmussen, inspired by Edna Hendershot of Colorado's Westminster Police Department, while Wever plays Detective Karen Duvall, based on Stacy Galbraith of Colorado's Golden Police Department.

Their outstanding performances exemplify the determination of both real-life detectives, and the narrative is rooted in the actual police work, such as reviewing forensic and surveillance evidence used to put O'Leary behind bars. O'Leary pleaded guilty to 30 counts, including sexual assault and rape, and received a 327.5-year sentence in Colorado and a 68.5-year sentence in Washington. He will spend the rest of his life in prison at the Sterling Correctional Facility in Sterling, Colorado​​​​​​.

Julia Garner leads Netflix's new 8-part true-crime drama about an $8 billion crypto scandal, an explosive romance, and the rise and fall of an empire.

While other exceptional detective series on Netflix, such as Mindhunter, focus intently on the psychology of the criminals, Unbelievable is far more interested in examining the psychological toll on the survivors, specifically Marie Adler. Collette and Wever deliver contrasting investigative styles through their performances, which make them one of streaming's best detective duos, in the same league as Woody Harrelson's Marty Hart and Matthew McConaughey's Rust Cohle in True Detective season 1.

Unbelievable is also comparable to Hulu's hit detective series, Furious, and HBO's crime masterpiece, The Night Of, both of which earned critical acclaim for their portrayal of moral ambiguity and institutional failures within law enforcement and the court system rather than delivering justice to its fullest potential. To witness a masterclass in detective work on Netflix, press play on Unbelievable this weekend.

#3429. How to Transfer Your Playlists to Tidal Music for Free

I recently switched music streamers from Apple Music to Tidal. I like Tidal's strict anti-AI features, the fact that it pays higher royalties to artists than other major streamers, and its focus on high quality audio. I wrote a post featuring eight hacks for Tidal users, but I wanted to highlight one in particular: How to transfer playlists without paying anything.

Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz, which are both easy to use, but they're subscription services, and they only transfer a few hundred tracks for free. I have thousands of tracks, saved in a ton of playlists. The easy solution was to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when the tracks were transferred, but it just didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music, Spotify, and any other service that lets you download your tracks as a text file to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee.

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

#3428. ‘Schmigadoon!’ and ‘Widow’s Bay’ land Apple TV two Grammy nominations

Apple TV today celebrated two Grammy nominations, one of which further establishes a canceled show as an unlikely awards success story. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, the Broadway adaptation of Apple TV’s ‘Schmigadoon!’ won four Tony Awards, including Best Musical, making Apple TV an EGOT winner by completing its collection of Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony awards.

‘Schmigadoon!’ premiered on Apple TV in 2021 and ran for two seasons, ending in 2023. In January 2024, show creator Cinco Paul confirmed that, although the third season had already been written with 25 new songs, Apple decided not to move forward with it.

Even before the Broadway adaptation’s Tony wins in June, a May report had raised hopes for the show’s return, revisiting an earlier interview in which ‘Schmigadoon!’ creator Cinco Paul revealed that there had been discussions about reviving it.

While there have been no further updates on a potential revival since then, fans got another reason to celebrate today, as the Broadway cast recording of ‘Schmigadoon!’ has been nominated for Best Musical Theater Album at the 2027 Grammy Awards.

It will compete against CHESS the Musical, The Lost Boys, Ragtime, and Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York).

Additionally, ‘Widow’s Bay‘ earned a nomination for Best Score Soundtrack for Visual Media, putting composer David Fleming up against the soundtracks of ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘One Battle After Another,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and ‘Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu‘.

The 2027 Grammy Awards will take place on Sunday, February 7, 2027. To check out the full list of nominees, follow this link.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

#3427. ‘9-1-1: Nashville’ Boss Teases What’s Next After That Shocking Season 2 Pharaoh Reveal

The first six episodes of 9-1-1: Nashville's second season have seen the first responders and other characters deal with a mysterious killer called the Pharoah (A.J. Buckley), who's been terrorizing Nashville with murders inspired by the Biblical plagues. The mid-season finale is an explosive episode that sees the Pharoah escalate things with his latest scheme after he catches Rogue (Ryan Phillippe) trying to lure him into a trap. As of the end of the mid-season finale, the first responders were able to save the group of children that the Pharoah just targeted, but Don (Chris O'Donnell) and Rogue are currently caught in his latest trap.

Following the mid-season finale for Season 2, 9-1-1: Nashville's showrunner, Rashad Raisani, sat down with Collider to talk about the episode and break down the first half of the season. Raisani discusses that shocking cliffhanger, 9-1-1: Nashville's expansion into the crime thriller genre this season, and the compelling character dynamics that have been at the center of this season. He also teases some storylines from the back half of Season 2, including the upcoming crossover with 9-1-1.

So, the Pharaoh has finally been revealed in this great moment where Don has stopped to help this stranger, right after viewers have found out what the Pharaoh looks like. We see Don weigh this decision for a moment, because he has ice and a cake in his car, and he's already cutting it close to the baby shower. Why do you think he ultimately chose to stop?

RASHAD RAISANI: I think Don stopped because that's who he is: if he sees somebody stranded on the side of the road with a smoking car, he's always going to help. And Pharaoh knows that 100%. That would be Don's greatest weakness: there's no way he's going to pass by somebody who needs help and not help them.

That cliffhanger was already very intense with the Pharaoh taking Don, only for it to then be revealed that he has Rogue as well. How early on in the season did you know you wanted to end the mid-season finale with both of them in danger, and why is it specifically these two characters?

RAISANI: I think we knew pretty early that we wanted there to be a big price that they had to pay. Pharoah warns them in the second episode, “Don't interfere, or else there will be consequences,” so I think we knew early that we were going to do something big with them. And I think it always had to be Don and Rogue because – along with Cammie (Kimberly Williams-Paisley), who's the dispatcher, who does the most to try and stop Pharaoh — Don's fire team has saved many of his victims, and Rogue is in charge of trying to catch this guy. So, it made a lot of sense for him to take two of the three most important people who were both firstborns as his way of exacting revenge and proving his point that there would be consequences.

There was an interesting clash this episode between Rogue and Nick, when they fight over Rogue’s unconventional approach vs. Nick’s by-the-book FBI approach, and Nick makes a comment about Rogue's past of rule-breaking in New York. We already know about Rogue’s wife's death and the Strangler case, but there's also been some mystery about why he moved to Nashville in the first place. How much can you tease about Rogue's past in New York and this reputation of his that Nick’s referring to?

RAISANI: Well, I think I can say it was a reputation well-earned, that Rogue did break some things, and that he bent the rules for some people, maybe a little too much. And so I think that will be definitely something that comes out and continues to get revisited, and we'll see that tendency of Rogue’s come out even more and lead to some issues in Nashville as well. So it's definitely in his character. Nick is right onto it when he says that, and it will lead to more clashes, frankly, between them. So, yeah, it's going to be a part of things.

Alongside the Pharaoh, there's this really compelling villain this season in Marcia Zellner (Camryn Manheim), who continues to make the disturbing prank calls to Cammie this episode while showing no remorse and still being her friend at work. How did you decide to have this additional villain in Zellner, who's completely separate from the Pharaoh, and is there anything you can hint about her motivation in targeting Cammie specifically?

RAISANI: Marcia is a direct inspiration from Ryan Murphy. It was one of the big things he wanted to do this season: he wanted to have a mysterious criminal; he wanted to have Cammie be tormented by somebody like Camryn Manheim, who ended up being Camryn Manheim, who, at a certain pivotal moment, would be prank-calling Cammie, and then take off a wig and reveal scars, and you [realize], “Oh my god, she has a big problem.” So, we knew early we wanted to do that, and we wanted to explore these two things, and we wanted these two balls in the air about Pharaoh and Marcia, and we're not necessarily saying that they aren't related.

Like, we want the audience to just wonder. It's possible, on the one hand, that bad things can be happening at the same time that they're unrelated; it's also possible that they're connected. It's also possible that Marcia might be using the stress of Pharaoh too, for her own motivation, to torment Cammie even more. So, I think that was part of what made us feel like it'd be fun to have another crazy thing from left field, to suddenly have multiple fronts of badness. And then Marcia is coming from a very specific place, a very specific incident that corroded her, and that led her to become the person she is now, and that has made her so determined to torment and torture Cammie.

Ryan (Michael Provost) showed a particular interest in the Pharaoh investigation, and we saw him do some detective work with Rogue this season. Was it just about this particular case for him, or does he have more of a real interest in this, and could he be more involved in this alongside Rogue once he goes back to work?

RAISANI: I think yes. I think, first, he was just taken by this guy who, Ryan – Michael Provost’s character – is very rule-following; he’s grown up as a rule follower, he was always trying to please Dad, and he's done a good job of that, but then he watches this guy from New York come in and just break all the rules and be a maverick, and there's something very alluring to Ryan, because he's so different than anything Ryan's ever seen, and so Ryan is really enchanted by him.

And I think it really starts from a character level that he was so fascinated by Rogue, and then he starts to get into the investigation, because he's so excited to be around Rogue. So I think that there is a definite chance that he'll continue to pursue law enforcement, and to continue working with Rogue. But Ryan has his own drama to get through; his wife has cancer, she's pregnant, he’s going to take time off from the firehouse… He's got to juggle that also with the things that he's interested in doing at work.

So, Ryan's going to be taking a whole month off work for Sam (MacKenzie Porter); how much of their journey are we going to see in the back half of the season while Ryan's away from the 113?

RAISANI: There's going to be some episodes where they’ll be offscreen for a bit, because they have to go and travel, as he said, but then we are going to do a really rich story devoted to what her surgery looks like, what the post-surgery looks like, what the caretaking looks like, and explore what that journey is for them, and how it also affects our other characters. So, it's going to be a huge part. And then, tracking her pregnancy and her cancer through the back half of the season is going to be a major driver for us.

Will another firefighter be brought in temporarily to replace Ryan at the 113?

RAISANI: No. But we will play, we will dramatize how the leadership void... him being gone, their Lieutenant's gone — that does change the pecking order a little bit, and it will force our other characters to see who's going to step up and fill that, and that's kind of where we play in those episodes.

Don and Blythe (Jessica Capshaw) had a major breakthrough last episode, and they seem to be on solid ground this episode. Blythe and Dixie (LeAnne Rimes) are still clearly in conflict with each other, but are Don and Blythe completely past the hurdle of Dixie in their marriage?

RAISANI: I don't know about completely… I mean, I think the wound is always there, but they're healing; that's what I would say. They are healing from it. And I think it's always going to be a memory. It's like, they say you can forgive without forgetting, and I think they're now in that stage, that they are getting back to solid ground.

It doesn't mean Dixie's going to disappear, and it doesn't mean Blythe and Dixie don't have their own relationship and their own frenemy status, because they are now hitched together with this record label that Blythe's in charge of, and we're going to play some stories in that world, where we're going to find out that those two women, as much as they can't stand each other all the time, they actually work really well together, and they complement each other. We're going to play the fun and the irony of them being kind of stuck together and thriving together.

What lessons did you learn while showrunning Lone Star that you've taken with you to Nashville?

RAISANI: That’s a great question. What I've learned, and it's still the hard way, is that you never have enough time to do all the things you want. And that you just end up... like, on Lone Star, our last season went from 18 episodes to 16 episodes to 12 episodes, and suddenly, the character arcs got smushed, and smushed, and smushed, so that Marjan (Natacha Karam) would have to meet the parents in the same episode that they introduced her fiancé, [and it's] the same episode where she has to get married, whereas that would normally take three or four episodes. So what I've learned is that you always need to have good drive for the characters, but you don't have to have them do a bunch of different things in tight clumps; the audience will go with them on their journeys.

And then the other thing I've learned is how to do these big action cases and how to interweave them, and that if you don't.... if the case is – and we've been guilty of it before, where we just did a big case for a big case, but the best cases have an emotional connection to what's happening in the characters' lives, and that makes them much richer. And I think that was the biggest lesson of Lone Star, we were at our best when those things were in sync with each other.

Rogue has been such a great addition to the season. The Pharaoh investigation has tied his storylines to that of the 113 thus far in every episode, but have there been challenges in navigating the process of weaving him into personal storylines as well and determining how he'll stay connected to them after this case?

RAISANI: I think so. I mean, I think that the good news is that because Ryan was so wrapped up in the case at the beginning, and because Don, as the season goes along, gets more inevitably put in the center of this, it hasn't been that hard to keep Rogue with our characters. I think the hardest challenge now is that if we're telling a call center story, and we're telling a story about Pharaoh, it just sometimes can be harder to play some of our — what I also love to do — firehouse family scenes. That's been our biggest juggling act, we're still turning the dials on how to balance everything with telling this hard-driven thriller mystery.

Cammie has this crazy boss, Marcia, who's tormenting her in a psychological thriller, but we also don't want to give short shrift to our beloved characters in the firehouse. And I think, to be honest, that's been one of the biggest things I've been wanting us to kind of figure out how to do better, frankly, in the back half of the season: just bringing some of that joy that comes from people like Taylor (Hailey Kilgore), and Blue (Hunter McVey), and Roxie (Juani Feliz), and the firehouse, because I think that's where a lot of the warmth of our show comes from. And so how do you balance them? How do you get Dixie in the show when there's this mysterious killer killing people?

The mid-season finale had me on the edge of my seat the entire time, and Season 2 in general has had really heightened stakes, both on the calls and outside of them, through the introduction of the Pharaoh. What's the process been like of expanding the genre of 9-1-1: Nashville this season beyond both the procedural model and the family drama aspect to include the crime thriller element?

RAISANI: Now, I’ve absolutely loved it. I mean, I've just been thrilled. I've always loved police thrillers. Whether it be, you know, True Detective, or Sherlock, or Seven, or Zodiac. And so I think to infuse that, I think it ended up being… I never knew how it was going to work, but I think that blend of taking our heightened Nashville fun and soap, and then giving it this bass note of a real high-stakes killer and thriller, and somebody like Rogue, who's very hard-bitten. I think it ended up, to me, making the chemistry all work better. And so, it's been a joy. I love crime thrillers, and I think that's one thing that's evident. Our writers love it, the actors love it, and so I think it's really elevated the show to have that.

And this episode revealed another piece of backstory for Rogue. We already knew about his sons, but he also has a little sister who's seven years younger. Is this a potential character that we could see in the future?

RAISANI: It is, as are his sons. And we will see one of his sons very soon. So yes, every time we make those little stray comments, we're trying to tell – and our audience is so smart, they're just like you, up on it. They always go, “Oh, I see what you're doing.” But yeah, we want to world-build, and we want to let people know that these people have lives off the few minutes of screen time they get in an episode, that they do have rich backstories and lives, and we will be bringing them in.

Can I ask, is his son going to be in the LA crossover with 9-1-1?

And then, Don and Rogue have come a long way from Don briefly letting him choke in the season premiere to them now having a friendship. What do you think the shift was for Don to finally trust him?

RAISANI: I think the shift was that Don began to respect that Rogue has integrity. He may not be everybody's cup of tea; he may be gruff, he may be a little bit more brusque than anything Don's used to, but Don sees what guides him is goodness, even if it has an interesting package, and they don't agree on how to do things, and they don't agree on how to talk to people even sometimes. At the end of the day, Don sees that Rogue is a force for good, in his own, sometimes misguided, way – at least, misguided in Don's opinion. And so I think he sees the light in Rogue, even if Rogue isn't the guy he would have imagined he'd want to hang out with.

The procedural is back with an intense opening emergency.

There are so many great dynamics amongst the main characters in Nashville, especially now that Rogue is also in the picture. Are there any dynamics we haven't seen yet between characters who haven't had much cause to interact, that you would love to play around with?

RAISANI: Yeah. I mean, there's a lot. One thing that we just scratched the surface of, funny enough, is Taylor with Don. I think Taylor and Roxie is one of the great friendships we just haven't had the time for yet, but that's coming in the back half of the season, is to play more of Taylor and Roxie's friendship, to play more of Rogue with people like Cammie, who I think — and Blythe — he has great chemistry with them.

I feel like we're just getting started. There's so many people who’ve never really had scenes, or certainly not stories, together. So I'd like to see Dixie meet Rogue. They have a brush in an episode that's coming up, so I like to think we're just getting started. There are so many relationships we haven't even… we haven't even seen Blythe’s dad, Edward (Tim Matheson), so far this season. So, like I said, I always feel like we're running out of time before we even get started.

9-1-1: Nashville will return to ABC on Thursday, January 7 at 9:00 P.M. EST.

#3426. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3423. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3419. Netflix Is Officially Removing Hulu’s Best 2-Part Stephen King Thriller

Stephen King's writing has inspired countless movies and television shows, and that trend shows no signs of slowing down. It: Welcome to Derry provides some surprising backstory for one of King's biggest novels, particularly the fact that the titular town of Derry's been terrorized for years by the malevolent Pennywise. Mike Flanagan has built his career on adapting King's work, including his adaptation of Carrie and a planned television series for The Dark Tower.Last year,The Long Walk andThe Running Man hit theaters. However,one of King's most underrated adaptations is set to leave Netflix in less than a month.

That series is Castle Rock. Originally airing on Hulu, Castle Rock is unique because it isn't based on a single King book or short story. Instead, it's set in the fictional town of Castle Rock, where most of King's stories take place. Despite its seemingly original story, Castle Rock pulls characters from King's work into a swirling web of murder, mystery, and magic. Horror fans will have to move quickly, as Castle Rock ​​​​​​departs Netflix on December 14. They won't want to miss it, because this series does something new with King's work rather than being a straight adaptation.

From the jump, Castle Rock isn't shy about showcasing characters and locations from Stephen King's work. Season 1's central mystery lies within Shawshank State Penitentiary, the titular prison in The Shawshank Redemption. Aspiring writer Jackie Torrance

(Jane Levy) is the niece of The Shining's protagonist, Jack Torrance, and Season 2 takes things a step further by introducing Lizzy Caplan as Annie Wilkes, who becomes the main villain in Misery. Co-showrunner Sam Shaw would later explain that he and Dustin Thomason wanted each season of Castle Rock to feel like its own separate story.

"The plan for the show, in the beginning, was to tell a different kind of original Stephen King story every season. This season is a ten hour story with a beginning, a middle, and an end, and we hope we will have a satisfying conclusion to all the trajectories that get introduced."

Indeed, both seasons of Castle Rock feel like two distinct stories. Season 1 focuses on Henry Deaver (André Holland), who's drawn back to Castle Rock after a mysterious Shawshank prisoner referred to as "The Kid" (Bill Skarsgard) requests his presence. As Henry uncovers the Kid's origins, he deals with the shadows of his past, including the death of his adoptive father. Season 2 deals with Annie's descent into mass murder while incorporating elements from Salem's Lot. Though Castle Rock lasted only two seasons, it captured the feeling of a good Stephen King novel.

Fans who enjoy Castle Rock or are sad that it's leaving Netflix are in luck, as the streamer has another great King adaptation in the form of 11.22.63. Like Castle Rock, 11.22.63 originally debuted on Hulu and was produced under J.J. Abrams' Bad Robot banner. But while Castle Rock is merely inspired by Stephen King's work, 11.22.63 is a straight adaptation of one of his novels, in which teacher Jake Epping (James Franco) discovers a portalto 1963 in his friend's diner. Jake is tasked with stopping the assassination of John F. Kennedy, entering a literal race against time and a thriller that'll have viewers on the edge of their seats.

One of Castle Rock's stars would reveal the plot for Season 3 last year, which would have hewed closer to one of King's novels than previous seasons. At Emerald City Comic Con in 2025, Jane Levy said plans were in place for Castle Rock to center on Jackie Torrance, especially since Season 1 ends with her on a journey to learn more about her family. Castle Rock proves that Stephen King's work can inspire unique stories beyond adaptations, as its approach showed a deep appreciation for allhis books.

#3418. Former Apple chairman Arthur Levinson files to sell $31.8 million in company stock

Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the company.

Today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

#3412. iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 update

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

After updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

#3410. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3409. This 10/10 Action Thriller Is Still Jason Statham’s Greatest Movie 8 Years Later

There are action stars, and then there is Jason Statham. There is no question that everyone has seen at least one of this performer's flicks, whether they know it or not. The English actor got his start as a Guy Ritchie favorite in movies such as Lock, Stock, and Two Smoking Barrels as well as Snatch. It was his entry into the classic Fast and the Furious franchise, however, that was not his most memorable role.

His part as the villain turned antihero contributed to him being an action star, but it still doesn’t compare to the action thriller to compare all action thrillers to. While it may not spring to mind with the greats such as The Transporter, Crank, or even the more recent Beekeeper, his magnum opus does what these other films only dream of.

At a certain point, Jason Statham has got to be in on the joke. The action star has been in too many different vocation-adjacent roles. It has become admirable how many times his characters can take another job where gunfights are necessary. The 2018 movie, The Meg, doesn’t quite fit into this category but also seems to be in on what Statham is selling. The Meg, of course, stands for megalodon, a prehistoric shark that is the focal point of the movie.

This is the type of narrative that is meant to be seen in theaters, but even if it isn’t, it is still a wild ride. The outrageous concept of a submarine crew encountering an extinct shark is a movie begging to be watched. This isn’t a self-serious journey into the waves. The Meg understands what it is about and doesn’t apologize for it.

Statham stars as Jonas Taylor, a renowned diver who has become known for crying megalodon. No one quite believes that his last crew was chomped to pieces by a giant shark, ushering him into a state of drunken retirement in Thailand. Of course, as these things go, no one can let sleeping sharks lie. Years later, another crew takes a journey into the treacherous waters and discovers that, yes, there is indeed a megalodon beneath the waters.

Even the characters in The Meg acknowledge the predicament they’re in. No one in their right mind would believe that Jonas saw a prehistoric shark, but they are all proven wrong when another crew gets endangered by its chomping jaws. They call in the only man who has claimed to see one, Jonas, himself. The Meg and its sequel are a fun ride, made purposefully for its underwater antics. It is a return to movies like Deep Blue Sea and even Jaws, where the most terrifying thing that exists is the rule of nature.

Statham chews the scenery as he is wont to do, and no one does it better. The ensemble made up of Cliff Curtis and Rainn Wilson brings together the humor that this sort of movie couldn't do without. The Meg doesn’t hold back on the visuals either. If people pay to see a big shark, they're going to see a big shark. It seems that all other attempts by Statham in later years were just a pale imitation of one of his best action thrillers. The Meg is quite literally all killer, no filler, and a visual treat for the senses.

#3405. Cincinnati Zoo Hippo Fiona Dies After Swallowing Child's Hat

Fiona -- a popular hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Gardens -- has died after swallowing a child's hat ... the zoo announced on Thursday.

The zoo posted photos paying tribute to Fiona on Facebook ... writing that she didn't make it despite the veterinary and keeper teams' best efforts.

The Cincinnati Zoo stated Fiona ate a hat last week. The vets tried to remove the hat from Fiona's system, but they ultimately couldn't.

The zoo is asking the community to keep Fiona's keepers and others who tried to help her in their prayers.

According to the local outlet WLWT 5, Fiona swallowed a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure after a child threw it into the air. It hit a fan and somehow slipped through a tiny gap into Fiona's habitat.

The zoo stated, "We probably couldn't make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident."

Fiona was born prematurely in January 2017 ... weighing just 29 pounds -- which is 25 pounds less than the previous lowest recorded weight for a member of her species.

Her recovery gained a national following ... and resulted in T-shirts and children's books being made.

Remember ... the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Gardens is the same zoo where Harambe -- a beloved gorilla -- was shot to death back in 2016 after a child fell into his enclosure.

Fiona -- who had a younger brother named Fritz -- was just 9 years old when she died.

#3404. Apple hears Liquid Glass feedback, tests small but welcome change

Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale.

Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling …

What am I supposed to be looking at here?

Are we talking about the barely-noticeable fade at the top of the screen?

Apple’s introduction of the Liquid Glass UI split the Apple community, some hailing it as one of the best improvements seen for many years, and others rejecting it as a usability disaster.

As is often the case with any change, the controversy dampened significantly once people had a chance to get used to it. That is not the same as everyone being happy with it, however. Apple later tried to please most of the people most of the time with a slider that allows people to customize the level of transparency, from a very frosted glass look to an almost completely clear one.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted that the company is currently testing a small but welcome additional choice.

They heard the feedback: Apple is testing the return of iOS 26’s softer scroll-edge effect in navigation bars when glass tint is set to 25% or lower.Currently disabled behind UIKit/clear_glass_soft_pocket. Applies to the default/auto style. pic.twitter.com/D2NvKfESYa

The difference is somewhat subtle, and some may consider it irrelevant, but as someone who has transparency maxed-out I’m a fan of the softer fade and would welcome the option to be able to reinstate this.

#3403. You Can Save More Than $1,300 on a Smart TV With These Early Black Friday Deals

Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing substantial discounts to smart TVs, with savings ranging from $200 to $1,350 across models from Samsung, LG, Hisense, Sony, TCL, and other major brands. Several of the TVs included are from this year's lineups, so you don't necessarily have to settle for an older model to get a good price. There's also a decent variety to choose from, whether you're looking for an OLED TV with excellent contrast for movie nights, a bright mini-LED display for a sunlit living room, or simply a bigger screen without spending a fortune.

We've rounded up some of the more interesting offers below, and you can check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage for more editor-vetted tech deals as the sale continues.

Samsung’s 65-inch S90H is down to $1,397.99 from $1,897.99, saving you $500 on the company’s mid-range OLED TV for 2026. It’s a solid option for movie enthusiasts and gamers alike, thanks to its self-lit pixels that produce deep blacks and excellent contrast, particularly in darker scenes where conventional LED TVs can struggle with a grayish glow. You also get a high-refresh-rate display for smoother gaming.

If you have room for a bigger screen, Samsung’s 77-inch S85H is also worth a look, especially now that it’s down to $1,797.99 from $2,197.99, saving you $400. Although it sits below the S90H in Samsung’s 2026 OLED lineup, it still delivers the deep blacks, excellent contrast, and wide viewing angles that make OLED TVs appealing. The larger screen also makes it a good fit for family movie nights.

One of the biggest discounts in this roundup, the 2026 75-inch Hisense U7 is now $997.99, down from $1,999.99. Its mini-LED backlighting and local dimming are designed to deliver brighter highlights and better contrast, making it an appealing option for rooms with plenty of natural light. Gaming-focused features also make it worth a look if you plan to connect a current-generation console or gaming PC.

For a more affordable 75-inch option, Hisense's 2026 U6 Pro is down to $699.99 from $1,399.99, saving you $700. Like the U7, it uses mini-LED backlighting to improve contrast and bring out more detail in HDR movies and shows, although it sits a tier below the U7 in terms of overall picture performance. It also comes with Fire TV and Alexa+ built in, making it a convenient choice for households already using Amazon's smart home ecosystem.

The C6 is LG’s mid-range OLED evo model for 2026, and right now its 65-inch model is $1,399.99, down from its $2,699.99 launch price. It combines excellent pixel-level contrast with gaming features designed for fast-paced titles, making it a versatile choice for both movies and consoles. LG also supports Dolby Vision, which gives it an advantage over Samsung's OLEDs for viewers who regularly stream compatible HDR content.

Sony’s 65-inch Bravia 6, the entry-level OLED in its 2026 TV lineup, is now $1,198, down from $1,999.99, saving you $802. It delivers the deep blacks and excellent contrast you'd expect from the display technology, thanks to its self-lit pixels. Sony's picture processing also helps bring out fine details and natural-looking colors in movies and TV shows, while Dolby Vision support makes the most of compatible HDR content.

For the same $1,198, you can get a considerably larger screen with the 85-inch Sony Bravia 3 II, which is down from $1,599.99, saving you $402. That said, this 2026 model uses a conventional LED panel, so it won't quite match the Bravia 6's deep blacks and contrast, but the extra 20 inches make it an appealing option for sports and family movie nights. It also has a native 120Hz refresh rate with VRR and ALLM for smoother console gaming, along with Dolby Vision support and Google TV with Gemini built in.

Toshiba’s 75-inch Z670R is down to $699.99 from $1,299.99, saving you $600 on a 2026 mini-LED TV. It combines full-array local dimming with QLED color technology for improved contrast and brighter highlights, while Toshiba’s REGZA Engine ZRi processor helps sharpen lower-resolution content. The native 144Hz refresh rate also makes it a good option for console and PC gaming, and you get Fire TV built in for streaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support.

Designed to compete with Samsung's The Frame, Toshiba's 65-inch G700 ArtVision is currently $899.99 at Amazon, down from $1,297.99, saving you $398. It's a 4K QLED TV, with a native 165Hz refresh rate, built-in Fire TV, and the same REGZA Engine ZRi processor found in the Z670R. But there's more to it than watching movies and shows, as its Ambient Mode can display over 3,000 curated artworks without a subscription, while the matte anti-glare screen and included white oak frame help it pass for a framed print on the wall.

TCL’s 98-inch F8D is down to $1,444.99 from $1,699.99, saving you $255 on a massive 2026 QLED Fire TV. It uses a high-brightness LED backlight, so you won't get the same level of contrast control as TCL's more expensive mini-LED QM models, but it still offers a native 144Hz refresh rate for smoother gaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support. And at nearly 100 inches, there's plenty of screen space to make movies, sports, and games feel more immersive.

TCL’s 75-inch QM64L is down to $699.99 after a $200 price cut—it’s the cheapest way into TCL’s 2026 QD-Mini LED lineup, and it pairs quantum dot color with local dimming for brighter highlights and better contrast in HDR movies and sports. That also makes it a good pick for a bright living room, where an OLED might not be the most practical choice. You also get a native 144Hz refresh rate for gaming and Fire TV built in

Roku’s 65-inch Plus Series is the most affordable TV in this roundup at $449.99, down from $649.99, saving you $200. This 2025 model combines a QLED panel with mini-LED backlighting and Dolby Vision support for improved contrast and richer colors when watching HDR content. It also runs the same Roku OS found on the company’s streaming sticks and comes with an Enhanced Voice Remote, so navigating apps and finding something to watch should feel familiar to anyone who already uses Roku.

LG’s 65-inch C6 OLED has the largest dollar discount in this sale at $1,350 off, which brings it from $2,699.99 down to $1,349.99.

There's no guarantee that Cyber Monday will bring lower TV prices, particularly when some of the early Black Friday deals are already offering discounts approaching 50%. Retailers sometimes carry the same promotions through the entire shopping weekend, while others introduce new discounts or change which models are on sale.

That depends on your budget, room size, and how you plan to use it. The LG OLED evo C6 and Samsung S90H are worth considering for movie enthusiasts and gamers who want excellent contrast and smooth motion, while the Hisense U7 and TCL QM64L offer mini-LED alternatives for brighter living rooms. For a large screen at a relatively affordable price, the 75-inch Hisense U6 Pro at $699.99 stands out, while the 65-inch Roku Plus Series at $449.99 makes sense for everyday streaming on a tighter budget. If screen size is your priority, the 98-inch TCL F8D is also worth a look, provided you have the room for it.
